Garey, majors of United States infantry and instructors at Plattsburg, wrote this handbook for military training, under a New York imprint in the late nineteen teens with more than two hundred pictures. It went through many editions in a single year as America raised new officers.

Chapters cover infantry and artillery in the fight, covering retreats, pursuit, and the new role of machine guns, once classed as emergency weapons. The manual is a clear snapshot of how raw recruits were taught to become officers in wartime.
1959-the-crown-of-thorns-a-token-for-the:
E. H. Chapin's Crown of Thorns, a token for the sorrowing, gathers discourses written for the bereaved. A preface explains that one sermon, The Mission of Little Children, was written just after the death of a dear son and first published as a pamphlet. The edition having become exhausted, Chapin reprints it here.

The sermons ask what mortal existence is, into which we crowd so much interest and over whose uncertain future we project our plans so confidently. They answer with Christian comfort. The book is a work of pastoral care rather than of argument, and its value lies in its tone: a minister speaking to grief without preaching at it.
1966-the-path-of-the-king:
John Buchan's Path of the King, dedicated to his wife and first read by a Cotswold fire. It traces a single idea through history: that a kingly spirit passes from age to age, carried by ordinary people. The chapters run from Hightown under Sunfell through the Englishman, the Wife of Flanders, and the Maid, to Eaucourt by the waters and beyond.

Travellers meet athwart their road and exchange greetings. On the second morning they reach a city populous in men but not in houses, with lines of skin tents stretching for miles. Buchan writes history as romance, and the book's charm lies in its chain of linked lives, each one carrying the same light a little further.
19869-while-caroline-was-growing:
Josephine Daskam Bacon wrote While Caroline Was Growing in 1906. Caroline is a girl whose heart outruns her lessons. She chants her geography by rote: bounded in the north by Massachusetts. Her eyes are not on the map at all. Like the gentleman in the poem, her thoughts are far away. Bacon watches girlhood with that divided attention in mind.

Bacon's stories of girls were praised for their truth. Caroline daydreams, schemes, and grows by small increments. Nothing in the book condescends to its young heroine. The New England setting stays light in the background. Readers meet a real child, not a lesson in skirts. The book charms by observation rather than event.
19875-the-bobbin-boy-or-how-nat-got-his-:
The Bobbin Boy tells how Nat got his learning, as an example for youth. Its opening is a bright May morning scene. A fenced patch of ground, a few trees, and birdsong frame it. Nat stands with his hoe in hand. His father gives directions for the work. The boy who hoes here will work in a textile mill. Nathaniel Peabody Banks is the bobbin boy of the title.

Banks rose from mill boy to Civil War general and congressman. William Makepeace Thayer wrote his life for boys to copy. Bobbin boys tended spinning frames for tiny wages. Thayer turns that start into a ladder of self-help. The book is pure nineteenth-century success gospel. It shows the genre's faith in industry and schooling.
19924-plain-facts-for-old-and-young:
John Harvey Kellogg wrote Plain Facts for Old and Young, a famous Victorian health guide. It treats sex, reproduction, and personal habits with unusual frankness. Kellogg prefaced the practical part with reproductive anatomy. He took special pains, he says, to avoid anything like indelicacy. The description stays concise and clinical by his era's lights. The book sold enormously for decades.

Kellogg ran the Battle Creek Sanitarium and preached total health reform. Plain Facts mixes sound advice with stern moral warnings. Its chapters on chastity and habit alarmed and fascinated readers. Historians of medicine and sexuality cite it constantly. It shows Victorian purity culture in its own words. Few health books reveal their age so completely.
19931-the-reckoning:
Percival Wilde wrote The Reckoning as a one-act play. A barber mixes his lather while trading life stories. His customer has moved around so much, he says, that he is neither Southerner nor Northerner. He lived a year in a little town near Savannah. The chair, the lather, and the talk set a trap of coziness. Wilde's one-acts usually spring such traps late. The reckoning of the title waits offstage.

Wilde specialized in short plays with a final twist. Barbershop talk lets strangers confess more than they mean. A razor in hand raises the stakes quietly. The Southern year will surely matter before the curtain. This piece shows Wilde's economy and menace. It is a small masterclass in one-act construction.
20069-caruso-and-tetrazzini-on-the-art-o:
Enrico Caruso and Luisa Tetrazzini were two of the great opera voices of their age. In Caruso and Tetrazzini on the Art of Singing, both share how they trained and sang. Tetrazzini sang Inez in Meyerbeer's L'Africaine before an Italian crowd. Queen Margherita heard her, praised her, and foresaw a great career.

The book mixes life tales with plain advice on voice and craft. A young singer then earned a hundred dollars a month, a rare start. Readers who sing, or love opera, get tips from stars. Their fame gives weight to each small point on breath and tone.
20146-engineering-bulletin-no-1-boiler-a:
Rufus T. Strohm wrote Engineering Bulletin No. 1, on boiler and furnace testing. The United States Fuel Administration backed daily checks of boiler plants. The simplest test, the bulletin says, is an evaporation test. It shows how well a boiler and furnace truly work each day.

Fuel was precious in wartime, and waste cost money and coal alike. Plant men could use these steps with tools they had at hand. The bulletin lays out method, care, and records in plain order. It stands as a neat piece of practical engineering from the fuel-saving era.
20187-on-christmas-day-in-the-morning:
On Christmas Day in the Morning is a Christmas tale of home and longing. Gay Nan reads a letter and feels a choke rise in her throat. She tells her husband Sam they must be there next Christmas. Sam agrees at once, with cheer and warmth in his voice.

Sam only wishes he still had a father and mother to visit. That wish gives the tale its ache beneath the holiday glow. Family homes draw grown children back each year at Christmas time. Readers get a short, tender tale of letters, loss, and promised returns.
20349-the-moving-picture-girls-at-rocky-:
Laura Lee Hope published The Moving Picture Girls at Rocky Ranch in 1914. Ruth De Vere is told that film work teaches words that mean something. Sign-post words, by contrast, merely point and carry no life in them. Her sister is glad to see her getting sensible at last.

Are you ready to go to the studio, she asks Ruth. At Rocky Ranch, the girls film western scenes among real cowboys. Great days among the cowboys, the subtitle promises its young readers. The book mixes film craft, ranch life, and sisterly banter throughout.
20367-the-coming-of-the-king:
Set in the ancient land of Judea under Roman rule, The Coming of the King tells a story from the time of Christ. A craftsman fashions a heavy yoke while word spreads of a grim order. Timber is being cut near Mount Tabor for two thousand crosses, and fear hangs over the workers.

The tale builds its drama from the lives of ordinary people living under that threat. Talk of mercy, dread, and a coming king runs through the scenes. Readers who enjoy Bible-era fiction will find a vivid picture of village life in a land waiting for change.
20386-embroidery-and-tapestry-weaving:
Mrs. Archibald H. Christie wrote Embroidery and Tapestry Weaving as a guide to the history and craft of needlework. The book covers both design and workmanship. It treats stitching and loom work as serious arts with long pasts.

Christie points readers to fine surviving pieces, including fragments worked in the tenth century. She singles out the great period of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, with many examples kept at the South Kensington Museum. Workers get practical help, while students of art get a clear survey of how the craft grew.
20519-highways-in-hiding:
Highways in Hiding, published in 1956, is a science fiction novel by George O. Smith. Its narrator, Steve Cornell, belongs to a world where some people hide powers of the mind. An underground network, the Highways, shields them from a hostile public.

Cornell knows what happens to the exposed. The Highways crowd, he says, had enough savvy to clean up any mess before their bodies got cold. Without that protection, men like him would not last. Smith mixes road adventure with telepathy and pursuit, in a tale from the golden age of magazine science fiction.
20526-short-story-writing:
Charles Raymond Barrett's Short Story Writing is a practical textbook for people learning to write fiction. Barrett breaks the short story into its working parts. Every element, he insists, must lead up to something in the finished tale.

A story needs for its structure a plot, a bit of life, an incident. Such an incident might come from a brief newspaper paragraph. Barrett shows how Richard Harding Davis could take the substance of just such a paragraph and build a story on it. The book served the many Americans who hoped to sell stories to the booming magazines.
20656-old-christmas-from-the-sketch-book:
Washington Irving's Old Christmas, drawn from his Sketch Book, describes Christmas at an English country hall. Irving visited England and fell in love with its old customs. The piece follows the squire's Christmas from the guests' arrival to the great dinner.

An old song in the text praises the season. A man might then behold, at Christmas, in each hall, good fires to curb the cold and meat for great and small. The neighbors were friendly bidden, and all had welcome true. The poor from the gates were not turned away. Irving's sketch shaped how America imagined the old English Christmas.
20728-space-viking:
Lucas Trask dreams of showing his bride the new house on Traskon, then taking a long trip among the Sword Worlds. H. Beam Piper sets that tender plan against worlds with names like Excalibur, Morglay, and Flamberge. War has already flared again on Durendal, so peace feels thin from the first pages.

Space Viking follows a wronged man who turns raider among rough star worlds. Piper mixes revenge, trade, statecraft, and battle in a tight plot. The book is famed for treating space piracy as real politics, not mere noise. It is a key work in Piper's future history.
20770-apple-growing:
Apples can be used in more ways than most fruits, says M. C. Burritt in Apple-Growing. Better knowledge of the fruit's worth has raised its use, he notes. New ways to prepare it for the table helped that growth along.

Orchard work fills the guide, from choosing ground to picking and selling fruit. Burritt wrote for growers who needed sound, plain advice in one book. Varieties, pests, pruning, and packing all get their share. The book shows a time when apples were big business for small farms. Its care with detail still speaks to anyone who tends fruit trees today.
20813-how-lisa-loved-the-king:
Palermo holds high festival in How Lisa Loved the King, a poem by George Eliot. Matrons and maidens watch a mock tournament where safe sport hints at danger. The scene takes a lift, as from epic song, the verse itself declares.

Eliot, famed for great novels, also wrote verse tales of real craft. Lisa's love for a king far above her rank drives this one. Sicily's sun, court pomp, and a maid's bold heart fill the lines. The poem shows the young Eliot testing themes of rank, longing, and women's inner lives that her novels later made immortal.
20836-ting-a-ling:
Aufalia takes a spring walk, veiled, with two grim slaves at her heels. Frank R. Stockton opens Ting-a-Ling, from 1882, in a town of secluded suburbs. Birds sing, crocuses bloom, and a fairy tale mood settles at once.

Stockton, famed for The Lady or the Tiger, wrote droll fairy tales with a twist. Ting-a-Ling, a tiny being, lends the book its name and spark. Magic, wit, and odd turns fill these tales for young and old alike. Stockton's dry humor sets his fairy work apart from sweeter fare, and this book shows it in full, playful flight.
20896-carry-s-rose-or-the-magic-of-kindn:
Caroline coaxes her lamb Daisy to wait, for wheels sound at the avenue gate. Mrs. George Cupples opens Carry's Rose, a tale for the young, with that bright arrival. Clapping hands and keen hopes set the tale's warm tone at once.

Kindness works like magic in Cupples's story of a girl and her rose. Small gifts, patience, and love turn hearts across the plot. Cupples wrote tales for children with a gentle, Scottish warmth. This one keeps her mark: home scenes, beast friends, and a clear moral that never needs to raise its voice to be heard.
21024-the-angels-song:
Bonfires blaze on hilltops and steeples ring as a king's heir enters life, The Angel's Song marvels. Nations feast while prayers rise to Him by whom kings reign, it says. All that pomp frames its turn to a far humbler birth.

Thomas Binney's famed sermon sets Christ's birth against the pomp of earthly thrones. No bells or feasts marked the manger, yet angels sang above it. Binney, a great Nonconformist preacher, builds that contrast with fire. The sermon became a Christmas classic in chapels, prized for its sweep from palace noise to the still, high song over Bethlehem.
21032-exercises-in-knitting:
Stitch counts head each pattern in Exercises in Knitting, so any piece can be resized at will. Open patterns suit Shetland shawls, Cornelia Mee notes, while chair covers run in coloured wools. White work, she adds, wants linen thread number one.

Mee's patterns teach doilies, covers, shawls, and trims stitch by patient stitch. Victorian knitters kept such books by the work basket for daily use. Colours and shades are named so each piece can be matched at home. The book keeps a whole craft dialect alive: counts, threads, and the small maths of the needle, set down with care.
21134-working-in-the-shade-lowly-sowing-:
Curiosity runs high in the small town of Franchope when Riverton Park, empty for twenty years, is to be occupied again. The Reverend Theodore P. Wilson builds his tale around the new arrival at Park House. The house is a fine old mansion on rising ground in a rich park. Episodes of selfishness and unselfishness drive the plot.

Wilson treats his theme almost as a sermon in story form: selfish acts lead toward disaster, while quiet, unselfish sowing leads upward. He had won a literary prize for Frank Oldfield some ten years earlier with the same method. The book stays short, direct, and intent on leaving readers with food for thought.
21372-steve-young:
Steve Young, sixteen and an orphan, joins a rescue voyage to the icy seas in George Manville Fenn's tale. His uncle, Captain Young, has vanished on a voyage toward Spitzbergen, and the captain's friends charter a Norwegian vessel, the Hvalross, to search for him. The ship's doctor thinks boys are a nuisance and says so.

Polar bears, killing cold, gales, ice floes, and the total dark of the arctic winter test the party. A cowardly young Highlander provides the comedy. At last they find Captain Young and most of his crew alive. Fenn fills the search with the practical detail of ice navigation he loved to teach.
21400-style-in-singing:
W. E. Haslam sets out what makes singing artful in Style in Singing, published by G. Schirmer in 1911. Haslam wrote the book for his own pupils, and he says the field lacked such a guide. Books on how to play instruments with style were common, but not books on song.

He ranks the parts of a singer's craft in clear order. Pose and technique must be sound before style can be learned, he argues. Yet skill alone is not enough without style to crown it. A well-chosen stock of songs, fitted to each voice, completes the training he lays out.
21534-textiles-and-clothing:
Kate Heintz Watson wrote Textiles and Clothing for the American School of Home Economics in 1907. Watson taught domestic art at the Lewis Institute and lectured at the University of Chicago. The book forms one part of a twelve-volume home-study course on homemaking.

The course claimed near three thousand pages and a thousand pictures across its set. Watson treats fibres, weaves, and the care and choice of cloth for dress and home. Experts in home economics across several colleges backed the series. Mothers, teachers, nurses, and house managers formed its target readers, in an age when home study promised a new profession for women.
21636-bluff-crag-or-a-good-word-costs-no:
Mrs George Cupples writes for the young in Bluff Crag, or A Good Word Costs Nothing, issued in 1872. Cupples also wrote The Story of Our Doll and The Little Captain. Nelson of London, Edinburgh, and New York published the tale.

Mr Lincoln hides behind his newspaper while children wait by the fire for his thoughts. His breathing soon shows he has fallen asleep instead of thinking. Small scenes of home life carry the book's lesson, set in the title. A good word costs nothing, and the tale shows its worth at Bluff Crag and beyond, in a gentle Victorian key.
21722-a-practical-discourse-on-some-prin:
Poet Robert Bridges turns critic in this short study of how hymns should be sung, first printed in a journal of theology in 1899. The booklet came out at Oxford in 1901, priced at one shilling. Bridges starts from Saint Augustine, who wept at the hymns sung in Milan in the year 386. That plain early music had few tools, yet it stirred Augustine deeply.

From that case, Bridges asks what makes church singing move a hearer: the tune, the words, or the singer's own feeling. He argues for care in how hymns are chosen, set, and sung in church. It is a brief, sharp piece by a poet who cared deeply about both music and verse.
21990-the-campaign-of-1776-around-new-yo:
New York's Revolutionary ordeal is mapped and documented in Henry P. Johnston's The Campaign of 1776 Around New York and Brooklyn, published by the Long Island Historical Society in 1878. Johnston calls the ground pre-eminently Revolutionary soil, where the war came to America's doors. His book gives a fresh, full account of the Battle of Long Island. It covers the loss of New York and reviews events to the year's close.

Maps compiled by the author, portraits, and original documents fill out the narrative. Spelling in quoted papers stands as written, down to the doubled letters marked with macrons. Johnston wrote as Brooklyn's own historian of its founding battle. The work remains a standard, source-rich history of the campaign that nearly ended the Revolution.
22029-spool-knitting:
Mary A. McCormack's Spool Knitting, published in 1909, teaches children to knit with a simple spool and pegs. McCormack compares the child at work to a spider moving round its web. The toy knitter makes cord in a round web, a flat web, or a circular mat. From those basics the lessons build quickly.

Projects include a ball and rattle for a baby, caps, mittens, slippers, and bootees. Dolls get muffs, hoods, coats, and collarettes of their own. Each piece needs only cord, patience, and a small pair of hands. The book is a neat window on the craft teaching once given to young girls.
22098-the-seventh-day-sabbath-a-perpetua:
Joseph Bates, a retired sea captain turned Adventist preacher, argued the case for Saturday worship in The Seventh Day Sabbath, a Perpetual Sign. Bates held that the Sabbath runs from creation to the end of time. His tract works through the Bible in order, text by text. When a questioner asks the way to eternal life, Bates notes that Christ points to the commandments.

He answers the common claim that the Sabbath was dropped or moved to Sunday. Scripture, he insists, nowhere leaves the seventh day out. Bates's little book helped found the Sabbatarian Adventist movement. It still states, in plain King James language, the core argument for keeping Saturday holy.
22325-the-art-of-modern-lace-making:
The Art of Modern Lace-Making teaches a craft with very old roots. Its opening claims lace, in one form or another, reaches back to the earliest ages. Even Scripture, it notes, mentions web-like fabrics of rude make.

Those early fabrics share their main traits with modern lace. Skill over centuries turned simple webs into fine, prized work. A practical manual like this one passed that skill to new hands. It treats lace as both art and trade. Readers interested in needlework get period instruction and pride in craft. The book also preserves how makers once explained their art to learners at home.
22379-masters-of-water-colour-painting:
Masters of Water-Colour Painting surveys British artists who worked in watercolor. Its plate list reads like a roll of honored names. Samuel Prout, Paul Sandby, and Thomas Rowlandson all appear.

Sandby's Windsor Castle shows the Round and Devil's Towers. Rowlandson gives the entrance to Vauxhall Gardens in London. James Holland paints a shrine in Venice for one plate. Samuel Prout sets a Venetian palace on the Grand Canal. William Henry Hunt contributes a homely scene, Plucking the Fowl. Francis Towne paints on the River Dart. The book lets readers compare these masters side by side, plate by plate.
22392-essentials-in-conducting:
Essentials in Conducting, issued by the Oliver Ditson Company, teaches leaders of bands and choirs. It defines the conductor's work at the start. He stands before performers and gives his whole effort to directing them.

A conductor of orchestra or chorus does not play or sing himself. His entire time goes to shaping the group's performance. The goal is a musically effective ensemble result. Clear beats, cues, and control make many players act as one. Manuals like this trained school and church musicians across America. Readers get the basics of a craft usually learned by watching. It preserves period teaching on tempo, gesture, and rehearsal discipline.
2240-much-ado-about-nothing:
In Messina, returning soldiers bring love and trouble in equal measure. Much Ado About Nothing pairs the sparring Beatrice and Benedick, tricked into love by their friends, with the young Hero and Claudio, whose wedding collapses on a villain's lie. Shakespeare weaves witty war between the sexes around a darker plot of slander.

Dogberry and his watch bumble toward the truth just in time, and the play ends with dances, forgiveness, and second chances. Its language sparkles, and Beatrice remains one of Shakespeare's liveliest heroines. The comedy still delights audiences who enjoy sharp talk and happy endings earned the hard way.
22482-men-in-the-making:
Ambrose Shepherd wrote Men in the Making, a book on forming character. One early passage follows a thinker who doubted the moon's worship. He did not fall in readily with that worship as he matured.

He became, Shepherd says, one of an order of doubters. The world owes much, he argues, to doubters of that kind. This youth suspected the moon was not a cause in itself. Priests taught otherwise, but he saw an effect needing a cause. Such stories model the growth Shepherd wants in his readers. Men are made, his title insists, by thought, faith, and questioning. The book offers period guidance toward sturdy, reflective manhood.
22554-as-it-was-in-the-beginning:
As It Was in the Beginning, dated 1912, is a novel issued under Desmond Fitzgerald's imprint. Grenville, its cool-headed hero, faces his friend's searching gaze. A glow of exceptional brilliance shines in Grenville's eyes then.

Grenville was not the type to be readily excited, the narrator notes. Yet that glow betrayed feeling as the two men met. He wondered if Fenton could be jesting with him at that moment. Such a charged meeting opens a story of strong emotions held in check. The title hints that first states of things govern later events. Readers get Edwardian fiction of friendship, love, and revelation. Its reserve makes its bursts of feeling count for more.
22574-the-best-portraits-in-engraving:
The Best Portraits in Engraving celebrates the art of the engraved portrait. Its author examined other collections in America before writing. In Paris, the great national cabinet of engravings became his daily medicine.

He underwent severe medical treatment during that Paris stay abroad. For weeks, the vast cabinet counted its holdings by the million. There was everything there to please or instruct a lover of prints. Thinking of those kindly portfolios, he records his gratitude now. They were benefactors to him in a hard season of illness. The book guides readers among master engravers and their sitters. It preserves connoisseurship of a kind photography was already displacing.
22603-rational-horse-shoeing:
Rational Horse-Shoeing, signed Wildair, is a practical manual on shoeing horses without harming their feet. The catalog record gives no year. The author blames many foot diseases on unnatural shoeing and promotes the Goodenough shoe as the sound alternative.

The system, readers are told, is meant for sound horses: to protect the feet and keep them healthy, not to cure disease. Rules in the author's circular cover ordinary cases, with disease treated as the exception needing special care. In an age when horses powered farms and cities, such advice carried real money value. The book now offers farriers and horse historians a clear statement of one reform school of shoeing.
22744-the-adventurous-seven-their-hazard:
Bessie Marchant wrote The Adventurous Seven: Their Hazardous Undertaking, a story of young people facing danger far from home. The catalog record gives no year. Marchant, who published as Bessie Comfort, wrote hundreds of adventure tales, many with brave heroines in wild places, at a time when such books were thought a boys' province.

The sample opens in a village schoolroom packed as full as it would hold, its air so thick that, as Sylvia said, a spoon could nearly scoop it. A stout lecturer perspires freely but means to do his duty, declaiming with tremendous vigor. From that stifling room the seven's undertaking launches. Marchant's pace is rapid and her young people resourceful, making her a pioneer of girls' adventure fiction.
23101-three-thousand-years-of-mental-hea:
George Barton Cutten traces mind cure through the ages in Three Thousand Years of Mental Healing, published in 1911. His epigraph, borrowed from Stowe, celebrates the mind's royal power over flesh. For a season, it claims, belief can armor nerve and muscle like steel, and make weak people strong.

Cutten, a psychologist, surveys the whole road from temple sleep and relics to Christian Science and the Emmanuel movement. He writes as a scholar of a craze, sorting faith, suggestion, and fraud with a cool hand. The book appeared when mental healing filled magazines and split churches. Cutten believed mental influence was genuine. He trusted its salesmen far less, and that double view makes his map of the movement unusually clear.
2315-the-flag-raising:
Kate Douglas Wiggin, author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, offers a patriotic story for children centered on a school flag raising. The Flag-Raising follows pupils and teachers as they prepare a ceremony honoring the flag, learning what it stands for along the way. Wiggin's warmth and her belief in children's civic feeling shape every page.

The book is short, earnest, and of its time, with songs and speeches woven into the school day. Modern readers will note its period patriotism. As a piece of children's literature history, it charms.
23185-the-glory-of-ippling:
The Glory of Ippling is a work of science fiction about contact between cultures. Its premise rests on a bold claim: no machine can match a group of humans for sheer complexity, even when those humans are drilled to work with machine-like precision. That idea frames everything the Ipplingers do.

One case follows an Ipplinger Cultural Contact Group handed a well-connected visitor, a Boswellister with important ties. Their orders are to place him on an assignment meant to test his maturity. Readers get a story about first contact, pride, and the strain of judging an outsider by home rules.
23577-taking-tales-instructive-and-enter:
W. H. G. Kingston gathered six tales in this volume, each first sold alone at a low price for families to read and discuss together. An English country miller, a boy who goes to sea, and a family settling in Canada fill the set. A boy soldier in the Crimea and the Indian Mutiny, an Australian shepherd, and a little boy working down a coal mine also fill the set.

Each tale aims to instruct as it entertains, giving young readers new thoughts about work, duty, and distant lives. Kingston writes with warmth and plain moral purpose, in the Victorian belief that a family story could teach as well as please. Modern readers may note how hard life pressed on very young boys, and will be glad, as Kingston hoped, that such demands have eased.
23625-the-magic-pudding:
Norman Lindsay wrote and drew The Magic Pudding, first printed by Angus and Robertson in Sydney in nineteen eighteen, here in a Dover republication. Bunyip Bluegum, a fine, round, splendid fellow, and his Uncle Wattleberry, more square than round with whiskers on his face, open the book in front, side, and rear views.

The pudding of the title, a magic steak and kidney pudding that regrows however much is eaten, draws a crew of Australian beasts into scrapes, chases, and songs. Lindsay's bold drawings go with them. The tale is a classic of Australian nonsense, rude, funny, and fond of its bush larrikins. Children and grown readers alike will enjoy the pudding's endless slices and the friends who fight, sing, and feast over it.
23649-the-sugar-plumb-or-golden-fairing:
Mrs. Margery Two-Shoes, governess of A, B, C, College, compiled this penny chapbook at York for the use of all her pupils. Each page pairs a letter of the alphabet with short rhyming verses and a picture, so that children learn their letters by chanting them aloud rather than by dry drill.

A stands for apples and ale, B for ball and batt, and C for cow and custard. The verses run on through the alphabet, with jokes, warnings, and small moral nudges tucked into the rhymes. Sold for one penny, it is a charming survival of early children's publishing: cheap, cheerful, and meant to be read, sung, and worn out by young hands.
24219-the-royal-guide-to-wax-flower-mode:
Emma Peachey, artiste to Her Majesty, wrote this craft manual, published and sold by herself in London in 1851. It is dedicated to the Princess Royal, in grateful acknowledgement of the fostering patronage of her august parent, the Queen. Peachey opens with verses on why flowers were made: to comfort man and whisper hope when faith grows dim.

An advertisement warns that Peachey must soon circumscribe or discontinue her lessons, making the book indispensable to any pupil. The guide teaches the art of modelling flowers in wax, flower by flower, for ladies who wish to keep blooms that never fade. Readers get a Victorian handbook of a fashionable, delicate craft.
24238-the-works-of-the-rev-hugh-binning:
Hugh Binning's collected religious writings fill this volume, whose contents open with a life of the author and an editor's preface. The main work is The Common Principles of the Christian Religion, clearly proved and singularly improved, also called A Practical Catechism, with its original preface. It sets out what the scriptures principally teach, in plain, ordered heads.

Later pieces treat God's glory as the chief end of man's being, and union and communion with God. Others cover the end and design of the gospel and the authority and utility of the scriptures. A third group treats eternal life through Jesus Christ and the ruin and recovery of man, closing with faith and love. Readers get a systematic Puritan divinity, written for teaching and devotion.
24476-the-nursery-march-1873-vol-xiii-a-:
Published in Boston in March 1873, this number of The Nursery was the third issue of its thirteenth volume. The magazine, edited for youngest readers by John L. Shorey, mixes short prose tales with verses and music. Its prose opens with pigeons and their friend, and goes on to obedient chickens, performing dogs, and a cure for sadness.

Other pieces tell of Kitty and the bee, Ida's mouse, and a child almost lost. Verses include Rowdy-Dowdy, The Sliders, and Mr. Prim, with Timothy Tippens set to music. Short, simple, and cheerful, the issue shows what American editors offered small children in the 1870s: kind stories, animal friends, and gentle lessons.
24477-the-nursery-april-1873-vol-xiii-a-:
Boston publisher John L. Shorey issued this April 1873 number of The Nursery, the fourth issue of its thirteenth volume. Its prose pieces urge readers to try, try again, and tell of a prisoner, Clarence's kittens, a tiger's toilet, and Peterlin on his travels.

Other tales follow George's boat, a little carpenter, Walter's dog, and a horse that loves children, with a visit to the maple woods. Verses include The Song of the Kettle, On the Gate, Where's the Baby, and The Birds' Return, with a Song of the Ducks set to music. The issue keeps the magazine's gentle mix of animals, work, and play.
24483-the-justice-of-the-king:
Hamilton Drummond published this historical novel in 1911, in the International Fiction Library. Its chapters take readers to the French court, where a king's despatch, a lesson in obedience, and a woman's sake set the plot moving. Later chapters are named for the justice of the king, for how Louis loved his son, and for the black dog of Amboise.

Poet and gallows-cheat Francois Villon appears among the characters, with Stephen La Mothe, Jean Saxe, and lovers caught between France and England. Drummond mixes court intrigue, theology, and romance into a tale of loyalty and power. Readers who enjoy swashbuckling historical fiction will find it rich in incident and old-French colour.
24547-in-the-wilds-of-florida-a-tale-of-:
W. H. G. Kingston wrote this tale of warfare and hunting in the wilds of Florida. It is set in the mid-nineteenth century, when fighting with the Seminole had not yet ended, and white settlers were still sometimes disturbed by attacks. Large areas of Florida were swamp, water, and densely overgrown plain.

Its hero is a school-leaver from Ireland, one son too many for his debt-encumbered squireen father to provide for. He visits relatives in America, and so comes to Florida. Kingston describes swamp travel, hunting, and frontier danger in detail. Young readers get a stirring tale of a boy making his way in a wild land.
24568-aboriginal-american-weaving:
Mary Lois Kissell, of the American Museum of Natural History in New York, wrote this paper on aboriginal American weaving. She read it before the National Association of Cotton Manufacturers at Boston on 27 April 1910. Her subject is the most primitive looms of the Americas, set against modern textile machinery.

Kissell argues that those early looms are just as surprising as machines that seem almost human in turning raw material into cloth. She describes how native weavers worked without factories, yet produced fine and durable fabric. The paper remains a clear, short introduction to Indian weaving, by a museum scholar who knew her material well.
24607-the-cycle-of-spring:
Sir Rabindranath Tagore wrote this lyrical drama, published at London in 1919, with a first edition in February 1917. The greater part of its introductory portion was translated from the original Bengali by C. F. Andrews and Nishikanta Sen, then revised by Tagore himself. He dedicated the book to his boys of Shantiniketan.

Those boys, Tagore says, freed a fountain of youth hidden in the old poet's heart, and Dinendranath guided them in their festivals. The play celebrates spring as renewal, with songs, dances, and the turning year. Readers get a beautiful example of Tagore's theatre, where nature, youth, and spirit meet in festival.
24643-a-treatise-on-the-art-of-dancing:
Giovanni-Andrea Gallini published this treatise on the art of dancing at London in 1772, printed for the author and sold by leading booksellers in Pall Mall and the Strand. Its contents cover the ancient dance, dancing in general, and the many requisites for perfection in the art.

Gallini, a dancing master of the London stage, writes for pupils, parents, and polite society, explaining steps, deportment, and the place of dance in education. His book preserves the grace and rules of eighteenth-century social dancing. Readers interested in dance history will find it a detailed and charming guide to a vanished art.
24644-harry-s-ladder-to-learning:
Published at London in 1850 by David Bogue and Joseph Cundall, this primer for children carries two hundred and thirty illustrations. Its first part is Harry's Horn-Book, teaching letters through pictures: boy, cat, dog, jug, cow, pig, bed, fox, cock, duck, mill, goat, stag, rose, hare, and bear.

Later parts climb Harry's ladder step by step, from letters and words to short lessons and stories, with a May-day dance among its pictures. The book is a handsome example of Victorian teaching by picture. Collectors and historians of children's books will enjoy its charm, and young readers can still climb its ladder today.
24681-opportunities-in-engineering:
Charles M. Horton wrote this vocational guide, published by Harper and Brothers at New York in 1920 as part of the Opportunity Books series. Sister volumes covered aviation, chemistry, farming, merchant ships, and the newspaper business. Horton's book tells young readers what engineering offers, and what it demands.

Chapters treat the branches of engineering, training, and the daily work of engineers, with advice on character and study. Horton writes plainly for boys choosing a career after school. The book remains a snapshot of American ambition in 1920, when engineering promised a path to useful, respected work.
24958-second-landing:
Floyd Wallace's gentle Christmas fancy sends two aliens, Ethaniel and Bal, toward Earth in a ship so far away that even the sun is only a twinkle. Intercepted radio broadcasts and early television signals let their machines compile dictionaries and translate the planet's languages, and the two must decide whether to intervene. Bal argues for leaving: Earth has fought two world wars in a generation, and a third, final one seems coming, driven by the big bomb.

Ethaniel pleads for a week, against Bal's reminder that they are due at Willafours in two months and twenty-nine days, with more than a hundred light-years still to go. The pair land, work through snow and cold, and return saying they did it, though how remains part of the wonder. The story's wistful twist suits the season it was written for.
24973-the-sun-king:
Gaston Derreaux's fantasy opens before the flood, when the world was divided among Jaffeth, Shem, and Arabin'ya, with lesser lands like Uropa and Heleste beyond. At the junction of the three great countries stands Oas, capital of Par'si'ya, where the people have forgotten God and worship murder and sin. King So-qi sends armies through Jaffeth gathering skulls for his Golgotha temples, gold, and slaves.

Virgin Too-che, alone among a million sinful souls, bears a male child without having been with a man, and So-qi laughs at her claim of divine fatherhood. His own decrees turn against him. Soldiers stone him when he cannot enforce his own law, and the philosopher Asha counsels a king whose infant son stands forfeit unless Too-che and her child are found. The tale runs wild, lurid, and strange.
25018-amusement-a-force-in-christian-tra:
The Reverend Marvin R. Vincent's 1867 discourses, published by Wm. H. Young of Troy, argue that amusement is a force in Christian training. The opening essay was delivered before the International Convention of Young Men's Christian Associations at Albany in June 1866. It faces a subject the church has left indefinite: pulpit evasion, wavering private Christians, and extremists thundering denunciations. Vincent insists the question be reexamined on fundamental gospel principles.

Later discourses take up the true nonconformist, the church and the young man, and thoughts for the clergy. Plain clothing served some Christians as outward proof of faith, because they read the rules word for word rather than by their intent. They forgot that sad colors could cost as much as gay ones, and scorned the man with a gold watch or the woman with a feather. Vincent pleads for inward regulation over outward rule.
25087-twenty-years-of-hus-ling:
J. P. Johnston's Twenty Years of Hus'ling, published in Chicago in 1902, is the comic memoir of a man who tried almost every kind of business before finding his footing. Johnston, author of The Auctioneer's Guide, first wrote his life sketch as an addition to that manual, then expanded it into a separate volume.

Readers follow Johnston through failures, odd jobs, travelling mishaps, and small triumphs, told with humor and a salesman's eye for character. The book's message is plain: energy, persistence, and honest purpose can carry a hustler through years of hard luck toward independence.
25166-what-the-left-hand-was-doing:
Darrell T. Langart's What the Left Hand Was Doing, illustrated by Freas, is a Cold War science-fiction novella about a secret organization hiding in plain sight. Its headquarters in Arlington, Virginia, bears the sign of the Society for Mystical and Metaphysical Research, a name so crackpot that nobody looks twice, and yet literally true.

Agents work behind that cover while a physicist named Ch'ien pursues controversial equations. First laughed at in 1980, his work is then taken seriously by the government and carried toward a physicists' conference in Peking. Langart's premise is neat: the best disguise is a truth nobody believes.
25269-elements-of-plumbing:
Samuel Edward Dibble's Elements of Plumbing, published by McGraw-Hill in 1918, is a textbook from the Carnegie Institute of Technology. Dibble headed its sanitary equipment department, and his book trains plumbers in both theory and handwork.

Chapters cover fixtures, the soldering iron and fluxes, solders and their melting points, wiping cloths and joints, sewers, drains, soil and waste pipes, traps, and pipe threading. Cold and hot water supply, insulation, and Durham screw-pipe work complete the course. Illustrations trace the bath tub and wash bowl from boxed wood to modern enamel.
25322-fables-in-slang:
George Ade's Fables in Slang, published in Chicago in 1901, collects comic moral tales first printed in the Chicago Record. Illustrated by Clyde J. Newman, the book reached its sixty-eighth thousand printing, a sign of Ade's popularity.

Fables include the visitor who got a lot for three dollars and the slim girl who tried to keep a date never made. The New York person who gave stage fright to Fostoria, Ohio, gets a fable too. A later fable stages a modern Solomon judging Flora and Adolph, whose wife proves a vampire of patience. Ade's slang morals still land with a wink.
2534-eugene-pickering:
Henry James sets this short tale at Homburg, a German spa town, in the days when its gaming rooms still drew fashionable crowds. The narrator meets Eugene Pickering, a young American of good fortune, and watches him fall under the spell of Madame Blumenthal, a brilliant older woman of the spa world.

Pickering sees in her a muse and a guide to a finer life, while the narrator doubts whether her charm hides a harder game. James writes with fine irony about youth, admiration, and the gap between what we dream of others and what they are. The story is a small, polished study of an American abroad learning to see clearly.
25353-the-ordinance-of-covenanting:
John Cunningham's Ordinance of Covenanting, published in Glasgow, is a book on the vows God's people make to him. It honors Andrew Symington, a teacher of divinity in the Reformed Presbyterian Church, and it sets out what a covenant, a vow, and an oath each mean.

Cunningham says those saved by grace stand in God's covenant, which has two sides and set terms but is not mere law. A vow is a free pledge to God alone, kept in line with duty, and it may first join or then renew that pact. He warns both those who pick the rite apart bit by bit and those who pass over it in vague terms.
25363-half-hours-in-bible-lands-volume-2:
The Reverend P. C. Headley's Half Hours in Bible Lands, volume two, Patriarchs, Kings, and Kingdoms, was published in Philadelphia in 1867 with many illustrations. Headley, author of Women of the Bible, retells Scripture stories with sketches of Eastern life.

Patriarchs appear as family kings, divinely appointed rulers of households, beginning with Abram and Sarai under Eastern skies. Later scenes follow Isaac and Esau, Job and his friends, and the kings David and Solomon. Solomon's luxury and idolatry split the kingdom between Rehoboam and Jeroboam, and Headley's plain narrative suits family reading.
25441-the-reckoning:
Robert W. Chambers sets this romance in the Revolution's northern frontier. The narrator, Carus, moves among spies, households, and soldiers, while Elsin Grey loves and suffers through divided loyalties. Walter Butler, the loyalist raider, haunts the story as a figure of charm and menace. Chapters carry the reader from an artillery ball to a sermon in stones, and on to Thendara.

The action builds toward the Battle of Johnstown and Butler's Ford, where old scores are settled. Chambers fills his pages with verse dedications, frontier detail, and the gossip of a countryside at war. Published in 1907 by A. Wessels Company, with copyright dated 1905, the book belongs to his series of American historical romances.
25620-asiatic-breezes-or-students-on-the:
Oliver Optic writes this student travel tale in his All Over the World Library, second series, following boys on the wing through Asia. A front picture shows the stern of the Fatima suddenly going down, promising a shipwreck scrape early in the voyage.

Optic, author of army and navy, boat club, yacht club, and lake shore series, sends his students from port to port, mixing sightseeing with mishaps and lessons in conduct. Asiatic breezes, strange sights, and foreign customs fill the journey, while the boys learn to meet danger with pluck and teamwork.
25626-the-girl-scouts-at-bellaire-or-mai:
Lilian Garis writes this 1920 Girl Scout story, published by Cupples and Leon, second in a series after The Girl Scout Pioneers and before The Girl Scouts at Sea Crest. Mary, the maid of the subtitle, awakens to scout life at Bellaire.

Chapters open with joys and joy riding, beautiful Bellaire, a broken marathon, and the eagle's feather. Trails, a little maid in clover, a mountain cave, a secret spring, new friends, and a cry in the night follow. A mysterious pet, a studio, Orchidia, and Professor Benson deepen the mystery before hidden trails resolve it.
2572-on-the-decay-of-the-art-of-lying:
Mark Twain read this essay to the Historical and Antiquarian Club of Hartford, offering it for a thirty dollar prize that it did not take. Twain insists the custom of lying has not decayed at all: the lie, he says, is eternal as a virtue, a solace, and a refuge in need.

What has decayed, he argues with mock gravity, is the art of lying well, with grace and skill. Twain's jokes land on politicians, prudes, and polite society, all while he pretends to defend his subject. The essay is short, sly, and very funny, and it shows Twain turning a club talk into a small masterpiece of mischief.
25773-on-the-portraits-of-english-author:
S. Felton writes this study of portraits of English authors on gardening, with biographical notices, in a second edition with considerable additions, published in London in 1830 by Effingham Wilson and Joseph Onwhyn. Felton had lately published Gleanings on Gardens, chiefly on the ancient style in England.

Shakespeare epigraphs open the book, on painting as almost the natural man and trifles snapped up unconsidered. Felton treats only deceased writers on gardening, tracing portraits taken of them and lives behind the gardens. The book suits gardeners who love old books, pictures, and the men who first wrote English gardening into art.
2590-guy-mannering:
Walter Scott sets this novel on the wild Scottish coast, where the astrologer Guy Mannering casts a child's horoscope and foretells danger at three ages. The child, Harry Bertram, heir to Ellangowan, is stolen away, and his family falls to ruin under smugglers and schemers.

Years later the grown Harry returns, unknowing, among gypsies, soldiers, and the fierce Meg Merrilies, who guards his secret. Scott mixes romance, law, and low comedy with a love of border country. The book stands as one of his liveliest tales of lost heirs, second sight, and home regained.
25908-washington-irving:
Henry W. Boynton writes the life of Washington Irving for the Riverside Biographical Series, printed in 1901. Boynton calls Irving's name the first landmark in American letters, a writer who won esteem at home and notice abroad early in life. Even after his copyrights ran out and cheap editions flooded the market, his first publishers sold more of his books year by year.

Chapters follow Irving from early years and town life through two periods as a man of letters, then as a public figure and as a man himself. A turn to steady, methodical work after the qualified success of Tales of a Traveler gave him keen pleasure, like building a small pyramid after castles in the air. The book gives a clear, fond portrait of a writer still widely read.
2602-queen-sheba-s-ring:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this adventure around a ring that comes to a modern Englishman, launching a journey to a hidden African kingdom. The contents promise a sergeant's advice, a professor out shooting, a death wind, and an escape from Harmac, with lions' dens and oaths along the way.

Haggard's heroes face a queen's shadow, a rescue that fails, and a fate that dogs their steps. The tale mixes lost world romance with imperial adventure, in the author's brisk, earnest style. Readers who love King Solomon's Mines will find the same thrills here, with a ring at the heart of the mystery.
26039-the-gold-thread-a-story-for-the-yo:
Rev. Norman Macleod tells a child's allegory of trust and duty in The Gold Thread, printed by Strahan in 1867 in an eighth edition. Dedicated to his children, for whom he first wrote and read it among the green hills of Moffat, the story later ran in Good Words. Macleod's lesson is plain: trust God, do right, and hold fast your gold thread through every temptation and danger, and God will lead you safe home.

The hero follows his thread up steps cut in rock, down to a raging stream where spray wets his cheek, and across a little bridge that appears just when drowning seems sure. He will not let go, come what may. Macleod tells children that God's voice in heart and word shows what is right, at home, at school, in nursery or playground, every day and everywhere.
26072-scotch-loch-fishing:
Black Palmer writes a practical treatise on Scotch loch fishing, printed by Blackwood in 1882 and dedicated to the Western Angling Club of Glasgow. The author claims nothing new, only a readable form, shunning fish history and habits and sparing technical terms. The edition is interleaved with blank sheets for the reader's notes, and suggestions sent to the publishers will weigh in future editions.

Advice runs hands on. Keep rod butts well at the boat's bottom, lest a loose rod go overboard. Troll with plenty of line, never less than thirty yards on one rod and forty on the other, so a fish missing one lure may see the second. Natural minnow, apt to foul, must be checked intact and spinning true. The book is a plain angler's companion for Scottish lochs.
26116-the-art-of-angling:
Printed in London in 1653 and reprinted at Leeds in 1817, this early manual teaches the craft of fishing with rod, line, and fly. It tells the angler to read sun, wind, moon, and season before setting out tackle. Bright flies suit dull days, and dark flies suit bright ones. It also gives plain rules for ground bait and for casting into a river.

Later pages show how to tie flies from scratch. The silver- or gold-ribbed Palmer and the May-fly are named as the two patterns from which all others follow. The book speaks straight to the reader in the plain voice of a working angler. It still reads as a window onto fishing tackle and river craft in the 1600s.
26186-when-the-birds-begin-to-sing:
Winifred Graham's 1897 novel, with sixteen illustrations by Harold Piffard, tells a love story through chapters titled with lines from Milton, Tennyson, Shakespeare, and Poe. A frontispiece shows a young woman lounging in a way that would shock the vicar's wife. Later pictures name Philip Roche, Mr. and Mrs. Grebby, and Eleanor, who climbs a hill breathless and rushes to a door with a wild cry.

Mid-book talk turns on a gaudily dressed widow, a man named Quinton always at her heels, and letters from a Madame Faustine that Eleanor dares not open. Gossip, jealousy, and guarded secrets drive the plot. The novel gives a vivid picture of late Victorian courtship, where reputation hung on a glance and a letter could change a life.
26308-hints-on-extemporaneous-preaching:
Henry Ware Jr., minister of Boston's Second Church, published this short treatise in 1824 for students of the Harvard theological seminary. Its preface defends a mode of preaching too much discountenanced and despised: speaking without a full written text, under proper limits. Ware cites Burnet on pastoral care, Fenelon on eloquence, and Quintilian on speaking off the cuff.

Three chapters weigh the advantages of free preaching, answer objections, and lay down rules. Ware promises to state benefits fairly while guarding against dangers and abuses, such as poverty of diction. He argues that faults blamed on free speech come from negligent study, not from the method itself. The book suits readers curious about pulpit craft in early America.
26309-the-high-calling:
Charles M. Sheldon's 1911 novel The High Calling, from the author of In His Steps, opens with Paul Douglas and his wife Esther debating their older boy Walter. Paul hoped Walter would join his office, but Walter's mind is set on electrical engineering. His room fills with models, and one device grabs Paul's hat, combs his hair, and sets another machine to blacking his shoes.

Walter calls it head treatment for nervous prostration, with shoe-blacking thrown in while the patient waits. Later, an angry committeeman rings Paul at the State House, demanding his presence. The novel treats a boy's freedom to choose his lifework, and a father's slow lesson that a calling must be the child's own, not the parent's plan.
26312-the-lost-art-of-reading: Gerald Stanley Lee's 1903 book, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons, takes up the reading habit and the forces that break it. Its first book names the literary rush, the bugbear of being well informed, and the art of reading as one likes. Later parts treat the imagination, the first person singular, and the habit of analysis. A second book turns to possibilities and first selection. Lee pleads for reading with freedom and wonder, not hurried duty.
26339-cupology-how-to-be-entertaining:
Clara's Cupology, published by the author at Cincinnati in 1904, promises to teach readers how to be entertaining. Its contents mix social hints, toasts, gems, and methods for telling age, with chapters on inspired cup reading, the woman's era, the mystical cup, and superstition. A reprinted piece insists the art is not mere fortune telling, but prophecy as a science of being able.

Later sections cover what eyes, thumbs, and finger nails reveal, beauty's seven nurses, birth stones for luck, strange wills, and laughagraphs. A peanut, an evening game, and a mysterious telegram all find places. The book offers parlour amusement of its age, with cheerfulness named as a woman's winning card, and luck, love, and laughter never far off.
26558-pennsylvania-dutch-cooking:
This cookbook gathers proven recipes for traditional Pennsylvania Dutch foods, opening with the arrival of the Plain Sects in William Penn's colony in 1683. Moravians, Mennonites, Amish, Dunkards, Schwenkfelds, and French Huguenots blended recipes from many homelands with new-world ingredients, handing dishes from mother to daughter for generations. Old measures such as butter the size of a walnut show a folk art.

Soups lead the book, from chicken corn soup at picnic suppers to rivel soup made from milk and flour alone. Fastnachts mark Shrove Tuesday, young dandelion greens mark Maundy Thursday, and dozens of Christmas cookies fill the house before the holiday. Pies appear at breakfast, lunch, dinner, and midnight snacks, with apple, rivel, and many more, in generous batches of six or eight.
26782-it-could-be-anything:
Keith Laumer wrote this tale of Brett, a young man who leaves Casperton because books have shown him a world beyond cornfields, cattle, and hazy blue hills. Aunt Haicey blames thick books with no pictures for the trouble, and Pretty-Lee, who loves movie magazines and their glamorous stars, stays behind as he boards the train. Brett wants to see cities, mountains, and ocean for himself, not merely read about them.

Where he arrives, the people move and speak like figures out of written stories, knitting brows, starting back in alarm, and trading knowing glances. Brett calls them golems, since real people never act that way. Illustrated by Finlay, the tale asks what meaning means when life itself starts to read like a book.
26835-where-the-souls-of-men-are-calling:
Credo Harris published this novel with Britton Publishing Company in 1918, with a frontispiece by John R. Neill. It opens in Hillsdale, a town somewhere in the United States, on a mild day in early April 1917. Two neat women, Miss Sallie and Miss Veemie Tumpson, are uncovering their tulip beds. Colonel Hampton stops at their fence with news that German submarines have torpedoed another American ship, and that war is certain.

Hillsdale sits on the fence between past and progress, its livery stables turned into a moving-picture house and a garage, its streets arched by elms, poplars, or live oaks. The novel follows its people from home-front talk into the war itself. There a young soldier leans on his rifle, knees ready to crumple, and learns that trouble looks far greater at a distance than once in action.
26862-howard-pyle-s-book-of-pirates-fict:
Merle Johnson gathered Howard Pyle's writings and pictures about pirates into this Harper and Brothers volume. It mixes fiction, fact, and fancy about the buccaneers and marooners of the Spanish Main. Pyle's own preface says he admires his pirate hero not for adventure, winds, or hidden gold, but because the man knew his own mind and his own wishes. Eight chapters carry that admiration across the Spanish Main.

The first chapter opens off Hispaniola, on the little hunch of island called Tortuga de Mar for its likeness to a sea turtle. Later chapters give the ghost of Captain Brand, Tom Chist and the treasure box, Jack Ballister's fortunes, Blueskin the pirate, Captain Scarfield, and the ruby of Kishmoor. Pyle's pictures run through the book, from the attack on a galleon to Blackbeard burying his treasure.
26865-the-corsair-king:
Maurus Jókai wrote this novel as A Kalóz Király, translated by Mary J. Safford and published by L. C. Page and Company of Boston in 1901. Four chapters divide it: Choosing a King, In Hispaniola, Revenge, and Retribution. It opens after a storm, with a battered brigantine limping over calm water off the Ladrones, its crew repairing damage and its captain checking his chart.

Captain Rolls summons the crew to judge what happened in the night, when the sick were thrown overboard as superfluous ballast. The surgeon Scudamore, smooth and gentle of face until mockery or greed transforms him, answers that the captain himself gave the order. From that shipboard trial the story moves toward the choosing of a corsair king and the vengeance that follows.
26928-ladies-in-waiting:
Kate Douglas Wiggin published this book of five stories with Houghton Mifflin of Boston and New York in 1919, with a frontispiece by Christine Tucke Curtiss. The stories are Miss Thomasina Tucker, The Turning-Point, Huldah the Prophetess, Two on a Tour, and Philippa's Nervous Prostration. The first opens at the Hoboken dock, where friends call good-bye to a young lady laden with bouquets and bonbons on the deck of an ocean steamer.

Miss Tommy, as they call her, sails with her belongings in the hold, her room given up, and her beastly uncle quarreled with at last. She leaves behind no home or kin to return to. She plans to sing her way from a modest Bloomsbury lodging to a gorgeous Ritz suite. Her courage, she says, is oozing out at the heels of her shoes as the gangplank lifts.
26960-famous-privateersmen-and-adventure:
Charles H. L. Johnston's 1911 volume, part of his Famous Leaders series, tells of privateersmen and adventurers of the sea: their rovings, cruises, escapades, and fierce battling for patriotism and for treasure. The book draws the line its old ballad draws, between those who sailed under letters legal and those under the cross-bones.

Among its subjects is Edward England, terror of the South Seas, met off the African coast in a brig. Johnston writes in brisk, boy-friendly prose, with cannon fire, boarding parties, and hard bargains, celebrating sailors who lived by daring on the open ocean.
27053-the-day-time-stopped-moving:
Bradner Buckner's science-fiction story The Day Time Stopped Moving begins with Dave Miller, drunk and despairing, pressing a revolver to his temple. Helen has left him after a year of late homecomings, and her brief letter of heartbreak lies on the drain-board.

Miller pulls the trigger, but what follows is all wrong: no St. Peter, no pearly gate, and everyone standing around like statues. A girl he pushes proves as unmovable as Gibraltar. The story turns a suicide attempt into a strange frozen world, where one man must learn what stopped time wants from him.
2714-long-live-the-king:
Mary Roberts Rinehart wrote this romance of a crown prince who runs away and sees the world, only to return disgraced and face terror at court. Chapters at a riding school, tea in a schoolroom, and a chancellor's visit mix boyish adventure with palace intrigue.

A letter, a fine night, and the right to live and love test the prince, while Nikky does a reckless thing and two prisoners wait in the park. Rinehart writes with warmth and suspense, in the Ruritanian manner. The book delights as a story of youth, duty, and a throne too heavy for a boy.
27268-ariadne-florentina-six-lectures-on:
John Ruskin's Ariadne Florentina gives six lectures on wood and metal engraving before the University of Oxford in Michaelmas term 1872. They define the art and its place among the arts in Florence. The lectures then take up the technics of wood engraving and of metal engraving in turn.

Design in the German schools, through Holbein and Dürer, and in the Florentine schools, through Sandro Botticelli, close the course, with an appendix on the present state of engraving in England. Ruskin's frog parliament, where leaping power lies in the hump-back as flying power lies in the breast-bone, shows his digressive wit.
27274-manures-and-the-principles-of-manu:
C. M. Aikman's Manures and the Principles of Manuring, third impression of 1910 from Blackwood, builds the science of manuring on Rothamsted results. Dedicated to Sir John Bennet Lawes and Sir J. Henry Gilbert, whose fifty years of investigations built the field, it fills a gap in English agricultural literature.

Part One gives a historical introduction, and Part Two takes up fertility of the soil in its physical, chemical, and biological properties. Tables of absorptive power by Schübler and rates of evaporation support a treatise meant for farmers and students of agricultural science.
27353-indian-conjuring:
Major L. H. Branson of the Indian Army wrote this small volume on the conjurers he watched in India, published in London by George Routledge and Sons and in New York by E. P. Dutton, with eight illustrations. Branson dedicates it to his wife, his best audience and keenest critic at his many sleight-of-hand performances, and reprints pieces first published in the Times of India.

Chapters take up the cup and balls, bamboo sticks, the ring on the stick, and the glass box. They also take up the bowl of rice, coloured sands, a rope trick, and the egg bag. The dancing duck, the mango tree trick, and the basket trick follow, with snakes and crocodiles besides. His old friend Shah Mahommed, aged 87, heads a family of itinerant conjurers. The book separates witnessed tricks from myths about Indian magic.
27456-the-mouse-s-wedding:
This Japanese fairy tale, number six in the Japanese Fairy Tale Series, was published by Griffith Farran in London and Sydney and by Kobunsha in Tokyo. Its hero is Kanemochi, a white mouse and servant of Daikoku, the God of Wealth. Onaga, his wife, shares his discreet life, safe from the cat by never venturing into parlor or kitchen.

Their only son Fukutaro, of a gentle disposition, is ready to marry, and his parents hire a go-between to treat with their relative Chudayu for his lovely daughter Hatsuka. Presents pass both ways: an obi, dried bonito and cuttle fish, white flax, seaweed, and sake. The tale gives a charming glimpse of Japanese wedding custom, told through mice.
27564-little-folks-july-1884-a-magazine-:
Little Folks, a magazine for the young in a new and enlarged series, published this number with Cassell in London, Paris, and New York in July 1884. Its lead story, A Little Too Clever, comes from the author of Pen's Perplexities and Maid Marjory.

That story opens on the moor, one broad expanse of purply heather kindled crimson by ruddy sunshine. The writer talks straight to children about crimson-lake from their paint-boxes, and the golds and greens no paint-box holds. A picture called A Queen of the Beach also appears. The number gives young readers stories and pictures together.
27576-little-folks-september-1884-a-maga:
Little Folks, a magazine for the young in a new and enlarged series, published this number with Cassell in London, Paris, and New York in September 1884. It continues the serial A Little Too Clever, by the author of Pen's Perplexities, with chapters called Escape, A Fairy Visitor, and The New Mother.

Elsie awakes after a dull, heavy sleep in a rude sleeping-place, lit only dimly through an aperture. Mrs. Ferguson is already up and busy, but Elsie's frock is not dry, so she must make shift with an old gown. Duncan's jacket has disappeared too. The morning is bright and warm after rain, and the children resolve to be on the road once more. Young readers follow their escape.
27645-the-beginning:
Henry Hasse wrote this prehistoric tale, illustrated by Finlay, of Gral, small and weakest of all the males of his tribe. Its blurb promises a relentless tale of early man, building toward a deadly climax.

Gral's existence is brute obedience to brute awareness, for only thus does one survive. There is the danger-sense when great-toothed cats roam the valley, and the hunger-sense when provender runs low and Gor-wah drives the males out to hunt wild-dogs, lizards, and lesser beasts. Who does not bring does not eat, by Gor-wah's dictate, until the others have gorged. Once, Gral scales the valley-rim and sees the little three-toed horses of the huge plain.
27693-little-folks-october-1884-a-magazi:
Little Folks, a magazine for the young, in its new and enlarged series, published this October 1884 number with Cassell and Company of London, Paris, and New York. Its serialized story, A Little Too Clever, by the author of Pen's Perplexities and Maid Marjory, runs through chapters twelve to fourteen.

Chapter twelve, An Unexpected Friend, finds Elsie thoroughly frightened and miserable for the first time since she left home. Her little attic high in a tall house full of people seems more dreadful than the bare loft in Sandy Ferguson's hovel. Loud voices, banging doors, hurrying footsteps, and the roar of traffic terrify the moor-bred Scottish lassie. She realizes her plan of running away was greatly mistaken.
27746-schedule-of-salaries-for-teachers-:
Issued by the Boston School Committee on January 20, 1920, this circular sets the salary schedule for teachers, supervising staff, and others in the public schools . It records the committee's orders fixing pay by rank.

The schedule lays out minimum and maximum salaries with annual increments, and rules for advancing staff already on the previous year's scale. As a document it captures a moment of postwar pay reform, when Boston raised teacher salaries and tied progress to years of service. The circular came from the secretary's office under orders adopted by the committee on January 5, 1920.
27823-little-folks-november-1884-a-magaz:
Little Folks, a magazine for the young published by Cassell and Company of London, Paris, and New York, appears here in its November 1884 number, in a new and enlarged series. The issue serializes A Little Too Clever, by the author of Pen's Perplexities, among other stories and pictures.

The excerpt opens in London, where Grandpapa Donaldson protests a warrant for John and Lucy Murdoch, while young Elsie listens with curiosity and hides her knowledge. The magazine mixes serial fiction, puzzles, and pictures, and it preserves Victorian children's reading in monthly form.
27925-the-art-of-disappearing:
John Talbot Smith, author of Saranac and Training of a Priest, published The Art of Disappearing with Benziger Brothers in 1902. The novel is arranged in sections on disappearance, among the exiles, the green against the red, an escaped nun, and the test of disappearance. The novel is long.

It opens with Horace Endicott, whose ten months with his young wife Sonia were roseate, then follows holy oils, the Dillon clan, a villa at Coney Island, and an invasion of Ireland. Smith blends Catholic feeling, Irish politics, and melodrama in a long, ambitious romance.
28007-little-folks-december-1884-a-magaz:
Little Folks, a magazine for the young, was published by Cassell and Company in London, Paris, and New York in a new and enlarged series. The 1884 volume's index lists amusements and recreations, a children's garden through the months, fanciful rhymes and fairy stories, and notices of the Little Folks Humane Society.

Contents include Little Miss Propriety, A Game of Cricket in Elfland, The Children's Own Garden, Little Margaret's Kitchen, and songs such as Three Little Squirrels and A Harvest Song. The magazine mixes instruction with play. Its crafts, stories, and moral tales show Victorian children's periodical writing at its most industrious.
28041-selections-from-the-poems-and-play:
Myra Reynolds, professor at the University of Chicago, edited these selections from the poems and plays of Robert Browning, published by Scott, Foresman and Company in 1909 in the Lake Library Edition. The introduction also treats Browning's life and poetry, with a bibliography and chronological table.

Selections also run from Songs from Paracelsus and Cavalier Tunes through My Last Duchess, The Pied Piper of Hamelin, Childe Roland, Fra Lippo Lippi, and Andrea del Sarto, with notes. The volume served students as a generous introduction to Browning's dramatic monologues and narrative verse.
28090-hints-on-driving:
C. S. Ward, the well-known Whip of the West, wrote Hints on Driving in London in 1870 from long practice with four-horse teams. Ward's father owned coaches and taught him the trade, and at seventeen Ward drove the Norwich and Ipswich Mail fifty-two miles a night to Colchester. He later drove the fast Quicksilver mail to Devonport.

The book teaches harnessing, handling reins, turning, and keeping horses sound, with stories from the road. Ward writes for gentlemen drivers, not only for professionals. It gives a vivid picture of coaching in its last great age, just before railways took the mails away.
28135-the-nursery-july-1877-xxii-no-1-a-:
The Nursery for July 1877, volume twenty-two, number one, opens a new volume of the Boston monthly for youngest readers. Prose tales include Percy and the Oxen, a Fourth of July morning, a fish story, Buttercup's Circus, and a sixth lesson in astronomy, with a drawing lesson and notes on the chamois. John L. Shorey published the magazine.

Verse runs from The Wild Bees' Home to songs of chipping birds, a kitten, and garden tools, closing with a bird song set to music. The pieces are short, plain, and full of animals, holidays, and country sights. The issue suits collectors of early children's magazines and readers of Victorian childhood.
28335-how-two-boys-made-their-own-electr:
Thomas M. St. John wrote How Two Boys Made Their Own Electrical Apparatus, eighth edition, as a manual for young makers. St. John, a teacher of great ingenuity, gives directions for 152 pieces of apparatus in 141 pages, with 125 pictures, priced at one dollar postpaid. Chapters cover cells, batteries, switches, magnets, coils, telegraph keys, bells, motors, and tools.

Boys learn to wind wire, build induction coils, and make galvanometers, bells, and buzzers from plain materials. St. John's tone is practical and encouraging, with clear steps. The book offers a classic guide to home electrical experiments, still useful for young builders.
28486-the-weakling:
Everett B. Cole's science-fiction story The Weakling opens with Naran Makun questioning a caravan master about his vanished brother. Dar Makun's whole train dropped out of sight on the northern swing. It left not a scrap of cargo nor the bones of a long-neck, though the null, a swirling danger, sometimes covers great territory in a hurry.

Suspicion falls on Kio Barra, master of a great mountain estate, who saw the caravan to his border. Barra is a psionic weakling, lord of the Mountain Lake more by title than by punch, yet the story's tagline warns that a weakling with a weapon is viciously deadly. Cole's tale turns on that paradox, with carnivores, pseudomen, and destructors in the background.
28533-the-king-s-post-being-a-volume-of-:
R. C. Tombs, ex-controller of the London postal service and late surveyor-postmaster of Bristol, wrote The King's Post as a companion to his Bristol Royal Mail. Published in Bristol in 1905, with a second edition in 1906, it gathers historical facts about the posts, mail coaches, coach roads, and railway mail services of Bristol from 1580 onward.

Chapters trace foot and running posts, the first Bristol postmasters Allen and Teague, the post house at the Dolphin Inn, Elizabethan posts, roads, and John Palmer's mail coach innovations. Tombs also honours Ralph Allen, Palmer, and Sir Francis Freeling. The book is a detailed local history of how letters moved before the modern post.
2885-the-house-of-the-wolfings-a-tale-of:
William Morris wrote The House of the Wolfings in prose and verse as a tale of the Wolfing house and all the kindreds of the Mark. The opening verses compare the world of men to a traveler passing a homestead left years before, its candles bright in a room beside the door that can never be entered again. The Mark's tribes face a Roman threat from the Mirkwood.

The story moves toward battle at the Slaughter Tofts, where tidings will tell whether the curse of the world has awakened and the serpent crawls in the thicket. Wood-wolves, shield people, spear kin, and horse kin march together. Morris's archaic style gives the tale its strange music, and it stands as a founding work of modern fantasy.
28954-this-is-klon-calling:
Walt Sheldon wrote this short science fiction story about Professor Lyman Dane, a practical joker who teaches by laughter. Dane, a tall, mournful, sly figure with wispy hair drooping like a tired willow, once jumped from a third-story window to teach terminal velocity, having rigged a canvas net below. He also loosed a mouse among women students to show chain reaction, and played boogie-woogie on a memorial carillon.

Dane claims that the absorption of knowledge grows in direct proportion to humor, with the belly laugh, measured in decibels, held constant. The story's warning opens it: one sure road to living dangerously is becoming a practical joker, and doubters might ask Professor Dane. Readers get a witty tale of a teacher whose jokes finally meet a danger no net can catch.
29022-mr-punch-awheel-the-humours-of-mot:
This volume, Mr. Punch Awheel: The Humours of Motoring and Cycling, gathers the cream of Punch humor on new machines, edited by J. A. Hammerton for the Punch Library of Humour. The book offers one hundred twenty pictures by Phil May, L. Raven Hill, Bernard Partridge, Tom Browne, and others, from Punch's run since 1841. One cartoon shows an owner of a violently palpitating motor car, promising all will be well once he finds the what-d'ye-call-it.

The Punch Library planned twenty-five volumes, from life in London and country life to Scottish, Irish, and Cockney humor. This volume treats the age when motors and bicycles changed the road, with jokes about breakdowns, speed, and new freedom. Readers get a funny, well-drawn record of early motoring, in the style that made Punch famous.
29206-happy-ending:
Mack Reynolds and Fredric Brown wrote this science fiction story about a man left alone after his world collapsed. Burned-out cities lie still and dead, and twisted bodies and souls give him their last salute in death. He waits, surrounded by memories, on a world that will never shout his praises again.

Four men come down in a lifeboat from a space-cruiser to Venusian shores. Three wear Galactic Guard uniforms. The fourth, bundled in a greatcoat and hat, his lower face bandaged, sits silent in the prow. Venusian trees seem to talk to him in soft, loyal voices. Readers get a bleak, moving tale of guilt, exile, and an ending that is happy only in the darkest sense.
29365-browning-s-england-a-study-in-engl:
Helen Archibald Clarke published this study of English influences in Browning in New York in 1908, as a companion to her Browning's Italy. Clarke, dedicating the book to her colleague Charlotte Porter, asks how England shaped Robert Browning, the poet long associated with Italy. Chapters move from English poets, friends, and enthusiasms to Shakespeare's portrait.

Later chapters cover a crucial period in English history, social aspects of English life, religious thought in the nineteenth century, and art criticism inspired by the English musician Avison. Illustrations show Shelley, Keats, Wordsworth, and Shakespeare's first folio portrait. Readers get a thorough literary study, useful for Browning readers tracing the English roots beneath the Italian poems.
29458-cost-of-living:
Robert Sheckley's short tale opens in a glittering plastic shower room, where easy luxury eases Carrin's mind. His clothes go into an automatic Kleen-presser, his breakfast is dialed and gracefully prepared, and his son grunts at the table. Yet Carrin cannot shake a vague, formless fear, traced to Miller's suicide last week. Miller had everything: wife, kids, a good job, and all the marvels of the age.
