Hester and Amy, Vavasor, and Major Marvel move through concerts, failures, and a journey that tests them all.

The title points to a soul weighed and found wanting, then remade by love and truth. MacDonald blends domestic realism with moral depth, and his characters grow through small acts of courage. The novel rewards readers who enjoy Victorian tales where character grows through trial and grace.
9328-cleveland-past-and-present-its-repr:
Published in 1869, this history of Cleveland joins biographies of pioneer settlers and prominent citizens to a history of the city. Commerce, manufactures, ship building, railroads, telegraphy, schools, and churches all get historical sketches, with photographic views and portraits by E. Decker. The preface notes how often Cleveland's founding has been told.

Colonel Charles Whittlesey's early history closes with the War of 1812, and this volume carries the story forward. Pioneer gatherings, newspapers, and directories had kept the tale alive. The book remains a rich source for Ohio history, and for the growth of a lake city.
9508-stories-worth-rereading:
Stories Worth Rereading, printed in 1913, gathers short tales and true sketches chosen for young readers and home reading. The pieces stress honor, pluck, kindness, and faith, in plain, earnest prose. Titles include Their Word of Honor, The Strength of Clinton, Jack's Fidelity, and Honor Thy Father and Thy Mother. True tales sit beside fiction, from David Livingstone to a San Francisco quake scene.

Other pieces warn against drink, praise a mother's ring, and tell of mission work from India to China. A boy without a reference, a mite box drive, and a sleigh ride all teach the same code: keep your word and stand by others. A reader gets a wholesome, old-style story book, rich in moral tales meant to be read aloud and kept in mind.
9608-the-cords-of-vanity-a-comedy-of-shi:
James Branch Cabell wrote The Cords of Vanity, a comedy of shirking, in a revised and expanded edition with an introduction by Wilson Follett. Follett calls the book an act of reclamation and fresh creation, and jokes that he may be its only known buyer. Cabell, famed for ornate fantasy, here turns to a hero who dodges duty with wit. The subtitle names the game: vanity's cords bind a man who will not face life.

Chapters follow confidences, loves, and evasions, as the hero talks his way past each call to act. Cabell's prose stays rich and ironic, half jest and half moral tale. A reader gets an early Cabell comedy, clever and bittersweet, on the art of getting by without growing up.
973-howard-pyle-s-book-of-pirates-fictio:
Howard Pyle wrote and drew these tales of buccaneers and marooners of the Spanish Main, compiled by Merle Johnson with a foreword by the compiler. The Ghost of Captain Brand, With the Buccaneers, and other pieces mix fact, fiction, and fancy, as Pyle imagined the pirate world of the seventeenth century.

Pyle's pirates are bold, cruel, and romantic by turns, and his pictures fixed the pirate image for generations: striped shirts, cutlasses, and treasure maps. The book gathers his best pirate work in one volume, with Johnson's notes to guide the reader. It remains a classic for lovers of sea adventure and of Pyle's art.
a-book-for-the-young: Sarah French offers a small book of poems and pieces for young readers. Its contents range from an address to the young and a dying horse to a ghost story, an embarkation scene, and the execution of Montrose. The verses treat courage, loss, and moral choice in plain and earnest language. French presents the collection as a modest gift meant to guide and entertain its youthful audience.
a-century-of-wrong: Jan Christiaan Smuts presents the Boer case in this account of a century of wrong. Its chapters run from the Cape of Good Hope through the founding of Natal, the Orange Free State, and the South African Republic. Smuts then treats the conventions of 1881 and 1884 and what he calls capitalistic jingoism. With a preface by Stead, the book asks readers to hear the other side.
a-course-in-wood-turning: Archie Seldon Milton teaches wood turning in a practical course for students. The book covers lathe speed, methods of fastening stock, spiral turning, and the making of plates and bowls. Illustrations and plates guide the learner through each process step by step. Milton's course serves schools and workshops where turning is taught by hand.
a-final-reckoning:
A Final Reckoning is an 1887 adventure novel by G A Henty. Its hero is a young English lad who, after a rather stormy boyhood, emigrates to Australia to start again. There he finds employment as an officer in the mounted police, a job that puts him on the colony's rough frontier.

A few years of active work bring him many brushes with both Aboriginal people and bushrangers, and promotion to a captaincy. In the end he settles down to the peaceful life of a squatter, a sheep or cattle farmer on his own land. The novel is classic Henty: a boy's colonial career told as a chain of frontier tests, ending in earned respectability.
a-king-and-no-king: Francis Beaumont writes a king and no king, a Jacobean tragicomedy of love and power. Its cast includes Mardonius and Bessus, two captains, the queen mother Arane, her daughter Panthea, and Spaconia. The first scene opens with the captains discussing the king. Beaumont's play mixes court intrigue, passion, and wit.
a-life-of-st-john-for-the-young: George Ludington Weed writes a life of St. John for the young. The incidents of John's life come chiefly from the Gospels, Acts, Epistles, and Revelation. Weed notes that some traditions about John are in harmony with scripture and some are not. The book gives young readers a clear life of the beloved disciple.
a-life-s-morning:
George Gissing's novel A Life's Morning follows a brilliant young scholar whose strength fails under his own ambition. Wilfrid Athel wins a scholarship to Balliol College at Oxford and drives himself without rest. A breakdown sends him home before he turns twenty-three. His father hopes quiet country life will restore him.

At home Wilfrid meets Emily, a young woman of strong mind and small means, and their attachment grows. Beatrice Redwing, wealthy and assured, offers a very different future. Family pressure, pride, and money pull the lovers apart. Chapters move through renunciation, parted paths, and a final reckoning at mid-day. Gissing writes a sober love story about talent, class, and the cost of surrendering one's own judgment.
a-rough-shaking: George MacDonald follows Clare Skymer in this story, from how the narrator came to know him, through his parents, a new family, and a new home. The chapter titles trace Clare as defender, farm boy, guardian of the poor, vagabond, and tramp, past a baker's cart, a blacksmith's forge, treasure trove, and justifiable burglary. Workhouse, magistrate, and policeman await a boy whose rough shaking comes from a world harder than himself.
a-text-book-of-assaying: Cornelius Beringer, with J. J. Beringer, writes this textbook of assaying for the use of those connected with mines, revised in a ninth edition with diagrams and tables. The first part treats the object and sampling of assaying, dry and wet gravimetric methods, volumetric assays, weighing and measuring, reagents, formulae, and specific gravity. The second part turns to metals in turn, beginning with silver, gold, platinum, cyanides, and mercury.
a-text-book-of-the-history-of-painting: John Van Dyke writes this textbook of the history of painting as one of a series of concise, teachable histories of art for classroom use in schools and colleges. Limited time for art study dictates a condensed style and a scope held to the general features of art history. Archaeological disputes and aesthetic theories are left aside. The main facts, as the best authorities have settled them, are given, with a bibliography at the head of each chapter for readers who want particulars.
a-young-girl-s-wooing: Edward Payson Roe tells a young girl's wooing in this illustrated volume of 1884, opening with a crescent of a girl and Graydon Muir. The contents follow a parting, effort, achievement, the secret of beauty, rival girls, a meeting, and old ties broken. Promptings of Miss Wildmere's heart, strategy, perplexity, and a declaration of independence carry the story on. An illustration asks whether Graydon is so bent upon winning her, in a courtship of gossamer threads and enemies' plans.
actions-and-reactions-by-rudyard-kipling:
Actions and Reactions is Rudyard Kipling's 1909 collection of short stories, presented here in an edition under his full byline. By 1909 Kipling was among the most famous living English writers, the author of The Jungle Book, Just So Stories, and Kim. This collection belongs to his later work, when his stories grew denser and more oblique.

The tales range across the worlds Kipling made his own: England at home, the empire abroad, and machines and men under strain. As in the companion edition, each story's action carries its reaction with it, often in a following verse. The book preserves Kipling's mature storytelling at the point where his fame rested as much on these crafted tales as on his early successes.
an-essay-on-medi-val-economic-teaching: George O'Brien writes an essay on mediaeval economic teaching, dedicated to Michael Cronin and issued from University College, Dublin. The study traces how medieval thinkers treated wealth, trade, and just price. O'Brien's clear survey joins economic history to the moral thought of the Middle Ages. The past here still speaks to how we judge wealth.
an-introduction-to-the-study-of-browning: Arthur Symons guides new readers into the study of Browning, in a short book on a great poet of his own time, given to George Meredith, novelist and poet. Symons walks through Browning's voice poems, his hard style, and his force, in plain terms. The study helped a new set of readers find their way into a hard but rich poet, and it still reads well today.
ancient-town-planning: Francis Haverfield writes on ancient town-planning, published by Oxford University Press, with plans and illustrations. The study shows how Greek and Roman towns were laid out, with streets, walls, and public squares following order and purpose. Haverfield's book founded the modern study of ancient urban design. Plans and views help the reader see each town whole.
anthony-wilding:
Anthony Wilding is a 1910 historical romance by Rafael Sabatini, set during Monmouth's Rebellion in the West Country of seventeenth-century England. The Duke of Monmouth, the ill-fated claimant called King Monmouth in the story, tries to rally troops who will not obey him. Against that failing rising, the hero Anthony Wilding pursues a private quest of his own.

Wilding sets out to woo a bride who does not want him, and his courtship becomes tangled with the rebellion around it. Sabatini weaves the political and personal plots together until each changes the other. Wilding emerges from the adventure wiser than he began, in a romance that mixes battle, intrigue, and love in Sabatini's swashbuckling manner.
areopagitica-a-speech-for-the-liberty-of:
John Milton addressed this speech to the Parliament of England against the licensing of books. Parliament had ordered that nothing be printed without official approval first, and Milton answers that free printing is the condition of a free commonwealth. The epigraph from Euripides sets the claim: true liberty is when free-born men may speak freely to advise the public.

Milton argues that licensing came from the very machinery of censorship England had thrown off. It cannot stop falsehood without also stopping truth. A virtuous reader, he says, is made by grappling with books of all kinds, not by being kept from them. He asks what it profits a nation to kill the thought in the book as well as the man. The speech failed in its moment and became the classic defense of a free press.
as-we-were-saying:
Charles Dudley Warner collected these short essays from his newspaper column, the Drawer, and this text comes from the Backlog Edition of his complete writings of 1904. The contents list twenty-six pieces, beginning with a defence of the rose against the fashionable chrysanthemum. Warner's persona is the fireside talker, and the first essay sets the tone of genial combat.

The subjects are the small change of civilized life. Fashion gets several essays: the red bonnet, the Directoire gown, frocks and the stage, and the clothes of fiction. Women in Congress and shall women propose treat the woman question with period caution. Chew on the list and you find chewing gum, dinner-table talk, altruism, and the burden of Christmas. It is journalism written to be re-read, in paragraphs of a column's length.
back-to-billabong:
Mary Grant Bruce's Back to Billabong returns her young Australians from London school to the station life they love. The book opens at Lancaster Gate in London, where red-haired Wilfred refuses to draw a beastly old map again, to his teacher's exasperation.

Chapters follow playing truant, coming home, sailing orders, watch dogs, a strange taxi, and the welcome of Australia itself. At Billabong come colonial experiences, the home on the creek, the Cungee races, and Wally riding a race. Bruce writes with the affection for open spaces that Dorothea Mackellar's epigraph celebrates. Young readers who love Australian station stories will find Billabong waiting, brown and dear, as ever.
baddeck-and-that-sort-of-thing:
Charles Dudley Warner gathered these light sketches of a summer trip to Baddeck, on Cape Breton Island, and addressed the preface to his travelling companion, Joseph H. Twichell. Twichell taught him the name, showed him the map, and produced a missionary's letter promising trout and salmon in the Bras d'Or lakes. The missionary, Warner reports, was never found.

The journey the two men actually made was mostly imposed on them by the arrangements of provincial travel. They crossed Nova Scotia by coach, rail, and steamer toward a week's fishing that kept receding. Warner's preface lays down his rule: the book contains only what they saw, no library compilation. The comedy is in the gap between the expedition planned and the one fate delivered, told in his gentlest manner.
bat-wing:
Sax Rohmer published this detective novel in 1920, sending his sleuth Paul Harley of Chancery Lane into a country-house mystery steeped in obeah. A frontispiece shows a woman raising her arms so her shadow on the blind resembles a bat. Chapters promise a voodoo swamp, a vampire bat, the call of M'Kombo, and a night walker at Cray's Folly.

Colin Camber, a recluse with a secret, stands at the case's centre while Inspector Aylesbury of Market Hilton cross-examines and theorises. Madame, lately widowed, apologises for the absent Colonel at dinner and arranges cigars with him after. A Spanish cigarette, a Lee-Enfield, and the wing of a bat serve as clues. Rohmer mixes West Indian terror with the classic English murder puzzle, narrated by Harley's friend Knox.
botchan-master-darling:
Yasotaro Morri translated Botchan, a Japanese novel by Kin-nosuke Natsume, and J R Kennedy revised the English text in 1919. Natsume, who wrote as Soseki, made the hero a brash Tokyo youth sent to teach in a country school. The translator's note warns that much tone must be lost.

Botchan clashes at once with Red Shirt, Badger, and Clown, the staff room rogues he names on sight. A grasshopper row and a whoop-la affair stir the school against him. Plain speech and quick fists are his only tools. Kiyo, the old servant who adores him, frames the tale with love. Kennedy's text keeps the comedy brisk. English readers met modern Japan through a school satire still read there today.
britannica-1911-agriculture-crops-and-cr:
Crops and Cropping reports a loosening of old rotation rules. Early twentieth-century farmers crop more freely than their fathers. Formal rotation systems bind them less closely now. Science underlies that new freedom, the section argues. Experiment stations have taught plant-life's real requirements. Rothamsted is the greatest and oldest such station. Lawes founded it at Harpenden in 1843. He and Gilbert published about one hundred and thirty reports. Their plots grew single crops for decades running.

Findings fill the long technical section. Wheat grew fifty-seven years in succession on one plot. Manured and unmanured plots ran side by side. Legumes like clover leave soil richer in nitrogen. Hellriegel and Wilfarth explained that mystery in 1886. Grass plots under different manures vary kaleidoscopically, it says.
britannica-1911-aidan-king:
Aidan, king of the Scottish kingdom of Dalriada, who died in 606, receives a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the son of Gabran, an earlier king of Dalriada. When his kinsman King Conall died, Aidan succeeded him. St Columba himself crowned him at Iona, a sign of the island monastery's weight in his world.

Aidan refused to let his kingdom stay dependent on the Irish Dalriada across the sea. Independence at home did not bring safety abroad. He came into collision with his southern neighbours and led a large force against Aethelfrith, king of the Northumbrians. The Scots were defeated at a place called Daegsanstane, probably in Liddesdale. The entry points readers to Bede and to Adamnan's life of St Columba for the record of his reign.
britannica-1911-albert-i-german-king:
Albert I, German king and duke of Austria, who lived from about 1250 to 1308, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Eldest son of Rudolph I, founder of Habsburg greatness, he was invested with Austria and Styria in 1282. A year later his father left him their sole government, which he ran with marked success.

Rudolph could not secure the German throne for his son, and the princes chose Adolph of Nassau in 1291, fearing Albert's power. Albert recognised his rival, then took the field when princes turned against Adolph. Adolph fell at Gollheim near Worms in 1298, and Albert was elected at Frankfort. He secured Bohemia's crown for his son Rudolph in 1306, pressed claims on Thuringia, and was defeated at Lucka in 1307.
britannica-1911-albert-ii-german-king:
Albert II packed three crowns into a reign cut short by war. Born in August 1397 to Albert IV of Habsburg, he followed his father in Austria in 1404 and took up rule in 1411. Good counsel helped him clear out ills that had grown while he was a child. He was king of Hungary and of Bohemia, German king, and, as Albert V, duke of Austria.

Albert fought beside the German king Sigismund against the Hussites, then wed Sigismund's daughter and heiress Elizabeth in 1422. Sigismund named him as his heir. Hungary crowned him in January 1438; Bohemia's crown came six months later, though the land itself never fell into his hands. Frankfort picked him as German king that March, an honour he had not chased. He died at Langendorf in October 1439, defending Hungary from the Turks, a keen, warlike prince whose brief reign held much promise.
britannica-1911-alcinous-king:
Alcinous, a king in Greek legend, is noticed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He ruled the fabulous Phaeacians on the island of Scheria, and he was the son of Nausithous and grandson of Poseidon, the sea god. His place in literature is fixed by one great act of hospitality. A storm cast Odysseus onto his island's shore.

The king's daughter Nausicaa relieved the shipwrecked hero, and Alcinous received and entertained him at court. Homer tells that story across books six to thirteen of the Odyssey. The gardens and palace of Alcinous were famous in antiquity, as were the wonderful ships of the Phaeacian sailors. Scheria was identified very early with Corcyra, where Alcinous was honoured as a hero. In the Argonaut legend his island home is called Drepane instead.
britannica-1911-amuck-running:
Despair, not madness, is the cause argued for running amuck. Jealousy at home or losses at play can leave a man weary of life, and the frenzy works, in effect, as the Malay form of suicide. Older opinion had blamed sudden insanity. The Malay term, more properly amok, names the fit itself: a man rushes out with a kris or other weapon and cuts at all he meets until he is killed.

In British lands the custom has died out, a quoted authority notes, since offenders dislike capture and a cold-blooded trial. The word may be Indian in origin, and Indian cases follow: a Rajput prince fell on Shah Jahan's court in 1634 and killed five officials. At Hyderabad, two envoys stabbed a prince and twenty-six attendants. Malabar's hired assassins end the survey.
britannica-1911-automatic-writing:
Automatic writing is writing performed without the agent's volition. Psychical researchers gave it that name. The writer may not know the words written. Some automatists know the word being written. Two or three words on either side register too. Clear perception of whole meaning is rare. Trance states can produce such writing. Hystero-epilepsy and morbid states can too. Normal wakefulness sometimes suffices, surprisingly.

Modern spiritualism made the phenomenon important historically. It appeared on a large scale about 1850. America was its first great stage. Numerous long writings purported spirit guidance then. Some were written in unknown tongues. Andrew Jackson Davis's Great Harmonia is notable. Charles Linton's Healing of the Nations followed. England's spiritualist newspapers filled with similar reports. Myers and Janet anchor the closing references. Podmore signs this psychical research survey.
britannica-1911-backnang:
Backnang is a German town in the kingdom of Württemberg, nineteen miles by rail north-east of Stuttgart, with 7,650 people in 1900. Its church dates from the 12th century and rewards a look, the entry says. History touched the town in 1325, when it was ceded to Württemberg by Baden.

Work defines the modern place: notable tanneries and leather factories, with woollen and cloth mills beside them. Nearby stands the Wilhelmsheim sanatorium for consumptives, patients with lung disease, set in the country outside town. Church, leather, cloth, and the sanatorium are the four facts this short entry gathers about Backnang.
britannica-1911-baking:
Baking is the action of the verb to bake. Forms of the word run through Teutonic languages. German backen is one such cousin form. Old English and Norse carry related forms too. Baking means cooking by dry heat. Bread making is its primary application. Loaves and cakes take their texture from it.

The term also covers firing by heat. Pottery hardens by that dry process. Earthenware takes the same name in workshops. Bricks are baked in kilns likewise. Moisture leaves the clay as heat rises. Hardness and lasting shape come from that change. The short entry points elsewhere for detail. Bread, ceramics, and brick articles carry fuller accounts. Dry heat is the single thread through all uses.
britannica-1911-baring:
Baring is the name of a family of English financiers and bankers. The firm of Baring Brothers was founded by Francis Baring (1740–1810). His father John, son of a Lutheran minister at Bremen, came from Germany to England. He set up a cloth manufactory near Exeter. Francis was born there and trained in a London commercial house.

In 1770 Francis and his brother John opened a London banking house. By his death in 1810 Francis was counted the first merchant in Europe. He directed the East India Company for years, chaired it in 1792–1793, and sat in Parliament as a Whig. The 1911 Britannica entry traces the firm's passing to his sons, above all Alexander, Lord Ashburton, who spread its work across America.
britannica-1911-barking:
Barking is a market town in Essex, England, on the river Roding near its junction with the Thames, eight miles east of the City of London by rail. Its urban district grew from 14,301 people in 1891 to 21,547 in 1901. The church of St Margaret is Norman with later perpendicular additions and holds many monuments.

Barking was famed for its nunnery, one of the oldest and richest in England. Erkenwald, bishop of London, founded it about 670. The Danes wrecked it, and King Edgar restored it in 970. Its abbess ranked as a baroness, and a turreted gateway survives. The 1911 Britannica entry adds the modern town: gas works at Beckton, rubber and chemical works, sewage works at Barking Creek, and a shipping trade.
britannica-1911-basilica-building:
Basilica, a word of Greek origin, is the subject of a very long architectural article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Strictly, a basilica was a large covered building near a city's business centre, arranged for merchants, litigants, and public business. In a looser sense the word covered audience halls, covered walks, riding schools, markets, and, in the age of Constantine, the great new buildings raised for Christian worship.

Form and history occupy most of the article. Drawing on Vitruvius and surviving remains, it sets out a normal plan: a columned hall with nave and aisles and clerestory lighting, the high windows above the aisle roofs. Rome's first basilica, the Porcia, dates from 184 BC, and the Basilica Julia and Trajan's Ulpia followed around the forum. Vaulted examples such as the Basilica of Maxentius close the Roman story, while provincial cities across the empire built basilicas of their own.
britannica-1911-battambang:
Battambang, also called Battambong and locally Phratabong, is the chief town of the north-western part of Cambodia, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in a rich plain on the river Sang Ke, which flows east into the Tonle Sap, the great lake of Cambodia. The town is a group of bamboo houses, but it has a walled ring of some past interest. Its people are about 5000, two-thirds Cambodian and the rest Chinese and Siamese.

Hands changed over the town by treaty. Siam took it when it overran Cambodia in the late 1700s, and France let Siam keep it when the frontier was fixed in 1867–1872. A treaty in 1893 barred Siamese armed forces there beyond police. In 1904 that deal was set aside. By a further treaty in March 1907 the district was at last ceded to the French, within whose protectorate of Cambodia it then lay.
britannica-1911-belvedere-building:
Belvedere, also written Belvidere, is Italian for “fair-view.” In building it names any structure placed high, in the top of a house or on raised ground, so as to command a fine prospect. The form changes with the builder’s fancy and the site.

A belvedere may be an angle turret, a cupola, or a loggia, an open gallery made for sitting and looking out. Sometimes the name covers the whole building that holds such a feature. The best-known case is the Belvedere gallery in the Vatican at Rome, home of the Apollo Belvidere, and the entry sends readers from this short note to the article on Greek art.
britannica-1911-bet-and-betting:
Bet and betting names the staking of money on a future event. The word may come from the French abeter, to instigate, kin to the English abet. The 1911 Britannica article says betting is as old as gambling itself. It began, it claims, with royal and noble gamblers in the East. It spread west and down through all classes. By the 19th century Britain needed laws to curb it.

Most betting, the article says, gathers around horse racing. Early backers often could not find anyone to take the other side. That gap created the professional bookmaker. He lays money against many horses and profits if he prices with care. The article then surveys turf practice, gaming law, and foreign systems. The French pari-mutuel pool, paying winners from a shared fund, closes the piece.
britannica-1911-billeting:
Billeting is the practice of lodging soldiers in private homes, with board provided. Troops on the march have always used village shelter and supplies, the 1911 Britannica article says. In England its history turns on protests against abuse of the system. Petitions under Elizabeth, James I, and Charles I led to the Petition of Right. That measure of 1628 declared forced billeting illegal. An act of 1679 repeated the ban.

James II still issued billeting orders in defiance of the law. The Bill of Rights listed such quartering among the kingdom's grievances. Once a standing army existed, legal rules for billeting had to be made. Later acts set rates, duties, and magistrates' roles in close detail. By 1911 barracks covered most needs, and billeting had shrunk to an emergency tool. The Army Act of 1909 kept it for Territorial forces in a national crisis.
britannica-1911-biltong: Biltong is a South African Dutch word for sun-dried strips of meat. The 1911 Britannica entry is a single line. It unpacks the word itself in a short bracket. Bil means buttock, and tong means tongue. The meat named is that of the antelope or the buffalo. It is cut into strips and dried in the sun. No curing method is given. No place or use is described beyond the word's roots.
britannica-1911-binturong:
Binturong, also called the bear-cat, is a mammal of southern Asia, with the scientific name Arctictis binturong. It is the single species of its genus in the civet family, the Viverridae. It ranges from Nepal through the Malay Peninsula to Sumatra and Java. Tufted ears set it apart from the rest of its family. So does its long, bushy tail, which can grip branches. That tail nearly equals the head and body in length, some 28 to 33 inches.

Its fur is long and coarse, dull black with a grey wash on the head and front legs. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it a night animal that lives in trees in the forest. It eats small vertebrates, worms, insects, and fruits. By nature it is said to be fierce in the wild. Taken young, though, it tames easily and turns gentle and playful. It is allied to the palm-civets, or paradoxures.
britannica-1911-birdsnesting:
Birdsnesting is the pursuit of collecting and preserving birds' eggs, with or without the nests. The 1911 Britannica article notes that wild birds' nests and eggs are now protected by law almost everywhere. Britain and the United States both guard them under local laws. Taking is allowed for science only, under special licence. Custom limits a collector to one egg from a nest. A nest itself should wait until the young have flown.

The article then gives the craft in practical detail. Each egg, unless hard-set, should be blown as soon as it is taken. A small drilled hole and a curved blow-pipe replace the old two-hole method. Cabinets keep eggs from light, which fades their delicate colours. A taken nest should be disinfected with hyposulphite of soda or insect powder. Handbooks by Newman, Kearton, and others close the how-to survey.
britannica-1911-bitterling:
Bitterling, in Latin Rhodeus amarus, is a little carp-like fish of central Europe. It belongs to the Cyprinid family. The 1911 Britannica entry presents it as a remarkable case of symbiosis, two species living to each other's gain. In the breeding season the female's genital papilla grows into a long tube, nearly as long as the fish itself. That tube works as an egg-laying organ, an ovipositor, for a special task.

Through it the fish lays her few, large eggs inside pond mussels, between the mussel's gaping valves. There, once fertilized, they develop in safety for about a month. The fry then leave their host and swim free. The mussel repays the favour in its own way. It casts its embryos onto the parent fish, where they stay encysted in the skin a while. Both species breed at the same season, the entry notes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alms-and-alms:
Alms and almsgiving, from the Greek eleemosyne, pity or mercy, means any gift to help the needy, prompted by charity. Almsgiving means much more than handing goods to the poor. The duty of almsgiving complements the right of property, which Leo XIII called not only lawful but necessary. Once ownership is admitted, rich and poor must both exist in society, and property lets its owner relieve the needy.

Scripture abounds in passages urging gifts for the needy's welfare, and the early Christians fully realized the duty. The Fathers frequently urged almsgiving, St. Cyprian devoting a whole treatise to it, and St. Thomas Aquinas summarized the teaching in the medieval period. As a rule, the poor of every class, saint or sinner, countryman or foreigner, friend or foe, have claims on the charity of those able to give. The entry then treats fruitful almsgiving, its phases, transitory almsgiving, and organized almsgiving.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-ble:
The Apostolic Blessing is the solemn blessing, urbi et orbi, which the pope himself gave before 1870 from the loggias, or open galleries, of St. Peter's on Maundy Thursday plus Easter, the Lateran on Ascension Day, and St. Mary Major on the Assumption. Popes often delegated the power to give it on petition and at mission closes. Clement XIII in 1762 restricted that delegated power to patriarchs, primates, archbishops, and bishops petitioning Rome for it.

Those prelates may give the blessing on Easter Sunday and some other feasts. Prelates with pontifical dress and territory of their own may give it only once a year, by a set formula. Superiors of certain orders, above all Franciscans, may give it twice a year in their own churches. Particular priests may also receive the faculty on return from Rome or at the close of missions and retreats.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustine-red:
Augustine Reding was Prince-Abbot of Einsiedeln in Switzerland and a theological writer, born at Lichtensteig in 1625, who died at Einsiedeln in 1692. He joined the Benedictines at Einsiedeln in 1641 and taught philosophy at twenty-four. He was ordained and made master of novices in 1649, and took doctorates in philosophy and theology at Freiburg in 1654. After teaching theology at Salzburg, he became prior at Einsiedeln in 1658 and Prince-Abbot in 1670.

As abbot he built the choir, the confession church, and St Magdalene's chapel between 1674 and 1684. His monastery took over the Bellinzona college in 1675 and ran it until 1852. He guarded monastic discipline, pressed thorough training for his monks, and saw their number grow from fifty-three to one hundred. As a temporal ruler his people loved him, and the poor revered him as a father. His chief work, a thirteen-volume scholastic theology, rests on the Summa of St Thomas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedictine-a:
Kilwinning, a Benedictine abbey in Ayrshire, Scotland, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. A church stood on the site centuries before the Benedictine house, linked in tradition to St. Winning, whom some scholars identify with the Irish St. Finnian. Others call him a Welshman named Vynnyn, while an early Scottish breviary makes him a Scot.

The Benedictine foundation itself came from Hugh de Morville, Constable of Scotland, between 1140 and 1162, on ground already home to a community of Culdees, early Celtic monks. The entry weighs these rival origins, then follows the abbey's medieval life. It is a short study in how uncertain a saint's story can remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-betting:
Betting, the backing of a claim by staking money or value on its outcome, receives a moral and legal entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. A bet pits one person's forecast against another's, each forfeiting the stake if wrong. No federal statute in the United States governs it, but many states punish bets on horse races, elections, or games of chance, and often void betting contracts.

In Britain, street betting and betting houses are forbidden, and wagering contracts are null. The moral judgment turns on stakes, skill, and harm: small friendly wagers differ from ruinous gambling. The entry joins moral theology to a comparative note on the law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-richa:
Richard Whiting, the last Abbot of Glastonbury, was executed in 1539 as Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries. Schooled at Glastonbury and a Cambridge graduate, he became chamberlain of his abbey. He was chosen abbot in 1525 through Cardinal Wolsey's choice, and ruled in peace for a decade.

A 1535 visit found all in order, yet his rule over the town was taken away and strict orders were laid on him. Still, he was assured the abbey would stand. In September 1539 royal agents seized him at Sharpham and carried him to the Tower for Cromwell to question. He was executed on 15 November 1539 on a treason charge that stays unclear, Glastonbury then being the last monastery left in Somerset.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessing:
Blessing, in its strict liturgical sense, is the Church's rite of setting persons and things apart for sacred service. It calls down God's favor on them. The entry first separates this narrow meaning from the wider biblical uses of the word. Those wider uses can mean praise, a wish for good fortune, dedication, or simply a gift.

Its five sections trace the practice from creation and the patriarchs through Christ and the apostles. They then set out who may confer blessings and what may receive them. They also cover what effect blessings have and the ceremony used. Readers find a compact guide to a rite the Church counts among her sacramentals, grounded at each step in Scripture and early custom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boycotting:
Boycotting, named for Captain Boycott of Connemara, began as the Land League's bloodless weapon against land-grabbers in Ireland. When tenants were evicted for unpaid rent, landlords needed new takers for empty farms, and a few grabbers could wreck the whole agitation. Violence tempted many, but Parnell offered a sharper tool at a public meeting in 1880.

Asked what to do with a tenant who bid for an evicted neighbor's farm, Parnell had an answer. He urged that the man be left severely alone, put in a moral Coventry, and shunned as a leper of old. The isolation struck not only the offender but anyone who dealt with him. First used against Boycott, Lord Erne's agent, it spread beyond land disputes and beyond Ireland into many other quarrels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Wilhering stands in the Linz diocese, Austria, on the Danube's right bank. Ulric of Willeheringen's castle housed regular canons at first, but when they failed his conditions he replaced them with Cistercians in 1146. Under its first abbot, Geraldus of Runa in Styria, the house was richly endowed and protected by Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg. Ulric's brother Colo completed the work.

The foundation languished until Henry, the third abbot, with only two subjects, handed it to Burkhard, Abbot of Ebrach, in 1185. Burkhard sent Henry back with twelve monks, and from then the abbey prospered, founding Hohenfurth, Engelszell, and Sausenstein. Reformation losses cut it to three monks and two novices by 1568, but Abbot Alexander's reform from 1587 restored property and observance. Fire destroyed the monastery in 1733, and it was rebuilt under Abbot Bonus Pomerl.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clemens-augus:
Clemens August von Droste-Vishering, Archbishop of Cologne, was born on 21 January 1773 at Münster and died there on 19 October 1845. Besides Münster University, Katerkamp tutored him privately. Young, he joined the learned circle around Baron von Fürstenberg and Princess Amelia von Gallitzin. 

In June 1796 he began an educational tour of Germany, Switzerland, and Italy under Katerkamp, returning in August 1797. Ordained priest on 14 May 1798 by his brother Caspar Maximilian, he was elected coadjutor to the aged Baron von Fürstenberg on 18 January 1807. He succeeded him six months later. As administrator he founded an independent congregation of Sisters of Mercy in 1808, the Klemens-Schwestern. Confined practically to Münster, it still numbered eighty-one houses and 1,126 members in 1904. When Napoleon made Münster part of his monarchy in 1813, he appointed Baron von Spiegel bishop without papal knowledge. After Napoleon's fall, Clemens August was restored by the pope in March 1815.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-comte-d-estai:
Louis Delamarre's entry follows Jean-Baptiste-Charles-Henri-Hector, Comte d'Estaing, a French admiral born at Ravel, Auvergne, on 28 November 1729. He died at Paris on 28 April 1794. First an infantry colonel, he became brigadier-general and sailed to the East Indies with Lally-Tollendal in 1757. Prisoner at Madras in 1759, he won parole, joined the French East India Company, and wrecked British factories in Sumatra and the Gulf. Caught again in 1760, he reached Plymouth, then freedom, rising to lieutenant-general of the navy in 1763.

Vice-admiral in 1777, he sailed from Toulon the next year with twelve battleships and fourteen frigates for the American colonies. Winds spared Howe's fleet, but he took Newport, then storm scattered both fleets. He seized Saint Vincent and Grenada in 1779 and mauled Byron's fleet, but failed, wounded, at Savannah. He backed the king in the Revolution, spoke for Marie Antoinette at her trial, and died on the scaffold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregationa:
Hugh Henry's entry treats congregational singing through Pius X's Instruction on sacred music, the Motu Proprio of 22 November 1903. Its third point urges special efforts to restore Gregorian chant among the people. The faithful may again take a more active part in ecclesiastical offices, as in ancient times. From that charge the entry frames four heads: ancient use, prohibition and decay, present-day revival, and the revival's character.

Ancient use rests on Ephesians 5:19, speaking in psalms, hymns, and spiritual canticles. Cardinal Bona reads this as witness that psalms and hymns sounded in assemblies from the Church's beginnings. A fourth-century Laodicea decree then marks prohibition's turn, and Baltimore's Second Plenary Council in 1866 voices the later American position. The quoted councils and pope point one way: restoration through instruction in Gregorian chant. Vernacular singing stays within stated limits, with training methods set out in the cited manuals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cursing:
A moral theology entry sorts out the many senses of cursing. In popular speech it blends with coarse and insulting words. In canon law it can mean the ban of excommunication. In its common biblical sense it is the opposite of blessing: a threat of God's wrath, its actual visitation, or its prophetic announcement.

Instances run from God cursing the serpent, the earth, and Cain, through Noah cursing Canaan, to Christ cursing the barren fig tree and foretelling doom for the damned. In moral theology, cursing means wishing evil upon God or creatures. Saint Thomas treats it as maledictio, and the entry weighs when such speech is grave sin and when it is mere petition for justice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dancing:
This entry traces dancing from natural gesture to art, and weighs its place in Scripture and church discipline. Strong feeling, it argues, lifts the body into rhythmic movement, and as speech grew into poetry and song, so movement grew into dance. Hebrew has eight verbs for dancing, and biblical dances were often women's joyful leaping and circling, from Miriam at the Red Sea to David before the Ark.

Later opinion held dancing unbecoming for men, a view shared by Rome, and the entry follows church cautions through the centuries. Yet it distinguishes spontaneous joy from formal art, and notes dances of many peoples. Readers get both the anthropology of movement and the moral questions it raised for clergy, parents, and pastors guiding their flocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dates-and-dat:
A chronological entry explains how documents came to be dated, from Roman letter formulas to the Christian era. In classical Latin, writers noted when and where they wrote, as in dabam Romae, I gave this at Rome, and from data, given, came our word date. Constantine's age made dating a condition of validity for imperial decrees, and by the twelfth century a Cologne instrument was challenged for lacking a date.

Yet practice lagged behind theory, and charters still went out undated into the twelfth century, Italian chanceries proving most careful. Sections then cover the Christian era, introduced by Dionysius Exiguus about 527. They cover the reckoning of years by indictions and other cycles. They also cover the reckoning of days by kalends, nones, ides, and saints' feasts, a system always apt to grow complicated and inexact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-bockin:
Edward Bocking was an English Benedictine whose zeal helped bring down Elizabeth Barton, the Holy Maid of Kent. Born of East Anglian parents near the end of the fifteenth century, he took degrees at Oxford in 1513 and 1518. He served as warden of Canterbury College. He became a monk at Canterbury in 1526. Sent with another monk to test Barton's claimed visions, he urged her on instead.

The entry calls him her chief instigator, moving her to Saint Sepulchre's convent at Canterbury and shaping her claim to speak against Henry VIII's divorce. After the king married Anne Boleyn, Cromwell arrested Barton, Bocking, and others. Bocking confessed the fraud, did public penance at Paul's Cross, and was hanged at Tyburn with six companions in 1534.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-egbert-king:
Egbert, also spelled Ecgberht, was King of the West Saxons, dead in 839, and is often wrongly called the first King of England. Of royal descent from Ine of Wessex, he was exiled by Beorhtric and Offa of Mercia, then chosen king on his return in 802. In 815 he ravaged Cornwall and beat the West Welsh there, and in 825 he turned back a Mercian invasion at Ellandune.

Kent, Surrey, Sussex, and Essex then accepted him, East Anglia bowed to his overlordship, and Mercia submitted after he drove out Wiglaf. In 829 Northumbria met him at Dore and owned him overlord, so that for the first time one man held sway over all the English peoples, though under-kings still ruled beneath him. At home he shaped the shire system, organised the fyrd militia, and befriended the Church at Kingston in 838.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernricus-pirh:
Ernricus Pirhing was born at Sigarthin, near Passau, in 1606, and his death fell between 1678 and 1681. Twelve years at Dillingen went to teaching canon law and Scripture, and he was still living there in 1675. His Jus canonicum in V libros Decretalium distributum, five volumes from Dillingen dated 1674 to 1677, marks a step forward for canonical science in Germany.

He kept the Corpus Juris's classical divisions while explaining his subjects' canonical legislation completely and synthetically. Seven pamphlets on the titles of the first book of the Decretals, cast as theses, also came from him and were resumed in his Jus Canonicum. An Apologia against two sermons of the Protestant Balduinus followed, at Ingolstadt in 1652 and Munich in 1653. After his death a colleague issued a Synopsis Pirhingana, a résumé of his Jus Canonicum, at Dillingen in 1695 and Venice in 1711.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-bour:
Francois Bourgoing, born at Paris in 1585 and dead in 1662, was the third Superior General of the French Oratory and an early companion of its founder, Cardinal de Berulle. From a family of magistrates, he served as cure of Clichy and resigned that post in favour of St. Vincent de Paul, also a disciple and friend of Berulle. Joining the Oratorians, he founded and directed new houses wherever bishops of France and Flanders called him.

In 1631 he became assistant to Superior General Pere de Condren. On Condren's death in 1641 he took the vacant office, organising and developing the congregation with unceasing zeal and opposing Jansenism energetically. His chief book, Truths and Excellences of Jesus Christ our Saviour, passed thirty editions, including one in 1906, and was translated into several languages, alongside four series of retreat exercises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-christo:
Franz Christoph Ignaz Moufang, born at Mainz on 17 February 1817 and dead there on 27 February 1890, was a German theologian and leader of the Mainz Catholic revival. He studied at Mainz, went to Bonn in 1834, first for medicine, soon turning to theology under Klee, Windischmann, and Walter, then to Munich. He took his theological examinations at Giessen, entered Mainz seminary, and was ordained on 19 December 1839. His uncle Adam Franz Lennig, pastor at Seligenstadt, stirred his broad interest in religious questions of the day.

After curacies at Seligenstadt, Bensheim, and Saint-Quentin in Mainz, he became religious instructor at the Mainz gymnasium in 1845. When Bishop von Ketteler restored the philosophical and theological school at Mainz seminary in 1851, Moufang became regent and professor of moral and pastoral theology. He became canon in 1854 and spiritual adviser to the diocesan court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-hei:
Friedrich Vering, a German canonist born at Liesborn in 1833, stood among the leading church lawyers of the nineteenth century. He studied law at Bonn and Heidelberg, taught Roman and canon law at Heidelberg, then held the canon law chair at Czernowitz from 1875. In 1879 he moved to the German University of Prague, where he taught until his death in 1896.

Though a layman, Vering staunchly defended Church rights against state encroachment. His best-known work is a broad textbook of Catholic, Eastern, and Protestant church law, first issued at Freiburg in 1876 and thrice revised. He also wrote on Roman private law and inheritance, finished a volume of Philipps on church law, and long edited the Archive for Catholic Church Law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gambling:
Gambling, the staking of money or value on a game of chance, belongs to the family of aleatory contracts, where gain turns on an unknown event. Bets on pure skill, like billiards, fall outside the term, while whist mixes skill with chance. Small stakes for zest hardly count as gambling at all, which connotes high play. The entry judges the practice by moral theology.

Theologians allow gaming only on four terms. The stake must be the player's own and free, play must be unforced, fraud is barred though bluffing is not, and the sides must stand roughly equal. Break any term and gaming turns wrong. Beyond that, excess breeds passion, lost time and money, idle company, and scandal. Betting on races, matches, or future prices stands under the same moral rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-keat:
Geoffrey Keating, an Irish theologian, historian, and poet born in Tipperary about 1569, kept Irish learning alive under persecution. Schooled in Munster and Leinster, he was ordained at twenty-four and sailed with forty students to Bordeaux's new Irish College in November 1603. There he took his doctorate in divinity, mourning Ireland in verse when the Earls fled in 1607.

Back in Ireland about 1610, Keating served Knockraffan parish and ended the abuse of delaying Mass for late gentry. Spies tracked him, a lady's anger drove him to a Galtee cave, and he spent six disguised years gathering history across Ireland. His history's preface came in 1629, its parts in 1631 and 1632, beside the Three Shafts of Death and his Key-Shield of the Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-baldung:
Swabian painter Hans Baldung, called Grien for his love of brilliant green in dress and pictures, was born at Gmünd about 1476 and died at Strasbourg in 1545. A lifelong friend of Dürer, who left him a lock of hair at death, he worked with Dürer at Nuremberg. His unsigned portraits have sometimes passed as his master's.

An exceptional draughtsman and good colourist with a fertile imagination, he spent seven years at Freiburg. There his great altarpiece shows the Coronation of the Virgin with Apostles inside the wings and scenes of Our Lady outside. Works fill galleries from Berlin and Vienna to Munich and Frankfurt, and he became a Strasbourg citizen in 1509 and a senator in the year he died.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hans-memling:
Bruges painter Hans Memling, born about 1430 and dead in 1494, was long wrapped in a romantic legend of a wounded soldier of Charles the Bold nursed by Hospitallers. The entry dismisses that tale as sacristans' fancy from the eighteenth century. Records instead show a prosperous burgher, owner of three houses in 1480 and among the city's highest taxed citizens, married with three sons.

His certain works run from a 1467 portrait of Spinelli through the Donne triptych, the St. John hospital altarpieces, and the shrine of St. Ursula to the Lübeck polyptych of 1491, some twenty exquisite pictures in all. Inferior to Van Eyck in nothing as a craftsman, he surpasses him in feeling. He paints velvets and flesh with a rarer, nobler tenderness that makes him the keenest poet of the Flemish school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-edward-:
Henry Edward Manning, second Archbishop of Westminster, was born in 1808 into a banking family and educated at Harrow and Balliol College, Oxford. There he took a first in classics in 1830 and shone in debate. After a short post in the Colonial Office he felt called to the ministry and was ordained in the Anglican Church in 1832. He spent seventeen years as rector of Lavington in Sussex, where his parish work showed zeal for the poor and for reform.

Appointed Archdeacon of Chichester in 1841, Manning threw himself into visitations and charges that foreshadowed his wider work, while the Oxford Movement drew him toward Rome. Newman's submission in 1845 came after years of conviction, and the account stresses that such a conversion is often a matter of time rather than a sudden step. The entry follows Manning through this Anglican period, tracing the path out of the Church of England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hong-kong:
Hong Kong island was ceded by China to Great Britain in January 1841 under restrictions, with cession completed by the Treaty of Nanking in August 1842. Gregory XVI named a prefect apostolic under the bishop of Macao in 1846. A vicariate apostolic was created in 1874 and entrusted to the Milan Seminary of Foreign Missions, present in the city since 1850.

Giovanni Timoleone Raimondi, Acanthus's titular bishop, served as first vicar apostolic until his death at Hong Kong in 1894. His successors were Luigi Piazzoli and Domenico Pozzoni, elected in 1905. The vicariate counted twelve European and ten native priests, over fourteen thousand Christians, twenty-six churches, and dozens of schools, plus Canossian, St. Paul, and native sisters, across Hong Kong, Lautau, and three mainland districts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hunting:
Hunting has been forbidden to clerics in one form or another from early times. The Corpus of Canon Law forbids all servants of God to hunt or range the woods with hounds, and to keep hawks or falcons. The Fourth Lateran Council under Innocent III interdicted hunting and hawking to all clerics.

Trent worded its decree more mildly: clerics should abstain from illicit hunting and hawking, implying not all hunting is illicit. Canonists generally split noisy hunting, called clamorous, from quiet hunting, allowing the latter but not the former. Ferraris held hunting lawful for clerics if rare, for sufficient cause such as need, use, or honest recreation, and with becoming moderation, though Ziegler disputed that reading.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-lelon:
French bibliographer Jacques Lelong was born at Paris on 19 April 1665. He died there on 13 August 1721. At ten he entered the Knights of St John of Malta. After a brief and unhappy stay in Malta, he studied at Paris. He left the knights and entered the Oratory in 1686. He taught at Juilly college in the Meaux diocese. He was ordained priest there in 1689.

Later he served as librarian at Notre-Dame des Vertus seminary in Aubervilliers near Paris. In 1699 he moved to the St Honoré Oratory at Paris. He remained its librarian until death twenty-two years later. His first famous work was the Bibliotheca Sacra, a two-part bibliography of sacred texts and versions in every language. It listed the best editions and manuscripts with historical and critical notes. The entry presents a librarian who mapped the Bible's printed world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jakob-wimpfel:
Jakob Wimpfeling, humanist and theologian, was born at Schlettstadt in Alsace on 25 July 1450 and died in the same town on 17 November 1528. He went to school at Schlettstadt under Ludwig Dringenberg. Starting in 1464 he studied at Freiburg university, taking a bachelor's degree in 1466. Afterward he studied at Erfurt and Heidelberg, taking a master's degree in 1471, and then he spent three years on canon law, followed by theology.

Speyer's cathedral preachership came his way in 1483, and in 1498 Elector Palatine Philip summoned him to Heidelberg as rhetoric and poetry professor. From 1513 he dwelt at Schlettstadt, where pupils and admirers gathered round him, until Lutheran disputes broke apart that literary circle. He died lonely and embittered. His early works pressed for synods held more often, for devotion to Mary, and for better clerical discipline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-bede-pol:
John Bede Polding was the Benedictine monk who became the first Archbishop of Sydney and Primate of Australia. Born at Liverpool in 1794, he was schooled at the Benedictine house at Acton Burnell and took the habit in 1810. He was ordained in 1819, serving as parish priest, prefect, novice-master, and sub-prior. First chosen for Madras, he was instead sent to New South Wales, consecrated in London in 1834.

Reaching Sydney in 1835, he found just three priests in New South Wales, plus one in Tasmania. He worked like a parish priest himself, saying Mass in stations and convict prisons, teaching, hearing confessions, and visiting the dying. Between 1836 and 1841 seven thousand convicts made retreats under his guidance. After a visit to Rome in 1841 he returned as archbishop of a new hierarchy, governing Australian Catholicism until his death in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-hardyng:
John Hardyng was an English chronicler and soldier whose chronicle is shadowed by his own forgeries. Born in 1378, he served Henry Percy, known as Hotspur, and Sir Robert Umfreville. He fought at Homildon Hill in 1402 and Shrewsbury in 1403, became constable of Warkworth Castle, and fought at Agincourt in 1415.

Henry V employed him to fetch Scottish documents proving Scotland's subjection to England, rewarding him with the manor of Geddington. Hardyng's conduct on this mission is indefensible: he forged many documents, some still in the Record Office, and claimed reward for the fraud. As constable of Kyme Castle he compiled his chronicle in three versions: Lancastrian to 1436, Yorkist, and a third dedicated to Edward IV running to 1461. It is valuable for his acquaintance with the leading statesmen of the age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-mensing:
John Mensing was a Dominican theologian and celebrated opponent of Luther in Germany. Born probably at Magdeburg, he entered the Dominicans in 1495, studied at Wittenberg, and took his licentiate in 1517 and doctorate at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder in 1518. He lived when controversy was rife and reformers' teachings spread rapidly through every province.

From 1522 to 1524 he held the Magdeburg cathedral pulpit and wrote his first defenses of the Sacrifice of the Mass. Enemy boldness then forced him to Dessau, where he aided Princess Margaretha von Anhalt against heresy. Professor at Frankfurt-on-the-Oder in 1529, theologian to the Elector at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530, provincial in 1534, and suffragan Bishop of Halberstadt, he took a leading part with Eck. He played that part at the Worms and Ratisbon conferences of 1540 and 1541. He died about 1541.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-ming:
John Ming was a Swiss Jesuit philosopher who wrote on evolution, socialism, and ethics for American Catholics. Born at Gyswyl in Unterwalden in 1838, he was educated at the Benedictine college at Engelberg, then entered the German Jesuit novitiate in 1856. At Aachen he studied philosophy, and theology at Maria-Laach, and taught theology at Gorz before coming to the United States in 1872.

After two years in pastoral ministry he taught theology at Milwaukee, then philosophy for twenty-one years, chiefly at Buffalo, Prairie du Chien, and St. Louis. Once he had mastered English he wrote for the Messenger and the American Catholic Quarterly Review on evolution and socialism, the two great questions facing American Catholics. He produced a treatise on the temporal power and his Data of Modern Ethics Examined, then studies of the characteristics, religion, and morality of modern socialism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-victr:
John of Victring was an Austrian Cistercian chronicler and confidential secretary to dukes of Carinthia. Born probably between 1270 and 1280, he became abbot of Victring in 1307 and served as chaplain and secretary to Duke Henry of Carinthia. After Henry's death in 1335 he defended the duke's daughter Margaretha's claims at Linz. Albert II and Otto of Austria took the lands and made him their valued counselor.

Frequenting Vienna as their secretary until 1341, he withdrew to his monastery to compose the history of his own age. His Book of Certain Histories, first a history of Austria and Carinthia from 1231 to 1341 based on Ottocar's rhyming chronicle and his own collections, grew in 1342. It became an imperial chronicle from 1217. In 1343 it grew into one from Carolingian times. Learned in Latin and Greek poets, lucid in narrative and impartial in judgment, he stands among the most important chroniclers of the late Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-epping:
Joseph Epping was a German Jesuit astronomer who decoded Babylonian sky records. Born at Neuenkirchen in Westphalia in 1835 and orphaned young, he studied mathematics at Münster, joined the Society of Jesus in 1859, and taught mathematics and astronomy at Maria-Laach. In 1872 he went to Quito to teach at Ecuador's new Polytechnic.

Driven home by unrest after President Moreno's murder, he spent his last years teaching younger Jesuits in Holland. With Father Strassmaier he found the key to Babylonian moon tables and matched ancient planet names to Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter. His 1889 book on Babylonian astronomy mattered for both astronomy and chronology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kwang-tung:
Kwang-Tung is a prefecture apostolic covering its whole Chinese province except districts held by Macao and Hong Kong. St. Francis Xavier tried to enter it in 1552 but died on Shang-sch'wan island before preaching there.

Father Melchior Barreto reached Canton in 1556 and debated science and morals with mandarins, and Father Ruggieri won leave to open a chapel in 1581. Matteo Ricci, the real founder of Christianity in China, arrived at Canton in 1582 and planted settlements toward Kiang-si and Nanking that still stand. After dependence on Macao until 1658, French mission priests joined Jesuits, Franciscans, and Dominicans. Persecution in 1742 expelled all missionaries, though native priests kept some 7,000 to 8,000 Christians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-linkoping:
Linköping, in Sweden, originally included Östergötland, Gotland, Öland, and Småland.

Benedict, 1220-1237, was the first of a long line of prelates who built and endowed the cathedral, begun in 1150 but unfinished at the Reformation. Among them was Blessed Nicholas Hermansson, 1374-1391, who had tutored St. Bridget's sons Charles and Birger, and received her body at Vadstena. He composed an Office in honour of St. Bridget. The last Catholic bishop was Hans Brask, bishop 1513-1527, died 30 July 1539. He championed the Old Learning, and had to leave in 1527, when the Diet of Westeraas made Lutheranism the state religion. The religious houses set up between the twelfth and sixteenth centuries included the cathedral chapter and the Cistercians. The Cistercians had three houses for men: Alvastra, Nydala, both founded in 1143, and Gutvalla, or Roma, in Gotland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luke-wadding:
Luke Wadding was an Irish Franciscan historian and theologian, born at Waterford in 1588 and dead at Rome's St. Isidore College in 1657. Eleventh of fourteen children, he learned Latin prose and verse by thirteen, lost both parents at fourteen, and studied philosophy in Ireland before Lisbon's Irish seminary.

Joining the Friars Minor at Matozinhos in 1605, he specialized in Scotist philosophy and theology, then built St. Isidore's College at Rome as a home for Irish Franciscans. His Annals of the Friars Minor, his edition of Duns Scotus, and his histories of the order made him the age's great Franciscan scholar. His work still anchors the study of Scotus and the Irish mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lying:
Lying, as Aquinas defines it, is a statement at variance with the mind. That beats the common formula of a false statement meant to deceive. One may lie while telling truth he believes false, and a known liar, believed by nobody, still lies when his words clash with his thought.

Following Augustine and Aquinas, moralists split lies into injurious, officious, and jocose kinds. Harmful lies, white lies of excuse or benefit, and jokes told for fun fall in these classes, though mere obvious jest carries no malice. Aristotle and Kant allowed no lie ever. Plato let doctors and statesmen lie for good, and modern writers split the same way, with Paulsen and most non-Catholics admitting the lie of necessity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-john-s:
Martin John Spalding was seventh Archbishop of Baltimore, born at Bardstown, Kentucky, in 1810 and dead at Baltimore in 1872. His forebears left England for Maryland in the seventeenth century, his grandfather moving to Kentucky in 1790. He entered St Mary's College, Lebanon, in 1821, taught mathematics there at fourteen, and graduated in 1826.

After four years at Bardstown seminary he entered Rome's Propaganda in 1830, was ordained in 1834, and won a theology doctorate defending 256 theses. Back at Bardstown he pastored the cathedral and edited the Catholic Advocate from 1835. He became Louisville vicar-general in 1844, coadjutor in 1848, and bishop in 1850. He brought Xaverian Brothers to Louisville in 1854 and founded Louvain's American College, opened in 1857. Succeeding at Baltimore in 1864, he organised the St Vincent de Paul Society, founded the House of the Good Shepherd and St Mary's Industrial School, and finished the cathedral. He presided over the Second Plenary Council of 1866, which backed his Catholic university idea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthew-lang:
Matthew Lang moved between chancery desk and bishop's throne with rare ease. Born at Augsburg in 1468, he studied at Ingolstadt, Tubingen, and Vienna, then served as secretary to Emperor Maximilian I in 1494, imperial councillor in 1501, and chancellor in 1508. Though named Prince-Bishop of Gurk in 1505, he stayed at court as a layman and never once visited that diocese.

Made cardinal in 1511, he ran imperial talks with France, Venice, Hungary, and the pope, and became Archbishop of Salzburg in 1519. He helped put Charles V on the imperial throne, pushed measures against Luther, crushed the Peasants' War in his lands, and held reform synods at Muhldorf. A lover of letters and a proud prince of the Church, he acted more from statecraft than from piety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthias-doer:
Matthias Doering, a Franciscan historian and theologian born at Kyritz in Brandenburg between 1390 and 1400, died there in 1469. He joined the Friars Minor at home, studied at Oxford, took his doctorate at Erfurt in 1424, and taught theology and Bible study. In 1427 his order chose him provincial for Saxony, and in 1443 the Conventuals made him minister general.

Doering threw himself into the Council of Basle's cause, backing a council's power over the pope, and he helped depose Eugene IV and elect the antipope Felix V in 1439. Excommunicated by Magdeburg's archbishop, he appealed to Rome, resigned in 1461, and spent his last years writing at Kyritz. Works tied to his name include a Confutation of papal primacy, a defence of Nicholas of Lyra, a lost book on church perplexities, and a chronicle continuation to 1464.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-men-of-unders:
The Men of Understanding, or Homines Intelligentiae, were a heretical sect cited before the Brussels Inquisition in 1410-11. Their leaders were Egidius Cantoris, an illiterate layman, and the Carmelite William of Hildernissen. The sect, kin to the earlier Brethren of the Free Spirit, taught the final salvation of all people and even demons. It held that bodily sin cannot stain the soul, and believed in a mystical illumination and union with God.

That union, they claimed, was so perfect it freed them from all moral and church laws and pledged salvation infallibly. Both leaders gloried in visions they claimed to enjoy. Cantoris, in religious exaltation, ran nude through Brussels streets proclaiming himself mankind's saviour. About 1410 Peter d'Ailly, Bishop of Cambrai, moved first against the heresy. William retracted, though doubtfully, in 1410, and again in 1411, when he was sentenced to three years in a castle and then exile outside the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-waddi:
Michael Wadding, also called Godinez, was a mystical theologian born at Waterford, Ireland, in 1591 who died in Mexico in December 1644. Orphaned young, he studied two years at Salamanca's Irish seminary and entered the Society of Jesus in 1609. After Villagarcia's novitiate he won leave for Mexico's missions, taking the name Godinez, by which he is best known. He made his profession in 1626.

He gave years to Sinaloa's rough mission, worked among the Mayos and Tephanes in 1620, took charge of the Comicaris, and with much labour won over the Basiroas to Christian tribes. In his Teologia mistica he recounts, as one who bore them, the missionaries' privations and sufferings. He taught for years in Mexican colleges. Famed for deep knowledge of supernatural states and rare prudence in guiding souls, his Practica de la teologia mistica, published in 1681, ran through ten editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-munich-freisi:
Munich-Freising is a Bavarian archdiocese that grew from the ancient Diocese of Freising. Its church goes back to Saint Corbinian, who came in 716 to organise Bavarian Christianity. He raised a Benedictine monastery and school on a mountain near Freising. When Saint Boniface ordered Bavaria's church affairs in 738, Corbinian's brother Erembert became first Bishop of Freising, suffragan to Mainz.

The diocese then stretched across the Upper Isar country to the Inn and the watershed, gaining convents at Tegernsee, Moosburg, Schliersee and elsewhere. Bishops such as Joseph of Verona and the learned Aribo shaped its early learning. The entry follows Freising through medieval prince-bishops, secularisation, and its union with Munich as an archdiocese in the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-of-freis:
Otto of Freising was a bishop and historian born between 1111 and 1114 and dead at Morimond in Champagne on 22 September 1158. Son of Saint Leopold of Austria and Agnes, daughter of Henry IV, he was half-brother of Conrad III and uncle of Frederick Barbarossa through his mother's first marriage. Destined young for the priesthood, he became provost at Klosterneuberg, studied at Paris, and with fifteen noblemen entered the Cistercian order at Morimond on his way home.

Within three years he was abbot, then bishop of Freising in 1137 or 1138, still wearing his order's habit. He founded and reformed monasteries, brought Aristotelian thought and Paris-style debate to Freising, and won back church lands lost in the investiture strife. His Chronicle frames history as a clash between the earthly city of Babylon and the divine city. His Deeds of Frederick, covering peace years 1152 to 1156, stays a prime source for Barbarossa's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-flemi:
Patrick Fleming was a Franciscan friar born at Lagan in County Louth on 17 April 1599 and dead on 7 November 1631. His father descended from Lord Slane's line, his mother from Robert Cusack, baron of the exchequer. In 1612, amid fierce Irish persecution, young Fleming went to Flanders, studying first at Douai, then at Louvain's College of Saint Anthony of Padua. He took the Franciscan habit in 1617 and made solemn profession a year later.

Baptised Christopher, he took Patrick as his religious name. After studies at Rome's Saint Isidore College and ordination, he lectured on philosophy at Louvain, winning repute for learning and administration. When Strict Observance Franciscans opened a Prague college, Fleming became its first superior and theology lecturer. Fleeing Saxon invaders in 1631 with Matthew Hoar, he was killed by armed Calvinist peasants on 7 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pickering:
Thomas Pickering was an English Benedictine lay brother and martyr, born about 1621 to an old Westmoreland family. Sent to St. Gregory's at Douai, he took vows as a lay brother in 1660 and went to London in 1665 as steward to the Benedictines serving the queen's chapel royal. There he became known to the queen and Charles II, and when Parliament drove the Benedictines out in 1675, he alone was allowed to stay, probably as no priest.

Titus Oates's pretended revelations of 1678 accused him of plotting the king's murder. No evidence but Oates's word appeared, and the queen publicly believed him innocent, yet the jury condemned him with two others to hanging, drawing, and quartering. Charles twice reprieved the three, then yielded to Commons' petition of April 1679. Pickering alone was executed, on 9 May 1679, his blood-stained cloth kept at Downside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-pai:
Religious painting has accompanied the Church's life since the Catacombs, serving ecclesiastical ornament, and for centuries after Constantine it was the only art in the Christian world. Until the Renaissance the Church monopolized painting: profane painting in Europe is only five centuries old and took the lead in the nineteenth century alone. Through the whole Christian era, then, the history of painting has been the history of religious painting, still fertile, though diminished.

The survey follows its changing faces, above all the Virgin, to whom art sang tender hymns. The Byzantine Panagia and the medieval Throne of God and Queen of Heaven gave way to the Mother. Bernard, Francis of Assisi, and Bonaventure made devotion to the Madonna a Christian devotion. Schools vied to paint the holiest Virgins, Siena's among the charming, and the entry closes wondering what future awaits an art that once expressed every shade of human nature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-son:
Religious song, or sacred song, is the name for poetical and musical creations used in public worship but kept outside the official liturgy for their freer, more subjective character. It springs from the faithful's desire, encouraged yet guided and controlled by the Church, to take an active part in ceremonies. While psalms were sung traditionally at early Eucharistic celebrations and love-feasts, the agapae, assemblies soon improvised songs of their own, religious in burden but spontaneous beside the psalms.

Missionaries turned the people's familiar melodies to Christian use, setting Christian texts to them to wean converts from pagan belief and practice. That habit led an emotional people to vent growing religious feeling in words and melodies of their invention. By the latter part of the ninth century vernacular words were mingled with liturgical chant. The name Leisen marks the vast song literature of the period that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-flemi:
Richard Fleming, Bishop of Lincoln and founder of Lincoln College, Oxford, lived through the turbulent years of the Wycliffite dispute. A Yorkshire man educated at University College, Oxford, he first came to notice as a young university officer. In 1409 he sat among the commissioners who examined the writings of John Wyclif. Later, as bishop, he carried out the order to burn Wyclif's exhumed body in 1428.

His enduring mark was educational rather than judicial. Fleming attended the Council of Constance and rose through church offices to the see of Lincoln. He used his position to found a college at Oxford meant to train clergy against heresy. The entry also traces his benefices and rectorships, including Boston, and notes that early suspicion of sympathy with Wyclif never hardened into doubt about his own orthodoxy. It is a useful portrait of a bishop-administrator in a divided church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-nutter:
Robert Nutter and Edward Thwing were English martyrs executed together at Lancaster on 26 July 1600. Nutter, born at Burnley about 1550, entered Brasenose College, Oxford, and then the English College at Reims. Ordained priest in December 1581, he returned to England and was committed to the Tower in 1584. There he spent forty-seven days in the pit, forty-three in irons, and twice suffered the scavenger's daughter torture.

Shipped to Boulogne with twenty priests in 1585, he revisited Rome, then was imprisoned again at Newgate under the alias Rowley, at the Marshalsea, and at Wisbech Castle. Thwing, of a Heworth family, studied at Reims and Pont-a-Mousson, taught Greek, Hebrew, rhetoric, and logic, and was ordained at Laon. After a stay at Spa for a knee ulcer, he went on the mission in 1597. Both men escaped to Lancashire, were arrested in May 1600, tried for being priests, and suffered on the same day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolph-willi:
Rudolph William Basil Feilding, eighth Earl of Denbigh and ninth Earl of Desmond, was born 9 April 1823 and died in 1892. He was educated at Eton College and Trinity College, Cambridge, where he took a Master of Arts. He entered the Church in 1850 and worked energetically for many Catholic charities under Cardinal Wiseman.

As Viscount Feilding he served as honorary treasurer of the Peter's Pence Association, jointly with Viscount Campden and Archibald J. Dunn. He showed great courage and independence of character. Such qualities were needed in the mid-nineteenth century, when English Protestant feeling ran high against the restored Catholic hierarchy. To mark his conversion with thanks, he built the Franciscan monastery at Pentasaph in North Wales.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-chrodegang:
St. Chrodegang, also called Godegrand, Gundigran, Ratgang, Rodigang, and Sirigang, was bishop of Metz. He was born at Hasbania, in today's Belgian Limburg, at the start of the eighth century, to a noble Frankish family. He died at Metz on 6 March 766. This entry follows a boy educated at Charles Martel's court, who served as his private secretary, then chancellor, then prime minister in 737.

On 1 March 742 he was appointed bishop of Metz, keeping his civil office at Pepin's request. In his influential position Chrodegang laboured earnestly for Church and State, and was ever solicitous to strengthen the union between temporal and spiritual rulers. In his diocese he introduced the Roman liturgy and chant, and community life for his cathedral clergy, with a special rule he wrote for them. He founded the Abbey of Gorze near Metz in 748, and remained its friend and protector.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-stephen-ha:
Stephen Harding, third abbot of Cîteaux, held the young Cistercian reform to strict observance through near collapse. Born at Sherborne in Dorset about the middle of the eleventh century, he studied at Sherborne, Paris, and Rome.
