Stopping at Molesme on his return, he joined Robert's community, practised great austerity, and became Robert's chief supporter.

He was one of twenty-one monks who retired to Cîteaux under Hugh of Lyons to found a stricter house. When Robert was recalled to Molesme in 1099, Stephen became prior under Alberic, and on Alberic's death in 1110 he was elected abbot. With monks few and the duke of Burgundy offended, he begged alms door to door rather than relax the rule. He died on 28 March 1134, after welcoming Bernard and his companions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-wolfgang:
Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg from 972 to 994, counts with Ulrich and Conrad among the three brilliant stars of tenth-century Germany. Born about 934 to Swabian counts of Pfullingen, he had a cleric tutor at seven and then attended the celebrated monastic school on Reichenau. There he befriended Henry, brother of Poppo of Würzburg, and followed him to Würzburg's cathedral school.

There he heard the noted Italian grammarian Stephen of Novara. When Henry became archbishop of Trier in 956, he called Wolfgang to teach in the cathedral school and labour for diocesan reform, despite enmity. Wolfgang's Trier years deepened his monastic and ascetic bent. Later bishop of Regensburg, he reformed clergy and monasteries and preached in Hungary and Bohemia. He died at Pupping on 31 October 994.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-temiskaming:
Temiskaming is a Vicariate Apostolic of Canada, suffragan of Ottawa, bounded by Hudson Bay and the Great Whale River in the north and by 72° and 91° west longitude. It was erected on 22 September 1908 by dividing the Diocese of Pembroke. Fathers de Bellefeuille and Dupuy first preached there in 1836, with yearly visits to Indians at Hudson's Bay Company posts. Oblates took charge in 1843 under Father Laverlochère, settling at Fort Temiskaming in 1863 and moving to Ville Marie in 1886.

Lumbering followed the fur trade, then agriculture drew settlers to Lake Temiskaming's fertile shores. Railways and the silver and gold finds of 1903 advanced the Ontario section. Catholics number about 20,000, including some 5,000 Indians. Haileybury is home to the first vicar, Elie-Anicet Latulipe, named in October 1908 and consecrated that November. The vicariate holds 17 parishes, 20 missions, and many stations, served by 21 secular priests, 4 Sacred Heart missionaries, and 9 Oblates, with convents, hospitals, and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-ewing:
Thomas Ewing, jurist and statesman, was born in West Liberty, Virginia, in 1789 and died at Lancaster, Ohio, in 1871. Raised in pioneer hardship in the Muskingum Valley, he learned to read from his sister and worked in the Kanawha salt works by furnace light. In 1815 he took the first degree ever given by a college in the western country, at Ohio University. He was admitted to the bar the next year.

Entering the Senate from Ohio in 1831, he stood with Webster and Clay against Jackson and backed Clay's protective tariff. The entry also follows his children, including sons who served as generals and a daughter, Eleanor, who married William Tecumseh Sherman and wrote her father's memorial in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-flemin:
Thomas Fleming, Archbishop of Dublin, was born in 1593, son of the Baron of Slane, and died in 1665. He studied at the Franciscan college of Louvain, became a Franciscan priest, and taught there for years before Urban VIII named him to Dublin in October 1623. His appointment angered opponents of the religious orders, and the priest Paul Harris attacked him in print.

Fleming called a provincial synod at Dublin in 1640. When the Confederate war broke out he backed the Confederates, sending a procurator to Kilkenny in 1642 and attending the general assembly that October. A man of peace by temper, he sought settlement at almost any price and opposed the thorough policy of the Old Irish party, signing the 1643 commission to treat with Ormond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-hardin:
Thomas Harding, a controversialist born at Combe Martin, Devon, in 1516, became the Catholic champion against Bishop Jewel. A Winchester scholar from 1528, he entered New College, Oxford, in 1534, became Hebrew professor under Henry VIII in 1542, and served as chaplain to the Marquess of Dorset. He first leaned to reform, but under Mary declared himself Catholic and took a divinity doctorate in 1554.

Elizabeth's accession cost him his preferments and brought imprisonment, and he retired to Louvain, where he served St. Gertrude's church and devoted himself to controversy. His 1564 Answer to Master Jewel's Challenge opened a long exchange with the bishop of Salisbury. Harding died at Louvain in September 1572.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-th:
Thomas Thwing was a Yorkshire priest executed at York in 1680 during the panic over the alleged Popish Plot. Born at Heworth Hall in 1635, he trained at Douai and worked in his native county, serving as chaplain at Carlton Hall, opening a school. Later ministering to the Institute of Mary community at Dolebank, where three of his sisters lived.

Arrested there in 1679, he was caught up in accusations by two dismissed servants who claimed a plot to murder the king. His relatives were acquitted in London on the same evidence, but Thwing, tried again at York, was convicted. The king first reprieved him, then issued the warrant after Parliament protested. On the scaffold he declared his innocence, his loyalty, and his charity to his neighbour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Eastern Shan-tung is a Chinese vicariate separated from Northern Shan-tung in 1894, covering the prefectures of Yen-chou, Lai-chou, and Teng-chou, with about ten million inhabitants and a very healthy climate. It was entrusted to the Franciscans under Mgr Caesarius Schang, resident at Chefoo.

Its modern history turned on violence: in November 1897 two German missionaries, Francis Xavier Nies and Richard Henle, were murdered at Chang-kia-chwang. The killings led Germany's fleet to occupy Kiao-chou days later. In 1899 the German-held territory was detached to Southern Shan-tung. By 1909 the mission counted twenty-two priests, nine thousand Catholics, nearly twelve thousand catechumens, thirteen churches, 138 chapels, and 350 stations, plus schools, hospitals, and orphanages.

Northern Shan-tung is a Chinese vicariate erected by Gregory XVI in 1839 under its first vicar apostolic, Louis de Besi, formerly pro-vicar of Hu-pe and Hu-nan. It endured many wars and persecutions, was divided into northern and southern Shan-tung in 1885, and lost its eastern portion to a new vicariate in 1894.

Entrusted to the Franciscans under a vicar apostolic resident at Tsi-nan-fu, it enjoys a salubrious, temperate climate and numbers eleven million inhabitants. Growth was rapid: in 1904 it counted eleven European Franciscans, eighteen native priests, 18,000 Catholics, 13,900 catechumens, and 134 churches and chapels. By 1910 twenty-nine European fathers, nineteen native priests, 28,000 Catholics, 20,000 catechumens, and 187 churches and chapels.

Southern Shan-tung is a Chinese vicariate. Its Catholic faith had scarcely been preached in its southern districts before Father John Baptist Anzer of the Steyl Seminary was sent there as pro-vicar in 1882. With another Steyl missionary he began the work, and in 1886 the vicariate was erected, later gaining the German-held districts of Kiao-chou, Tsi-me, Kau-mi, and Chu-chong in 1898.

Entrusted to the Divine Word priests of Steyl under Mgr Augustine Henninghaus, resident at Yen-chou-fu, it held twelve million inhabitants in a temperate climate. In 1908 it counted forty-six European and twelve native priests, over 35,000 Catholics and nearly 40,000 catechumens. 131 churches and chapels, seminaries, Chino-German and catechumen schools, a college for European girls, asylums, and a hospital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wheeling:
Wheeling is a diocese comprising West Virginia except eight eastern counties in Richmond diocese. It also covers twenty-four Virginia counties and part of Craig County, 21,355 square miles in West Virginia and 7,817 in Virginia, 29,172 in all. Formed from Richmond by apostolic letters of July 1850, its first bishop was Richard Whelan, transferred from Richmond, where he had been consecrated its second bishop in March 1841.

The earliest Wheeling chancery record notes Francis Rolf appointed pastor in 1829, recording a baptism on 3 November 1828, with evidence of earlier priestly visits. Wheeling town, established in 1795, is said by one vague tradition to take its name from a Father Whelan who ministered occasionally to his flock. Western Virginia, which became West Virginia in 1863, never held many Catholic settlers nor many professing any religion. In 1912 its Catholic population, institutions, and clergy are set out in the entry's closing statistics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wood-carving:
Wood-Carving covers making art objects from wood with knife, chisel, file, or drill. This entry treats only artistic work: plastic pieces such as statues and crucifixes, called wood-sculpture, and arabesques and rosettes for cabinets, called wood-carving proper, though the two often merge. Wooden god-statues served religion in antiquity, above all in Egypt, but wood-carving flowered only in the Christian era.

Perishable timber leaves scant early Christian remains, yet wood served church uses as today: Bawit saints at Cairo, Saint Sabina's door at Rome, wooden reliquaries, and Maximianus's ivory-clad chair at Ravenna. German art began in wood, churches and fittings alike, dressed with animals and interlaced geometry. Almost all is lost save Radegunde's desk at Poitiers and a Lombard door at Parma, with low-relief chests like Terracina's and Puy's door signed Godfredus made me.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wyoming:
Wyoming, the forty-fourth state, takes its name from the Delaware word Maughwauwama, mountains with large plains between. It spans 41 to 45 degrees north and 27 to 34 degrees west of Washington, bounded by Montana, South Dakota, Nebraska, Colorado, Utah, and Idaho. It measures 355 by 276 miles across 97,883 square miles, larger than New York and Pennsylvania together. Its face is mountainous, with valleys, plains, and plateaux.

Ranges run northwest to southeast in broken spurs: the Rockies end in the Wind River Range, with Big Horn, Owl, Rattlesnake, Medicine Bow, Teton, Yellowstone, and Black Hills beside it. Rivers rising here include the Yellowstone, Big Horn, Snake, Green, Cheyenne, Belle Fourche, and Powder, none navigable but prized for irrigation and timber. Lakes include Yellowstone, Jackson, Shoshoni, Lewis, Madison, and Fremont, and Yellowstone Park, set apart by Congress at 3575 square miles, shows geysers, springs, lakes, and woodlands.
chekhov-tales-garnett-1916-darling:
Constance Garnett published The Darling and Other Stories in 1916, a volume of Anton Chekhov's tales in her translation. Garnett's many volumes introduced Chekhov to the English-speaking world. Her Chekhov arrived in the middle of the First World War and found eager readers.

The title story follows Olenka, a woman who takes on the views and work of each man she loves, losing any self of her own. Other stories in the volume show Chekhov's doctors, teachers, and clerks in quiet crises. His scenes end without verdicts, leaving readers to judge. Garnett's plain English let that restraint speak, and the volume helped change what English short fiction could be.
children-s-internet-protection-act-cipa-:
The United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania issued this opinion on May 31, 2002, striking down parts of the Children's Internet Protection Act. Chief Circuit Judge Becker wrote for a three-judge court with Judges Fullam and Bartle. The American Library Association and Multnomah County Public Library led the plaintiffs. Federal library funding, through the E-rate and LSTA programs, stood behind the law.

Findings of fact run for hundreds of pages: how the Internet is indexed, how much explicit material exists, and how filtering software harvests and sorts web pages. Overblocking, the court found, was inherent to the technology. The analysis applies strict scrutiny to a content-based limit on a public forum. The government appealed, and the Supreme Court reversed the judgment a year later. As hosted, the opinion is a landmark record of libraries and the early web.

The baron is partly an imposture, and his friend Mr Bunker manages the performance.

eugene-pickering:
Henry James introduced Eugene Pickering at the German spa of Homburg, where his narrator puzzles over a young man with one chair too many and a face half remembered. Eugene is an American kept in childhood by a possessive father, now tasting freedom among the roulette tables. He falls for a charming widow whose past the spa gossips over, and the narrator watches the experiment with affectionate alarm.

James, in this early novella taken from the 1887 collection named on its title page, studies what a sheltered upbringing does to judgment. Eugene's father dies mid-story, and inheritance, liberty, and love arrive together, faster than wisdom. The ending refuses easy rescue. It is young James, already exact about the price of innocence abroad.
every-soul-hath-its-song:
Hurst's Every Soul Hath Its Song is a story collection by Fannie Hurst. The title page lists her earlier book, Just Around the Corner. The contents hold nine named stories. Sea Gullibles opens the volume, followed by Rolling Stock and Hochenheimer of Cincinnati.

Other stories include In Memoriam, The Nth Commandment, T.B., and Summer Resources. Sob Sister and The Name and the Game close the list before the title story. The opening story follows Simon Binswanger, a steerage immigrant child. He first sees the Statue of Liberty from his mother's side. Decades later he has crossed the city divide to the Upper West Side. Hurst writes urban immigrant life with dense, vivid detail.
family-pride-or-purified-by-suffering:
Holmes's Family Pride, or Purified by Suffering, is a domestic novel of New England life. Mary J. Holmes also wrote Lena Rivers, Meadowbrook, and Cousin Maude. The opening chapter enters the farmhouse at Silverton. Uncle Ephraim Barlow anchors that household in the first pages.

Barlow is a deacon of the orthodox church in Silverton, Massachusetts. He clings to old-time customs and scorns new-fangled notions. Born among Bay State rocks and hills, he shares their roughness. Yet his character, like the wild scenery, holds beauty and grandeur. All who know him respect him, the narrator says. His seat before the altar each Sunday marks the town's order. The subtitle promises suffering that purifies family pride.
fielding:
Austin Dobson's Fielding is a short biography of Henry Fielding, the novelist and magistrate, written for the English Men of Letters series. Dobson confines himself strictly to the biographical side, leaving the critical estimate of Fielding's works to other writers.

His task is to verify scattered anecdotes, correct misstatements that crept into earlier lives, and add details he discovered himself. Dobson weighs Arthur Murphy's early life of Fielding, prefixed to the 1762 collected works, against Watson's life and other sources, noting where tradition misled and where facts could still be checked. The memoir suits readers who want Fielding the man, set straight, before turning to Tom Jones and his other novels.
four-months-among-the-gold-finders-in-al:
Vizetelly's name stands over this diary of the California gold districts, kept on the spot by J. Tyrwhitt Brooks, M.D. The expedition sails from San Francisco into the diggings at the rush's first heat. The preface says the diary went home for family entertainment before reaching the public.

By July the aspect of things is anything but cheerful. Miners sink exhausted under the sun by the river, and dysentery appears from unwholesome food. The party hires Snake Indians to work the ravines, paying them in provisions and drams of pisco. The diary was published in London in 1849.
from-the-valley-of-the-missing:
White opens this melodrama on a canal boat in late October. Lem Crabbe, a one-armed boatman, rules his wife Scraggy by fear. She nurses a baby as the mules drag the boat along. Crabbe mutters that it is time for her to go. Cruelty and drink shape their floating home.

Years later, stolen twins stand at the plot's center. Fledra, called Flea, shields her brother Flukey fiercely. The squatter Lon Cronk claims the twins as his. Horace Shellington bars his door against the man. Ann Shellington foresees evil in the struggle. White wrote the story of the missing children as high melodrama. A photo-play version supplied the book's pictures.
fruit-gathering:
Rabindranath Tagore's Fruit-Gathering is a book of short prose poems that the author himself translated from Bengali into English. The poems speak in a quiet, devotional voice, addressing a listener or a divine presence in images drawn from gardens, rivers, seasons and the day's labour.

Tagore returns to ripening fruit, falling petals, evening light and the river's call as figures for a life growing older and ready to give itself fully. Some pieces are only a few lines long, while others unfold like brief prayers or songs. The Macmillan edition presents them as a single gathering, meant to be read slowly. Readers who know Tagore's Gitanjali will recognise the same mood here, gentler and more autumnal in tone.
god-the-invisible-king:
H G Wells set out his personal religion in God, the Invisible King. His preface states that the belief is not orthodox Christianity, nor Christianity at all. Yet it holds a personal and intimate God. Chapters cover the cosmogony of modern religion, heresies defined as the things God is not, and the likeness of God. An envoy closes the book.

Wells imagines God as a finite, struggling king within human hearts, calling believers to a coming happier earth and a church without creeds or priests. Truth and justice, he argues, are elemental claims of this faith. Written during the First World War, the book scandalized churchmen and remains a key document of Wells's thought.
govdocs-archive_org-julius-evola-tao-te-:
Julius Evola, the Italian Traditionalist philosopher, produced a commentary on the Tao Te Ching, the ancient Chinese Book of the Way and Virtue. His edition presents the text together with his own reading of it, plus a bibliographic guide and an index of names.

Evola reads the Tao through his doctrine of Tradition, treating its teaching on action and stillness as an ancient wisdom above modern decay. The commentary shows a European esoteric thinker meeting a Chinese classic on his own terms rather than the academy's. It remains one of the stranger and more argued-over meetings of East and West in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ArmstrongJohn_J: nsia-ArmstrongJohn John Armstrong: the made public government document on John Armstrong, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the collection.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Bugging_Bugging:
The Center for National Security Studies was a Washington group that kept watch on the intelligence agencies in the years after Watergate. This mailing from its office at 122 Maryland Avenue NE belongs to the file's subject area of bugging: state wiretapping and electronic spying.

The Center published and lobbied against illegal spying at home, and its mailings carried that campaign to supporters and researchers around the country. Files like this one show how the oversight movement organized itself in print during the Church Committee era. The mailing is preserved as campaign literature from the fight over domestic spying.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GervaisPershing:
Rosemary James wrote in November 1971 about Pershing Gervais, a former investigator for Jim Garrison who had vanished from public view. Gervais spoke to her from what the headline calls his unknown hideaway. A man who once hunted witnesses for the district attorney was now the one being hunted for a quote.

Gervais had been a colorful figure in the New Orleans investigation, and his disappearance fed the case's atmosphere of flight and hiding. The article preserves his voice from exile, still talking while his old boss's case unraveled back home.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ImmunityCongres:
Timothy J. Robinson reported for the Washington Post on a ruling from the D.C. Circuit court of appeals. The court held that the Constitution's speech and debate clause does not give members of Congress or their aides absolute immunity from civil suits. The ruling came in the McSurelys' case against Senator John McClellan's subcommittee.

The McSurelys had been targets of a Senate inquiry, and their suit tested how far congressional armor reaches. A limit on immunity meant staff work could be answered for in court. Robinson's article preserves the decision and what it changed for Capitol Hill.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KleinsSportingG:
On October 20, 1984, an unnamed writer sent this letter to Gary Mack of KXAS-TV. Mack was a broadcast journalist who covered the Kennedy assassination for the Dallas station. The letter discusses FBI letters and the records of Mary Moorman. The author's name cannot be recovered from the text.

Moorman stood in Dealey Plaza and took a well-known photograph as the motorcade passed. The letter shows how, twenty years on, private researchers were still trading documents and tips with reporters. It also shows the limits of the file: a reader learns what the letter covers, but not who wrote it or what reply it received.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LaneMarkMLKing_:
Mark Lane wrote this magazine article in November 1977 about the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. Lane introduced it as 'the reason for the book,' meaning the book he was then publishing on the King case. He had built his name attacking the Warren Commission's account of the Kennedy assassination.

Here he turns to Memphis, where James Earl Ray pleaded guilty to killing King and then took the plea back almost at once. Lane argues that the official story does not hold. The article is part summary and part notice of his larger work. It also shows how the King case drew the same researchers who had spent a decade on Dallas.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NorthAdvertisin:
Charles Nicodemus wrote about a fight over advertising between the National Rifle Association and North Advertising. The NRA was counterattacking against gun-control advertising. The article quotes Donald Nathanson, the president of North Advertising, whose agency stood on the other side of the campaign.

Gun politics in print ads was a new front in the 1970s. Advocacy groups had learned to buy space and frame the argument themselves. The NRA's counterattack treated an ad agency as an opponent worth naming. Nicodemus covers the exchange as a media story: who bought which message, and how the other side answered. The piece preserves both the quarrel and the names of the men running it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ParkTonsung_Par:
Maxine Cheshire wrote this Washington Post article about Tongsun Park. Park was the central figure in the Koreagate investigations, the scandal over South Korean influence-buying in Washington. Cheshire examines his ties to two intelligence services at once: the Korean CIA and the American CIA.

Park was a socialite and businessman whose parties and payments reached members of Congress. Reporters like Cheshire had to map a man who belonged to several worlds: Seoul's agency, Washington society, and the hearing rooms. The article presents what was known of those ties at the time. It stands as a period account of a scandal that tested how foreign money moved through the capital.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Right-wing_Righ:
An article titled 'Washington's Right Wingers' surveys the capital's extreme conservatives. In its account, these right wingers see liberalism as 'creeping socialism.' They revere Barry Goldwater, the Arizona senator who led the conservative movement. The article's cast includes the Statue of Liberty bombing plotters and armed Minutemen.

Washington journalism of the 1960s treated the far right as a subject to be mapped for puzzled readers. A single survey that runs from Goldwater admirers to bomb plotters shows the era's wide definition of the fringe. The piece preserves the movement's public faces as a reporter lined them up. It also records the language of the time, in which socialism was the charge and Goldwater the standard.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StateofLouisian:
Clay Shaw, a New Orleans businessman, was the only person ever tried for conspiring to kill President Kennedy. District Attorney Jim Garrison brought the case, and it went to trial in early 1969. The record here preserves the court proceedings of February 19, 1969, held in open court before Judge Edward Haggerty in the Criminal District Court for the Parish of Orleans.

A trial transcript keeps the exact words spoken in the room: lawyers arguing, witnesses answering, and the judge ruling as the case moved forward. Shaw was acquitted, but the trial remains a central event in the history of the Kennedy assassination debate. Reading the raw proceedings lets students judge the evidence and the courtroom claims for themselves, without a narrator in between.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-VoicePrinting_V: An FBI airtel dated August 2, 1968, sent a tape from the Charlotte office for voice printing. It belonged to MURKIN, the bureau's case name for the hunt for Martin Luther King Jr.'s killer. The Charlotte special agent in charge submitted a Code-A-Phone tape recording for comparison. The airtel shows new voice technology entering a major manhunt in its first months.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_climate-:
In 1983, scientists at Lawrence Livermore studied what a nuclear war would do to the world's climate. Their study warned that a nuclear exchange could dramatically affect the temperature of the atmosphere. This briefing book presents that early official work on the climate effects of nuclear war.

The finding belonged to the first wave of nuclear winter research. It meant the danger of nuclear war was not only blast and radiation in the cities hit. Smoke and cooling could harm farming and life far from any battlefield, a point later climate studies kept testing.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va:
Boris Hagelin built cipher machines, and William Friedman was America's leading codebreaker. Their private understanding helped shape the Crypto AG story, later called the intelligence coup of the century. Michael Martelle and Ian Sotnek edited this briefing book, number 697, published in February 2020.

Documents from the Friedman collection give historical context to how Crypto AG machines reached governments worldwide. A 1955 memorandum authorizing the key proposal was released through a freedom of information request. The posting reaches back before the scandal broke, to the handshake-level arrangements that made a rigged cipher business possible.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: 80th Anniversary of the Atomic Bombings: Revisiting the Record - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records.

President Ronald Reagan received a formal briefing on how a nuclear war with the Soviet Union could unfold. Its outline, first classified top secret, has been declassified, and this posting presents it. The briefing walked through possible Soviet acts of aggression, in the planners' phrase, what the Russians could do to us.

One figure stated the stakes plainly. Without civil defense, a massive Soviet attack could kill eighty million Americans. A briefing written for a president has to compress the unthinkable into pages he can absorb. Reading it now shows both the era's fears and the cold arithmetic officials used when they described escalation to the man who would decide.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
In March 2016, the Obama administration promised a broad effort to declassify American records on Argentina's dirty war. The National Security Archive marked the pledge by posting examples, edited by Carlos Osorio, of the kinds of material such an opening could release from United States files.

Argentina's military ruled from 1976 to 1983 and murdered thousands of its own citizens, many of them secretly seized and never seen again. American agencies watched closely and wrote much of it down. Files of that kind can confirm fates, support court cases, and correct the public record. The posting explains what might surface, and why families still waiting for answers watched the promise so closely.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_colombia_Former_C:
In July 2018, the National Security Archive reported striking testimony about a ranch in Colombia. The ranch, owned by former president Alvaro Uribe Velez and his family, allegedly served as the working base of a deadly paramilitary group. The witnesses were people who had worked for the Uribe family during the 1990s, when paramilitary violence was tearing through Colombia's countryside.

Uribe later became Colombia's president and its most powerful hard-line figure, so testimony tying his family's property to a paramilitary base carries heavy political weight. The posting lays out what the witnesses said and when they said it worked there. Readers get a careful, sourced account of an allegation at the center of Colombia's long argument over Uribe's past and the armed groups of that era.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Cyber:
When the Taliban retook Afghanistan in August 2021, American biometric devices fell into their hands, according to reporting gathered in a National Security Archive cyber brief published on August 20, 2021. The devices held identity data gathered over years of war, including records on Afghans who had worked beside coalition forces.

Coalition partners feared that data could now enable persecution of those very people. The brief draws a wider parallel, noting that worries over civil liberties and human rights in Afghanistan mirror concerns raised about China's treatment of its Uighur population. Readers get a short, sobering case study in what happens when identity databases built for war outlive the side that built them and change hands in defeat.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_mexico_Truth_Comm:
A Mexican truth commission spent years documenting state violence during the country's dirty war, and in August 2024 the National Security Archive reported its findings. The commission's verdict was blunt: human rights abuses in Mexico were systematic and widespread, not the work of a few bad apples, across twenty-five years of state violence.

The commission also pointed north, recommending declassification of American dirty war records, since United States agencies watched Mexico's repression closely and wrote much of it down. Findings like these matter because they settle the official story: patterns ordered from above, not rogue behavior from below. Readers get the commission's conclusions and the next fight they set up, opening the foreign files that can confirm or extend what Mexico documented about itself.
guy-mannering:
Walter Scott built Guy Mannering, his second novel, around an astrologer who casts a horoscope and a child who vanishes. Guy Mannering, a young Englishman visiting the Scottish estate of Ellangowan, predicts the heir's future on his fifth birthday. That same night the boy is stolen. Suspicion ruins the exciseman who hunted smugglers nearby. Years later Mannering returns to Scotland as a colonel from India, and the lost heir's story restarts.

Gypsy Meg Merrilies, the lawyer Pleydell, and the farmer Dandie Dinmont crowd the stage as identities unravel. Scott mixes astrology, kidnapping, smuggling, and law with Border scenery and dialect. The novel confirmed that Waverley was no accident: Scott could make Scotland's recent past into romance at will, and readers across Europe demanded more.
hebbel-gyges-und-sein-ring:
King Candaules, proud of his wife's beauty, secretly shows her unveiled to his friend Gyges, and the insult can be washed out only in blood. Hebbel's Gyges und sein Ring, given here in German, draws its tragedy from Herodotus. Honor, shame, and necessity lock the three figures in a pattern none can escape.

The queen, shamed without her knowledge, demands the king's death at Gyges's hand as the price of her honor. Gyges, who never sought any of it, becomes the instrument of fate. Hebbel called the play his purest tragedy, and its clean lines support the claim. Characters crushed between irreconcilable moral laws fill its brief scenes. The ring of invisibility becomes a symbol of every hidden act that still corrupts.
henrietta-s-wish-or-domineering: Young Henrietta's wishes drive this Yonge novel. The domineering of the subtitle cuts both ways. A Victorian family story. Writers of history may cite it later. The book preserves that tale. Kept for readers. Kept for readers.
himalayan-journals-complete-or-notes-of-:
Joseph Dalton Hooker's complete Himalayan Journals gathers his notes as a naturalist travelling through Bengal, Sikkim and Nepal, with the Khasia Mountains also covered. The journal form lets Hooker mix plant hunting with geography, geology and daily travel, and the full edition brings his separate volumes into one long account.

Inside, Hooker moves from Calcutta and the Sunderbans toward high passes, naming new plants and noting soils, hot springs and local customs as he climbs. Chapters follow rivers, forests and mountain villages, and readers meet Lepcha guides, traders and missionaries along the road. Rhododendrons, orchids and pines recur throughout, tied to altitude, rainfall and soil rather than shown as mere curiosities. The result suits anyone curious about how a working field botanist saw the eastern Himalayas before roads and railways changed them.
himalayan-journals-volume-1-or-notes-of-:
Himalayan Journals, Volume 1, by Joseph Dalton Hooker, holds the notes of a naturalist in Bengal and the Sikkim and Nepal Himalayas. Hooker first published the work in 1854. He dedicates it to Charles Darwin, his affectionate friend, in a page dated at Kew in January of that year. Hooker had sailed with Sir James Ross to the Antarctic, where botany was his chief pursuit. Home again, he wanted the tropics.

His choice lay between India and the Andes. Dr Falconer at the Calcutta botanic garden promised every assistance. The geography of the central and eastern Himalaya was then unknown, Hooker says. All to the north was mystery, attractive equally to traveller and naturalist. Volume 1 records the approach, through Bengal toward the mountains. The journals mix botany, altitude, politics, and weather into the great Victorian form: the scientific expedition narrated by the man who measured it as he walked.
himalayan-journals-volume-2-or-notes-of-:
The second volume of Joseph Dalton Hooker's Himalayan Journals carries his naturalist's record into a second Sikkim trip, after the first volume's travels in Bengal and the lower hills. Hooker writes as a working botanist on the move, noting plants, weather, roads and the people he meets in the same daily entries.

This volume follows the Teesta valley, the climb to Tendong, and the long approach toward the high peaks, with leeches, landslips, rain and scarce food slowing the party. Rhododendrons, oaks, orchids and yews appear again and again, each tied to its height and climate, while Lamas, Lepcha porters and local officials shape what the travellers can and cannot do. The grand view of Kinchinjunga anchors the middle of the trip. Anyone tracing Hooker's route, or the plant life of Sikkim, will find the ground covered step by step.
howard-pyle-s-book-of-pirates-fiction-fa:
Merle Johnson compiled Howard Pyle's Book of Pirates from the writing and pictures of Howard Pyle, the artist-author who, Johnson says, defined pirates for the modern imagination. The contents mix history and tale: Buccaneers and Marooners of the Spanish Main, the ghost of Captain Brand, Tom Chist and the treasure box, and Jack Ballister's fortunes. Blueskin and Captain Scarfield close the volume.

Pyle's stories send boys and sea rovers from Delaware Bay to the Spanish Main in search of prizes from the Indian seas and Africa's coast. His illustrations, famous in their own right, shaped every pirate costume since. The book gathers decades of magazine work into one salt-water treasury for young and old readers.
idylls-of-the-king: Tennyson's life work: twelve long poems retelling the rise and fall of King Arthur and his Round Table. Noble ideals rot from within as Lancelot and Guinevere betray Arthur, until the kingdom falls in a final doomed battle. Written across fifty years, these musical, melancholy poems fixed the Arthurian legend in the Victorian imagination and remain the most famous English telling of the story.
if-i-were-king:
Justin Huntly McCarthy's If I Were King opens in the Fircone Tavern in Paris, where Master François Villon holds ragged court. Villon, poet and thief, drinks with the city's underworld while the king's men watch. The Coming of Katherine brings the high-born Katherine de Vaucelles into his orbit. Enter Thibaut, the Grand Constable who is Villon's enemy and double.

King Louis XI, disguised in the tavern, hears Villon boast what he would do if he were king for a week. The king grants the wish in earnest: Villon wakes as Grand Constable, with the gallows waiting if he fails. McCarthy built the novel from his own successful play. Romance, duels, and the shadow of the gallows fill the sixteen chapters. Villon's week of power is a fairy tale with a rope in it, and his love for Katherine its impossible prize.
joy-and-power-three-messages-with-one-me:
Joy and Power gathers three messages by Henry van Dyke, all with one meaning, as his subtitle says. Van Dyke delivered the title talk in Los Angeles in May 1903, opening the Presbyterian General Assembly. The Battle of Life followed at Princeton's baccalaureate Sunday in June. The Good Old Way closed the set at Harvard a week later.

In his preface, dated July 5, 1903, van Dyke admits the three say about the same thing. Each urges the same course of action and appeals to the same motive. The title talk takes its text from John's gospel: happy are those who do what they know. Van Dyke calls the message nothing new, but the best he had learned in life.
joy-in-the-morning:
Joy in the Morning is a book by Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews, published by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1919. The sample shows the author's long list of earlier books. They include The Perfect Tribute, her famous Lincoln story, plus Crosses of War and Her Country. An illustration shows a man pinning 'the thing men die for' on a guide's shabby coat.

That caption, from page 135, hints at the book's wartime feeling. Andrews wrote often of courage, sacrifice, and American ideals in story form. The Eternal Feminine, The Militants, and The Courage of the Commonplace stand in her list. This 1919 volume belongs to her war-era writing for general readers. Its title promises the turn from sorrow toward morning, a theme her readers knew well.
just-so-stories-rudyard-kipling:
Just So Stories is Rudyard Kipling's book of tales for children, published in 1902. Twelve stories explain, in Kipling's playful way, how things came to be. How the Whale Got His Throat opens the set, and How the Camel Got His Hump follows. The Rhinoceros gets his skin, and the Leopard his spots, in the same spirit.

The Elephant's Child asks questions until his nose stretches into a trunk. Other tales tell how the first letter was written and how the alphabet was made. The Cat That Walked by Himself and The Butterfly That Stamped close the book. Kipling addresses his reader as Best Beloved throughout. These stories, told aloud in their making, remain nursery classics.
landscape-and-song:
Edith Nesbit selected and arranged the poems in Landscape and Song. The book was printed in London, with a New York issue as well. A handwritten note shows one copy was a Christmas gift in Toronto in 1887.

The opening poem dreams of flower cups, meadows, and April mists. Cottage gardens and wood smoke appear in its lines. Poems throughout join outdoor scenes with song-like verse. Nesbit, later famous for children's books, shows an early editor's taste here. The anthology suits readers who like gentle nature poetry. Many poems pair a place with a mood or memory. The anthology favors feeling over formal display throughout.
life-and-letters-of-robert-browning:
Mrs. Sutherland Orr built this life of Robert Browning from letters. Many letters came from the people who had received them. Others were copied by Miss Browning from originals in her care. Her memory, Orr says, was the only record of Browning's boyhood.

Without his sister's help, Orr writes, the book could never exist. Friends assisted her through the press, and Dykes Campbell revised proofs. The preface to this second edition thanks them all by name. Readers get a biography resting on family memory and correspondence. Mrs. Bridell Fox supplied letters written to her father, the Reverend Fox. Miss Flower's correspondence with Browning also reached Orr through her.
life-of-robert-browning:
William Sharp wrote this life of Robert Browning. Project Gutenberg issued it as one of its early electronic texts. The etext was typed twice and compared for accuracy. Alan Light prepared that careful electronic edition.

The biography traces Browning from youth through his long career. His courtship of Elizabeth Barrett holds a central place. Years in Italy shaped both the man and the poems. Sharp writes with sympathy for readers discovering the poet's story. The publishers hoped the comparison method yielded a very clean text. Readers could request the file as 656.txt or 656.zip.
long-live-the-king:
Mary Roberts Rinehart opens this novel with a runaway crown prince. The boy sees the world and lands in disgrace quickly. The Terror and a riding-school visit build the intrigue. A chancellor's visit and tea in the schoolroom follow.

Two prisoners, a park meeting, and a mountain road chase ensue. Nikky does a reckless thing in chapter fourteen. A committee of ten and a delegation raise the politics. Romance and revolution share Rinehart's Ruritanian stage throughout. Father and daughter and the fortress carry the middle chapters. The right to live and love titles the tenth chapter.
love-me-little-love-me-long:
Love Me Little, Love Me Long is a novel by Charles Reade. Its heroine, Lucy Fountain, is a young lady of beauty and standing. Left an orphan, she passes into the care of two trustees. One is Edward Fountain of Font Abbey; the other, Mr. Bazalgette, a merchant.

Lucy spends half the year with each trustee in turn. Reade warns that his tale is mild, and told much in chit-chat. Characters reveal themselves in talk, as people do in life. In his preface he hopes these figures may return in stronger scenes. The book is a gentle comedy of love, money, and guardians.
lucia-rising:
Lucia Rising presents E. F. Benson's famous Lucia comedies in one Penguin volume. Benson, son of an Archbishop of Canterbury, wrote over a hundred books. His Lucia tales became cult favorites from the 1920s on. This edition joins Queen Lucia, Miss Mapp, and Lucia in London.

Lucia Lucas rules the social life of her village like a queen. Music, Italian phrases, and dinner parties are her weapons. Miss Mapp watches her rival with sharp and jealous eyes. Benson turns tiny snubs into high comic warfare. The stakes are small, but the battles feel grand. Readers who love witty social satire will delight in Lucia's rise.
luther-open-letter-on-translating:
Critics attacked Luther's German Bible for adding the word alone to a key verse about faith. His Open Letter on Translating, from 1530, answers the charge head-on. The short piece became a founding document of translation theory, studied far beyond theology.

A translator, Luther argues, must listen to common people in the marketplace, not only to scholars in libraries. Words serve sense, and sense must land in the hearer's own speech. His defense of freedom in rendering made modern vernacular Bibles possible. The letter also opens a window into the mind that gave Germans their literary language. Short, combative, and brilliant, it still settles arguments about how translation should work.
mankind-in-the-making:
Mankind in the Making is H. G. Wells's book on society's future. His preface links it to his earlier Anticipations. Together with 'The Discovery of the Future,' it forms one argument. That essay first appeared in Nature and the Smithsonian Report.

Wells views politics and society as parts of one evolving scheme. Here he turns to how children are born, raised, and taught. Schools, homes, and the state all come under his reforming eye. He asks what kind of people the future should make. His answers are bold, impatient, and full of Edwardian confidence. The book is a landmark of his social thought.
manners-customs-and-dress-during-the-mid:
Manners, Customs, and Dress covers the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. Its author, Paul Lacroix, wrote as P. L. Jacob, the Bibliophile Jacob. He kept the Imperial Library of the Arsenal at Paris. Nineteen chromolithographs and over four hundred wood engravings fill the book.

One plate shows the Queen of Sheba in fifteenth-century costume before Solomon. Lacroix opens the daily life of courts, towns, and homes to general readers. Dress, feasts, trades, and ceremonies pass in rich review. The work grew from his popular Arts of the Middle Ages series. French editions had already won wide appreciation. It remains a splendid picture book of medieval life.
marcus-aurelius-meditations-long:
Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome from 161 to 180, wrote his Meditations in Greek on campaign along the Danube. The notes were never meant for publication; they are orders he gave himself. George Long's English translation is the text here, long a standard version.

In twelve short books, the emperor drills himself in Stoic practice: accept what fate sends, watch the mind's judgments, and remember how brief life is. He thanks his teachers, scolds his own temper, and steadies himself for death. Few books let a reader this close to a ruler's inner life. It is the most read work of Stoic philosophy today.
marx-capital-vol-1-moore-aveling:
Karl Marx published the first volume of Capital in German in 1867. Samuel Moore and Edward Aveling translated it into English in 1887, under Friedrich Engels's eye. This volume treats the production of capital; the later volumes on circulation and the whole system came after Marx's death.

Marx starts from a single commodity and builds his case step by step. He argues that profit springs from surplus value: the gap between what labor makes and what labor is paid. Chapters on the working day draw on factory inspectors' reports to show the human cost. The book is the core text of Marxist economics and a giant of social thought.
mates-at-billabong:
Mary Grant Bruce set Mates at Billabong at a wide Australian homestead. Chapter one presents Norah's home under a low western sun. Red roofs hide among pine, box, and tall blue gum trees.

Jim comes home, a thunderstorm breaks, and a dance fills chapter nine. Christmas, poultry, and station doings fill the middle of the book. A cricket match, Cunjee against Mulgoa, adds sport and local pride. The long quest and the final chapter, Mates, close the tale of the station folk. Two points of view get a chapter of their own early on. Bruce keeps bush work, sport, and home talk in close balance.
mathias-sandorf-een-model-volksplanting:
Jules Verne's Mathias Sandorf appears here in Dutch, dated 1885. Robbers of Rotterdam printed it in the Wonderreizen set. The sample picks the tale up at the Presidio of Ceuta.

Three weeks after fierce events in Sicily, a fast steam yacht sails on. The Ferrato passes between Gibraltar and Cape Almina on October 9. Two comic friends talk of Hercules and his famed pillars of stone. The French note in the record tells of Sandorf, betrayed while he fought to free Hungary, who fled prison and came back for revenge. The Dutch text keeps Verne's own chapter shape and pace.
missing:
Mrs. Humphry Ward set this novel in the First World War. Its frontispiece reproduces a dreaded telegram: a husband reported wounded and missing. The opening chapter waits in a lodging house for an expected couple. The landlady, Mrs. Weston, has entertained dozens of brides and bridegrooms, and displays their picture postcards proudly.

The sharp-tempered Miss Cookson fusses over the rooms before her sister arrives. That sister, Mrs. Sarratt, is the bride whose husband the war will take. Ward, famous for Robert Elsmere, turns from theology to wartime grief here. The novel follows a young wife suspended between hope and the official word, missing.
mistress-wilding:
Rafael Sabatini first published this historical novel in 1910 as Arms and the Maid. American publication renamed it for its hero, Anthony Wilding. The setting is the Duke of Monmouth's Protestant rebellion against James II. The contents open with pot-valiance, Sir Rowland's rescue, and Diana's schemes.

The nuptials of Ruth Westmacott stand at the story's center. Chapters promise Mr. Trenchard's counterstroke, a meeting at the ford, and counsel with His Grace. The motto Pro Religione et Libertate, for religion and liberty, heads a key chapter. Sabatini mixes bright humor with historical accuracy, keeping readers unsure who will win the heroine.
modern-painting:
George Moore gathered these art essays from chapters first allowed to appear in The Speaker. He dedicates the book to Sir William Eden, his companion in art talk. The contents open with Whistler, then Chavannes, Millet, and Manet. An essay called The Failure of the Nineteenth Century states his quarrel with the age.

Moore champions Monet, Sisley, and Pissarro against the academicians. He writes on art education, picture dealers, patrons, and the camera in art. Burne-Jones and the New English Art Club get chapters of their own. The book is a fighting critic's record of the impressionist revolution, written by a novelist who had painted in Paris himself.
much-ado-about-nothing:
William Shakespeare's comedy is set in Messina, at the house of Leonato. This text keeps old print spellings, like u for v. An editor's note explains why printers swapped letters in that age. Type was dear, and shops reused set blocks of words.

The play pairs two love plots in one bright house. Beatrice and Benedick trade sharp wit and swear off love. Hero and Claudio fall fast, then face a cruel slander. Tricks, spying, and a foolish watch sort truth from lies. The old spelling in this file lets readers see the text close to its first printed form.
nasa-tm-19650012155-effects-of-gust-indu:
Prepared for a May 1964 aerospace medical meeting in Miami, this study asks how hard acceleration affects a pilot's work. Gusts and sharp maneuvers both push on the body. At the same time, the pilot must keep control of the vehicle. The authors used a piloted motion simulator to study that strain at low level.

Advanced missions, they note, can push a pilot near the limits of tolerance. Reentry forces were a recent example. Their approach joined engineers, stress specialists, and flight surgeons. A simulator lets that team study the problem safely, long before a real flight faces it.
nasa-tm-19660003576-evolution-of-o-stars:
Richard Stothers, at the Institute for Space Studies in New York, follows a giant star through the burning of helium in this third paper of a series. The star weighs thirty times the Sun's mass. Its life is traced from helium ignition, through depletion, to exhaustion. Helium burning begins with a brief phase, after which the onset of burning halts the star's slow squeeze under gravity.

O stars are the most massive and brightest normal stars. Their fast lives test theories of how stars age. Tracking one star's computed path through helium burning shows what such a theory predicts. Stothers presents that path for specialists in stellar structure.
nasa-tm-19670006715-an-experimental-inve:
Thomas H. Cochran, John C. Aydelott, and Charles M. Spuckler, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for an environmental sciences meeting in Washington, D.C., in April 1967. It reports experiments on how boiling from a flat heated surface changes when gravity is removed. The question matters for fuel tanks in space.

Zero-gravity data came from letting the test package free-fall down a 100-foot drop tower. The team varied fluid cooling, fluid properties, and heat input, working in the range where separate bubbles form. High-speed films showed boiling did not depend on gravity when the fluid was well cooled. The change away from separate bubbles, though, came at a lower heat input in zero gravity. Analysis pointed to a pressure force as the main driver of bubble release.
nasa-tm-19670008308-the-evolution-of-the:
William R. Corliss wrote this history at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, where it appeared in January 1967 as Goddard Historical Note Number 3. It traces the growth of STADAN, the Satellite Tracking and Data Acquisition Network. The catalog record notes that the network grew out of the pre-IGY and Minitrack facilities built to follow the first satellites.

Corliss explains that STADAN did more than its name suggests. Alongside tracking satellites and receiving their data, the network radioed commands up to spacecraft. It also ran the ground communication links that funneled data from stations worldwide into the nerve center at Goddard in Greenbelt, Maryland. Position and pointing records traveled with each measurement, he stresses. Scientists cannot interpret instrument data without knowing where the satellite was and which way it faced.
nasa-tm-19670028135-a-method-of-soft-tet:
B. S. Perrine Jr., of the Aero-Astrodynamics Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this memorandum on July 31, 1967. It studies two spacecraft joined by a flexible tether line in a near-circular orbit. Different air drag on each craft would slowly pull them apart or push them together.

Perrine derives the equations of motion through a closed-form solution. He then devises a method of pulls on the tether, applied in a repeatable sequence. The pulls keep the two craft near each other despite the unequal drag. The method is applied to a workshop case drawn from Apollo-era planning.
nasa-tm-19700003737-the-midlatitude-ioni:
N. J. Miller of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this August 1969 preprint, numbered X-621-69-330, on the midlatitude ionization trough. Explorer 22 Langmuir probe measurements from three winters supply the data, gathered at one thousand kilometers. The trough is a nightside band of thin ionization at midlatitudes, watched here while solar activity was rising.

As solar activity increased, the trough's position stayed put, Miller reports. Its electron density nevertheless rose threefold across the period studied. Electron temperature kept a nightside peak right at the trough, barely changing in height, width, or place. He ties that warm peak to heat conducted down field lines from the hot protonosphere. Beyond the plasmapause, thin plasma chokes that heat flow off again.
nasa-tm-19700004964-apollo-11-water-serv:
Apollo 11 Water Servicing is a Kennedy Space Center report dated November 10, 1969. It records how the water supply for the Apollo 11 spacecraft was serviced and checked before flight. Clean, safe water mattered both for the crew and for the craft's systems.

The report sets out its purpose and scope, then gives the analysis, the results, and a discussion. Added lists track water sample reports from the launch countdown. Two more lists cover chamber tests with the command module and the lunar module. A table gives the volumes of the water samples tested at each center.
nasa-tm-19700025390-lm-controllability-d:
An engineer named Kaupp at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this internal note on December 7, 1967. It asks whether the lunar module stays controllable while its descent engine fires. The worry is a disturbance torque from the engine thrust itself.

The note names three ways that torque could grow too strong. The engine's gimbal trim system could fail, or the autopilot could send a bad trim command from noisy readings. Sloshing fuel could also shift the craft's balance point during the coast. If thrust torque beat the control system, the module could tip past recovery on its way down.
nasa-tm-19710011468-the-practical-use-of:
G V Brown, head of the Cryophysics Section at the Lewis Research Center, wrote this paper for an August 1971 refrigeration congress in Washington. It asks whether magnetic cooling can now work beyond tiny laboratory setups. Strong new superconducting magnets changed the case. Fields once limited to near absolute zero work can now order magnetic materials at far higher temperatures.

Brown argued that a magnetic refrigerator could rival gas machines at low temperatures. Gas machines lose efficiency badly in the cold. He also described related devices. They include a magnetic pump for helium or hydrogen vapor, a regenerator for use below twenty kelvin, and an adjustable heat source or sink.
nasa-tm-19710016954-analysis-of-a-contro:
S M Seltzer of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this analysis on April 30, 1971, as NASA TM X-64601. He worked in the Astrionics Laboratory there. The subject is a control system with two nonlinear elements. Nonlinear parts break the simple rules used for steady control design. Designers still need to know if such a system will settle or keep oscillating.

Seltzer showed how the system can be studied in parameter space. The catalog record ties the work to limit cycles, the steady oscillations a control loop can fall into. The analysis addresses whether those cycles exist and whether they are stable. It also gives their size and frequency, key facts for safe guidance design.
nasa-tm-19710022685-lining-metal-tubes-b:
William L Maag and William F Mattson described a new way to line metal tubes in this August 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2347. A lined tube pairs a strong outer wall with a special inner surface. Their method forms the lining and bonds it in one high temperature process. It relies on creep, the slow stretching of hot metal under steady pressure.

A thin walled tube inside is pressurized until it creeps outward. That pressure squeezes layers of thin metal foil between the inner and outer tubes. Heat bonds the foil into a lining. After bonding, workers remove the inner tube by chemical or mechanical means. The report gives worked examples of the method.
nasa-tm-19710024070-calculation-of-cambe:
William B Igoe of the Langley Research Center wrote this September 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2311. It gives a way to calculate wing camber, the curve of a wing's center line, using slender wing theory at Mach 1.0. Designers of near sonic wings needed the camber shape that spreads lift as planned. The method covers wings with straight edged, many sided outlines.

Igoe assumed a steady chordwise load and a freely chosen spanwise load pattern. Charts supply the functions the calculation needs. He also worked an example for a variable sweep wing. Compared with test data, the method caught the size and trend of spanwise twist. It still could not fix fine camber details for supercritical wings.
nasa-tm-19720006378-computer-controlled-:
Eugene J Manista of the Lewis Research Center reported this converter study in January 1972, as NASA TM X-2480. A computer swept and recorded the output curves of a thermionic converter automatically. The flat converter used an etched rhenium emitter and a niobium collector. A guard ring surrounded the collector to keep edge effects from spoiling readings. Manista asked how voltage imbalance on that ring distorted the results.

With the normal guard ring wiring, distortion stayed minimal in the power range. Shorting the emitter to the guard ring was far worse. It bent the curve badly and lowered the striking voltage of the hot mode. An improved computer program also gathered a limited performance map. The map covered set emitter, collector, and cesium conditions.
new-forces-in-old-china-an-inevitable-aw: New Forces in Old China, subtitled An Inevitable Awakening, is a book by Arthur Judson Brown. The hosted sample holds only a Project Gutenberg header, so it preserves no readable content from the book itself. The title and subtitle alone frame the subject: new forces at work in old China, and a waking the author calls sure to come. No year for the book is given in the sample or the record. Readers should treat this note as a title level guide only.
on-anything:
Hilaire Belloc published this essay collection in London in 1910. Constable and Company issued the book that year. Most essays first ran in the Morning Post newspaper. One piece first ran in the Morning Leader instead. Belloc dedicated the book to George Macdonald Lemmi.

The contents open with building castles in Spain. Belloc writes short, bold essays on almost any topic. His topics range from travel and food to faith and folly. He argues with humor, force, and strong opinions. Readers meet Belloc as a lively public essayist. Page views of the first print sit free for all to view online. Clay and Sons of London printed the book, its title page says.
on-christmas-day-in-the-evening: Grace Smith Richmond wrote this Christmas story, copyrighted in 1910. Charles Relyea drew the pictures for the book. The hosted sample preserves only front matter and picture captions. Captions quote lines about imagination and a steam calliope. One caption names Billy and his anxious sister Margaret. Readers can confirm author, artist, and date from the sample. The sample gives no readable text of the story itself.
on-something:
Hilaire Belloc wrote this second book of miscellaneous essays. He dedicated it, with a joke, to Somebody. The contents promise a plea for simpler drama. Other pieces treat notebooks, unknown people, and threepenny bits. A Norfolk man and odd people receive portraits.

Later essays advise a young burglar with mock gravity. The monkey question appeals to common sense, he says. An empire builder and King Caedwalla also appear. No topic is too small for his lively mind. The book mixes humor, history, and sharp opinion. Heads add a Van Tromp sketch and the Tree of Knowledge. A unit of England and a relic close the list.
on-the-art-of-reading:
Arthur Quiller-Couch wrote these lectures on the art of reading. Cambridge University Press first issued the book in 1920. The sample shows reprints through the year 1939. Lecture one introduces his aims for young readers. Lecture two contrasts apprehension with full comprehension.

Two lectures treat how children should read books. Another lecture treats reading for examinations at school. Quiller-Couch taught English literature at Cambridge for years. He urges slow, loving attention over mere cramming. The contents alone show his range and his method. The book remains a warm guide for teachers and parents.
on-the-decay-of-the-art-of-lying:
Mark Twain read this comic essay to a Hartford club. It was offered for a thirty dollar prize there. A footnote admits it did not take the prize. Twain insists the custom of lying has not decayed. Only the art of lying has grown sloppy, he says.

He calls the lie a virtue, a grace, and man's surest friend. Judicious lying is what the world needs, he argues. Awkward lies fail as badly as blunt truth, he warns. He jokes that lying should be taught in public schools. He cites the old saw that children and fools speak truth. Wise adults, by that rule, do not speak it plain.
on-the-improvement-of-the-understanding:
Baruch Spinoza wrote this treatise on improving the intellect. R. H. M. Elwes translated it into English. The contents list rules of life and modes of perception. Spinoza asks what the true and final good is. He sets ordinary desires against that higher aim.

The method part teaches readers to form clear ideas. True ideas must be split from false and fictitious ones. Doubt, memory, and careless words can hinder the mind, he says. Good definitions are the means to clear understanding. It lays out the program of his later Ethics.
organic-gardener-s-composting: Steve Solomon's Organic Gardener's Composting is a practical gardening book. Its title promises instruction in composting for organic gardeners. The hosted sample, however, contains none of the book's text. It consists entirely of the Project Gutenberg header and license matter. That header gives the title, the author's name, and an August 2003 release date. Because no page of Solomon's actual guidance appears, this note reports only what the front matter establishes. It makes no claims about the book's methods or advice.
our-foreigners-a-chronicle-of-americans-: Samuel P. Orth's Our Foreigners appeared in 1920 in the Chronicles of America series. Its subject is immigration as the making of the American people. The hosted sample shows the title pages and a contents list only. The chapters open with Opening the Door and The American Stock. Utopias in America, The Irish Invasion, and The Teutonic Tide follow. No chapter text appears in the sample.
pagan-and-christian-creeds-their-origin-:
Edward Carpenter's Pagan and Christian Creeds argues that the religions of the world are variations on one root fact of universal life. His contents map the case. Solar myths and Christian festivals come first. The symbolism of the zodiac and totem sacraments follow. Food magic, expiation rites, and pagan initiations build the argument. The savior-god and virgin-mother stand near its peak. The genesis and exodus of Christianity close it.

The introduction warns that the very abundance of material tempts students of religious origins to rush in with plausible theories. Carpenter proceeds anyway, gently. Creeds and rituals, he holds, symbolize the redemption of our own most intimate natures. We may understand them consciously, or not at all.
parent-and-child-volume-iii-child-study-:
Mosiah Hall wrote Parent and Child, Volume Three, on child study and training. The Deseret Sunday School Union published it at Salt Lake City in 1916. Hall taught education at the University of Utah. He also inspected high schools for the state. The introduction frames home-making as the world's fundamental business. Rearing children well demands understanding, it argues.

Loving parents suffer for mistakes, the introduction says. Loving intelligence might have prevented them. We cannot save our children in ignorance. The volume's keynote is a more enlightened parenthood. Its lessons study child nature and its laws of development. References accompany most lessons. A parents' class library list closes the book. The Union offered the course to guide children into righteousness.
personal-recollections-abridged-chiefly-: A hosted sample showing only the front matter of Charlotte Elizabeth's Personal Recollections, the title page and a detailed contents, with no letter text visible. The edition is abridged chiefly in parts on political controversies in Great Britain. The contents arrange her life as letters: childhood and a martyrs' prison, youth and loss of hearing, travels and a storm at sea. Nova Scotia, Ireland, and religious progress follow, each letter's topics spelled out in full.
philaster-or-love-lies-a-bleeding: The sample hosted for this entry shows only the front matter of Philaster, or Love Lies a Bleeding, the title and list of persons, with no dialogue visible. The play is credited to Francis Beaumont and John Fletcher, and the scene is set in Sicily. The persons include the King, Philaster the heir to the crown, Pharamond, prince of Spain. Arethusa the king's daughter follows, and Eufrasia, a lord's daughter disguised as a page and called Bellario.
piano-and-song:
Friedrich Wieck's Piano and Song, translated from the German and published at Boston in 1875, tells how to teach, how to learn, and how to judge musical performances. The translator's preface introduces Wieck as a distinguished teacher who died in the autumn of 1873. He was father and teacher of Clara Wieck, the celebrated pianist who became Clara Schumann, and Robert Schumann himself had been his pupil.

His second daughter, Marie Wieck, was also a known performer. The translator believed Wieck's views would prove as valuable in America as in Germany. The little book preserves the method behind one of music's famous families.
piano-tuning: The hosted sample stops at the front matter of the Dover edition of J. Cree Fischer's Piano Tuning, the copyright pages and the start of its preface, with no instruction text visible. The Dover pages explain that this 1975 edition republishes the work first published at Philadelphia in 1907 by Theo. Presser, leaving out the dated chapters on the tuning profession and advertising. The title calls the book a simple and accurate method for amateurs.
podcast-joerogan-ELGY6HfkENg:
Author Michelle Dowd joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2137 to talk about her memoir of a hard childhood. Dowd grew up in a survivalist family in the mountains, under strict rules and deep poverty. Her book turned that hidden life into a public story.

She tells Rogan what daily life in that world was like, and how she found her way out through reading and school. Rogan asks about faith, fear, and the family she left behind. The episode is a quiet, gripping life story, and a look at the off-grid childhoods that exist far from public view.
podcast-joerogan-UlRHECIUNng: Bill Thompson with Rogan for episode 2473. The day's guest in a long, open talk. The full conversation as aired. A deep dive. One episode, dated, from the podcast shelves, kept for listeners and the curious.
podcast-tuckercarlson-BRgll1YUuNg:
A UFO whistleblower joins Tucker Carlson and says his life was in peril for speaking out. The episode title quotes his stark line on the risk. The guest is not named in the title, which fits the fear at the core of the talk.

The guest tells what he claims to know of the craft programs and what befell him when he spoke. He argues the state guards the secret with threats that cross into harm. Carlson asks why he speaks at all at such cost. Listeners get a tense first hand tale. The library holds the talk as an archive record of his account.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rH3QGv2L9ng:
A whistleblower joins Tucker Carlson to claim the state has run the largest spy program in all of history. The episode title also warns of a coming slave state. The guest is not named in the title, which adds to the sense of risk.

The guest lays out the scale of the watch net as he says he saw it from inside. He warns that the tools built for war abroad now turn on the home crowd. Carlson asks what can still be done to break the net. Listeners get a stark alarm in the guest's own words. The library holds the talk as an archive record.
pragmatism-a-new-name-for-some-old-ways-:
William James delivered the lectures printed here at the Lowell Institute in Boston in the winter of 1906 and at Columbia University in January 1907. Published them as Pragmatism, a new name for some old ways of thinking. He dedicates the book to the memory of John Stuart Mill. From whom he first learned the pragmatic openness of mind, and pictures Mill as the movement's leader had he lived. The preface confesses he does not like the name pragmatism, but it is too late to change it.

James unifies in broad strokes the tendencies suddenly precipitating out of the air in many countries: truth as what works in experience, beliefs judged by their fruits. He points beginners to Dewey and to F. C. S. Schiller's Studies in Humanism. Few philosophy books traveled further into ordinary speech.
principles-of-teaching:
Adam S. Bennion, superintendent of church schools, wrote a manual of teaching for class teachers in the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. The book first appeared in 1921 and was reprinted in 1952 by the general boards of the church's aid groups.

Early chapters ask what teaching is, why it is done, and what joy it brings, then turn to the teacher's own character and growth. Two chapters deal with personality and one with attainment. Church teachers get short, direct counsel on aims, preparation, and conduct in the classroom.
public-speaking:
Clarence Stratton, a director of English in a Cleveland high school, wrote a school text on speaking printed by Henry Holt with a copyright of 1920. The course treats a speech as a skill that can be broken into parts and practised.

Chapters cover speech itself, the voice, words and sentences, beginnings and endings, gathering material, planning, and making an outline or brief. Later chapters treat explaining, proving, refuting, debating, special occasions, and dramatics. Pupils get exercises and rules meant to turn shy speakers into clear ones, with appendixes and an index for class use.
queen-sheba-s-ring:
Queen Sheba's Ring is an adventure novel by H. Rider Haggard, told in twenty chapters by a narrator who begins by defending his friend Professor Ptolemy Higgs. Higgs had written of the tableland of Mur in North Central Africa. He had written of an ancient underground city in its ring of mountains. He had written of the strange tribe who live there. The tribe is of Abyssinian Jewish descent.

Higgs's rivals, the narrator says, have written him down as a man who strains the truth, and the tale that follows is the proof of his account. Chapter titles promise Sergeant Quick's advice, a death wind, an escape from Harmac, a den of lions, a burning palace, starvation, and a trial.
quit-your-worrying: Quit Your Worrying!, by George Wharton James, published at Pasadena, California, in 1916, is shown here by its dedication and contents. James calls to those standing on the banks of worry before the ocean of God's love to come on in, the water is fine. Twenty-three chapters name worry a curse of the age, then sort its kinds: health, parents, marital, religious, envy, ambition, jealousy, suspicion, impatience, and anticipation.
resonance-in-singing-and-speaking: Thomas Fillebrown, M.D., D.M.D., is named on the title page of this third edition of a book on resonance in singing and speaking. He served twenty-one years as professor of dentistry and oral surgery at Harvard, and lectured on voice development. Oliver Ditson issued the book, copyright 1911, in the Music Students Library. Fillebrown dedicates it to William Haskell Stockbridge, his instructor in voice culture. The opening pages shown are title and dedication only, so the book's chapters on the voice are not displayed here.
response-in-the-living-and-non-living:
Jagadis Chunder Bose, professor at Presidency College, Calcutta, published this study of response in living and non-living things with Longmans, Green in 1902. A line from the Rig Veda heads it: the real is one, though wise men call it variously. Bose dedicates the work to his countrymen.

A list of his earlier papers maps the research behind the book. He reported to a Paris physics congress in 1900 on how like the effects of electrical stimulus are in inorganic and living matter. Discourses at the Royal Institution and the Royal Society followed in 1901, with work on the electric response of plants under stimulus in 1902.
robert-browning:
Edward Dowden, professor of English literature in the University of Dublin, wrote this life of Robert Browning for the Temple Biographies in 1904. A portrait in oil, for which Browning sat to R. W. Curtis at Venice in 1880, fronts the book. The editor's preface, by Dugald Macfadyen, defines its task.

What readers want in Browning's case, the preface says, is a biography of the mind, in Gladstone's phrase. His life's events were achievements of the spirit more than public incidents. The book ties his poems to their dates and origins to show his inward growth. Browning's tonic optimism, it argues, clears the fog of materialism from life.
rough-and-tumble-engineering:
James H. Maggard wrote Rough and Tumble Engineering for men who run farm and traction engines, not for engineers of large fixed engines in fine engine rooms. In his preface he promises plain, everyday field terms and no science terms. His readers, he says, may do eight horse work one day and sixteen horse work the next. They may work one day with all in their favor and the next day in mud holes.

Maggard is frank that reading alone will not make an engineer of anyone. He asks for close reading, good judgment, and common sense. He claims that in one month a learner who follows the book can be, for real work, better than most so-called engineers. The opening pages address young men who wish to learn most of all.
rudyard-kipling:
John Palmer wrote Rudyard Kipling, first issued in New York in 1915 by Henry Holt and Company, with a front picture of Kipling. The contents list an opening survey, then chapters headed Simla, The Sahib, Native India, Soldiers Three, The Day's Work, The Finer Grain, and The Poems. Book lists for Britain and America and an index close the volume. Palmer's plan treats the Indian tales as a large bloc, then moves to later work and verse.

In the Simla chapter Palmer divides Kipling's Indian stories into three groups: tales of Simla, Anglo-Indian tales, and tales of native India. Kim, he adds, is more, much more, than a tale of India. He warns that the Indian stories tend to fill a share of space out of line with their weight. They count for less, he argues, than their number or the notice they have won would suggest.
schnitzler-casanova-s-homecoming:
An aging Casanova returns to Venice and finds himself a weary man haunted by his own legend. Arthur Schnitzler's novella Casanova's Homecoming, from 1918 and presented here in English, studies that return with melancholy precision. Desire has outlived desirability, and wit curdles toward bitterness in the old seducer.

Younger rivals, old flames, and the city's unchanged beauty all measure his decline. Schnitzler refuses both mockery and sentimentality, holding his hero in clear, cold light. The result ranks among the finest short works of twentieth-century European literature. Growing old has rarely been anatomized so gracefully. The novella shows a master of psychology working at novella length with perfect control.
school-and-home-cooking:
Carlotta C. Greer wrote School and Home Cooking while she led the foods and household management program at East Technical High School in Cleveland, Ohio. She shaped the book as a classroom text that pupils could follow step by step, both during lessons and later in their own homes. Its front pages picture the kitchen at Mount Vernon.

Greer begins with dishes and materials that beginners already know, then builds new skills on that ground. She puts off naming and sorting the food groups until pupils have worked with each one. Every section ends with related tasks covering table service, full meals, and projects to try at home. Those closing lessons also weigh meal cost, food value, wise choosing, and thrifty buying.
sermons-on-evil-speaking:
