Isaac Barrow preached these sermons against loose and harmful talk, with an opening life of Barrow by Professor Henry Morley. Contents list pieces against foolish talking and jesting, against rash swearing, and two parts on the folly of slander. Barrow's own text treats evil speaking in general.

Morley traces Barrow from his London birth in 1630, through Charterhouse and Felstead schools, to Cambridge in 1643. Barrow won a Trinity fellowship in 1649 beside his friend John Ray, the plant scholar. The sermons apply that learning to daily speech, urging care with the tongue as a Christian duty.
sixteen-months-in-four-german-prisons-we:
Henry C. Mahoney told this tale of sixteen months in four German prisons, written down by Frederick A. Talbot for Sampson Low in London in 1917. The prisons named are Wesel, Sennelager, Klingelputz, and Ruhleben. A photograph shows Mahoney as he looked on his release day, taken by the German government itself.

A transcriber warns that gaps in the text stand as printed, cut by author, editor, or printer on purpose. Mahoney's account of arrest, hunger, and camp life in the Great War reached British readers while the war still raged, as first-hand proof of a civilian prisoner's lot.
sixty-years-of-california-song:
Margaret Blake-Alverson published this record of sixty years of California song at Oakland in 1913, from her own address on Second Avenue. A photograph by Webster of Oakland, dated 1912, shows the author. She dedicates the book to her friends everywhere, with a verse on singing through work and love.

Blake-Alverson states her terms plainly: if her singing and teaching bettered persons and communities, her work was well done. Pioneer concerts, teachers, and choirs fill her pages. The book preserves a woman musician's own account of how song grew with California from rough early days onward.
ski-running: Katharine Furse wrote Ski-Running, dated 1924, with a map and four photos. The opening pages give the contents alone. Heads cover the past of ski-ing, the cost of a ski-ing holiday, winter centres, clothing, and gear and its care. Later heads treat first steps, manners on the snow, snow and light, falls, tests, guides and teachers, maps and route finding, snow slips, mishaps, and the pull of the sport.
sport-and-work-on-the-nepaul-frontier-tw:
An indigo planter who signs himself Maori wrote Sport and Work on the Nepaul Frontier, dated 1878, as twelve years of sporting memories. A front picture shows tiger hunting and the return to camp. His preface says he went home in 1875 for a few months after some twelve years in India. There he met such deep ignorance of daily Indian life among folk at home that he saw room for a chatty, plain book.

His plan is to picture planter life in the mofussil, the country districts of India. He will tell of hunting, shooting, fishing, and other sports, and of work and play and plain daily events. He will also describe the natives as they show in close daily dealing: their ways, customs, bent, rites, and sayings, so far as these touch the planters' own social life. The book aims at friends at home, in a familiar and unshowy voice.
stage-confidences-talks-about-players-an:
Clara Morris, author of Life on the Stage and The Pasteboard Crown, writes Stage Confidences as talks about players and play acting. Charles H. Kelly printed the London book in 1902, with pictures, and Morris gives it to Mary Anderson. A front picture shows Morris herself in 1883. Her greeting speaks first to the dear girls who honor her with their liking and their confidences.

Morris grants the girls one edge over her: numbers. They can ask more questions in an hour than she can answer in a week, and fly into a hundred fits of vexed hope while she frames one soft answer. Their name is Legion, and their homes scatter between the two oceans. Some are grave, some gay, some well-off, some very poor, some wise. The greeting sets up a book of counsel drawn from a life on the stage, told as friend to friend.
stories-worth-rereading:
Stories Worth Rereading, dated 1913, is a set of short moral tales for young readers. No editor or author is named on the pages at hand; the contents alone carry the book, and they lean toward conduct, home, and faith.

Titles tell the drift: Their Word of Honor, What Rum Does, The Bridal Wine-Cup, My Mother's Ring, Honor Thy Father and Thy Mother, and Fighting the Good Fight. Other pieces praise song, a doctor's cow, and a boy's faithfulness to a dog, and the set closes with short lives of Samuel Smiles, the author of Self-Help, and David Livingstone. Temperance and duty are the steady themes.
studies-in-song:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Studies in Song was printed at London by Chatto and Windus in 1880. The contents begin with a Song for the Centenary of Walter Savage Landor, Swinburne's great elder and friend, and a grand chorus of birds drawn from Aristophanes.

The poems that follow include Off Shore and After Nine Years. They include a piece for a portrait of Felice Orsini. Evening on the Broads and The Emperor's Progress come next. The Fourteenth of July and The Launch of the Livadia follow. Six Years Old, A Parting Song, and the long By the North Sea close the book. Sea wind, public events, and private grief meet in verses built for sound as much as sense, hallmarks of Swinburne's art.
successful-methods-of-public-speaking:
Grenville Kleiser, once an instructor in public speaking at the Yale Divinity School, wrote Successful Methods of Public Speaking for Funk and Wagnalls of New York and London. Kleiser wrote a shelf of such manuals, from How to Speak in Public to Fifteen Thousand Useful Phrases, and this volume sums up his system.

The method treats speaking as a trainable power: building self-confidence in speech and manner, shaping ideas, using the voice, and holding an audience. Kleiser wrote for ministers, lawyers, salesmen, and club speakers in an age when platform skill could make a career. His books sold widely to self-improvers learning by mail and by practice at home.
swan-song:
Anton Chekhov's short play The Swan Song appears here in Marian Fell's English version, printed with her introduction and a chronological list of his works. The play's Russian author is spelled both Checkov and Tchekoff on the opening pages.

Fell's introduction sets the scene. Russia's last nineteenth-century years were grey with doubt and gloom. Its peasants were enslaved by want and toil. Its educated class was enslaved by idleness and tedium. Its idealists hoped for happiness two or three hundred years ahead. Chekhov, born at the Black Sea port of Taganrog on January 17, 1860, made that world his subject. The Swan Song itself is a one-act piece for an old actor alone in a dark theatre after the audience has gone.
talks-on-talking: Grenville Kleiser, once a teacher of public speaking at Yale Divinity School, wrote Talks on Talking, held under rights in 1916 by Funk and Wagnalls Company. Kleiser also wrote guides on how to speak in public and how to gain faith in one's own speech. Parts listed cover the art of talking, types of talkers, the speaking voice, how to tell a story, talking in sales work, and how to speak in public.
the-advancement-of-learning:
Francis Bacon wrote The Advancement of Learning, here copied from an 1893 Cassell and Company printing in London, Paris, and Melbourne. A front essay recalls the first title page of 1605, which named the work as two books on the growth of learning, divine and human, addressed to the king.

The essay hails it as a book still alive, one that opened a fresh world of thought. Bacon used it early in the reign of James the First to clear ground for his New Organon, his new tool of knowledge. Against it stood Aristotle's Organon, long drilled into students as the core of logic. Readers get Bacon's famed map of all learning, its gaps, and its blocks.
the-art-of-money-getting:
P. T. Barnum lays out golden rules for making money in this lecture. In the United States, he begins, land outnumbers people, so a healthy person willing to take any decent work that offers can find well-paid employment. Roads to success stand uncrowded on every side.

Yet Barnum grants that keeping money is the hardest thing in the world. The road to wealth, he quotes Dr. Franklin as saying, is as plain as the road to the mill: spend less than you earn. He invokes Dickens's Mr. Micawber as a comic witness to that simple rule, and builds his counsel on thrift joined to steady, chosen work.
the-art-of-public-speaking: Title pages alone present The Art of Public Speaking by J. Berg Esenwein and Dale Carnagey, copyrighted in 1915 by the Home Correspondence School of Springfield, Massachusetts. Esenwein is billed as author of How to Attract and Hold an Audience and works on the short story and the photoplay. Carnagey is named as a professor of public speaking at Baltimore. He also taught in Y.M.C.A. schools across several cities.
the-art-of-soul-winning:
J. W. Mahood wrote this handbook for personal workers. He was an evangelist and author of The Missing Wheel Found. Jennings and Pye printed it at Cincinnati in 1901. Eaton and Mains printed it at New York. A line from the Gospels heads it: he brought him to Jesus. Mahood's preface sees a crying need for a mighty revival in all the churches.

The key to such a revival, Mahood argues, is earnest personal work, and most church members are not ready for it. Many know nothing of a personal Pentecost; many are simply careless of their duty. He urges pastors to place a copy in every home a month before set revival meetings, with daily study, memory verses, and thought on the texts.
the-boy-allies-in-the-trenches-or-midst-:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies in the Trenches, or Midst Shot and Shell along the Aisne, dated 1915. The first chapter is called With the Army. It opens as two lads walk in on Field Marshal Sir John French, chief of the British force sent to help France. French is stunned to see them alive.

Lieutenant Paine and Lieutenant Crawford tell him they are not so easy to kill. They have been in Russia, they say, where they rode with a Cossack unit and saw much hard fighting. They came back by airship. Hal gives French a dispatch from Grand Duke Nicholas, chief of all the Russian hosts in the east. French, once the tale is told, puts both lads on his own staff at once. Rooms are to be made ready for them on the spot.
the-brain-and-the-voice-in-speech-and-so: F. W. Mott wrote The Brain and the Voice in Speech and Song, dated London, July 1910. Mott's name bears the marks F.R.S., M.D., and F.R.C.P. The list of heads starts with views on how speech began. The voice's three traits, loudness, pitch, and timbre, come next, then its three parts: the bellows, the reed in the larynx, and the resonator. The brain's work in speech and song, speech and right-handedness, and the seat of speech in the brain close the heads shown.
the-complete-works-of-robert-burns-conta:
Robert Burns's complete works, holding his poems, songs, and correspondence, appear here in an edition from Phillips, Sampson, and Company of Boston and J. C. Derby of New York, dated 1855. The title page promises a new life of the poet, with critical and biographical notices, by Allan Cunningham. The book is described there as elegantly illustrated.

A transcriber's note warns that hyphenation and accent vary through the book and have been left unchanged. The placing of poems, epitaphs, and songs also follows the printed original, indent for indent. A dedication to Archibald Hastie, Esq., member of Parliament for Paisley, begins after the title page, though its text is cut off in what is present. Cunningham's life was a standard doorway into Burns for nineteenth-century readers, and this American edition carried the Scots poet's songs and letters to a wide market in that form.
the-cords-of-vanity-a-comedy-of-shirking:
James Branch Cabell calls The Cords of Vanity a comedy of shirking. This revised and expanded edition carries an introduction by Wilson Follett. Follett frames the new edition as both a rescue job and an act of fresh creation, since Cabell reworked the novel rather than merely reprinting it.

Follett jokes that Cabell calls him the only known purchaser of the first edition. He quotes the old reviews with relish. A Cleveland paper found the book slushy and disgusting. A New York paper called it sterile, malodorous, and dull. Ainslee's Magazine found it rambling and at times nauseating. Such dull verdicts, Follett argues, cannot touch a writer who never counted them among his rewards or his penalties.
the-crossing: Winston Churchill's The Crossing is shown here only through its contents, split into two books. Book I, The Borderland, runs from The Blue Wall through Charlestown, the Nollichucky Trace, Harrodstown, and Kaskaskia, ending with The Hair Buyer Trapped and The Campaign Ends. Book II, Flotsam and Jetsam, takes its hero to Danville, across the mountains again, and on to St. Louis, with chapters on a keel boat and a strange city. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-crown-of-thorns-a-token-for-the-sorr:
E. H. Chapin subtitled his book The Crown of Thorns a token for the sorrowing. In a preface dated May 1860 he explains that one discourse in it, The Mission of Little Children, was written soon after a dear son's death. It was printed as a pamphlet. That printing sold out faster than the demand, so the piece returns here with others of like cast, most born of the same loss.

The contents list sermons on the three tabernacles, the shadow of disappointment, the Christian view of sorrow, consolation in loneliness, and resignation. Chapin offers the volume with his sympathy, hoping it may teach a troubled soul to endure and hope, and help the grieving weave the thorns that wound them into a crown.
the-crucifixion-of-philip-strong:
The Rev. Charles M. Sheldon, author of In His Steps: What Would Jesus Do?, published The Crucifixion of Philip Strong with Street and Smith under an 1899 copyright. Chapter I finds the minister unable to decide what is best to do. The postman has brought two letters, and Philip sits in his study, hands clasped over his knee, staring out the window in hard thought.

He calls his wife Sarah up from below. She comes teasing: he only summons her in great distress. The last time she had to cut him loose after he shut the tassel of his dressing-gown under the lid of his writing desk. Philip smiles and answers that he is fast again, in a strait between two choices, and begins to read her the letters.
the-dance-by-an-antiquary-historic-illus:
An unnamed antiquary wrote The Dance, printed in London by John Bale, Sons and Danielsson in 1911 and dedicated to Dr. Eleanor Maxwell. The subtitle promises historic illustrations of dancing from 3300 B.C. to 1911 A.D. In the preface the author calls the work a sketch of the picture-record of the dance, not a full history of the subject.

At most, he says, it sums up the history of posture, since a whole dance cannot easily be shown in pictures. A thorough treatment would take years and volumes; two writers alone gave eight hundred dances in four volumes. The old art of writing dances down, as music is written, is lost, and tries at reviving it have failed. He hopes the book will still serve readers studying the costume, positions, and gear of the dance across many periods.
the-deacon-of-dobbinsville-a-story-based: John A. Morrison subtitled The Deacon of Dobbinsville a story based on actual happenings. A preface by Lawrence D. Pruitt, dated March 1966, explains that the tale was first printed forty-five or fifty years earlier. It contrasts professors of religion with people converted and filled with the Holy Spirit. Pruitt quotes Morrison's leave to reprint, dated October 26, 1965. He notes that the author died at Anderson, Indiana, on December 23, 1965, in his seventy-third year, before the reprint appeared. Only that preface and the heading of Chapter I are present here.
the-eve-of-the-revolution-a-chronicle-of:
Carl Becker's The Eve of the Revolution, a chronicle of the breach with England in the Chronicles of America set, was printed by Yale in 1918. In his preface Becker owns that deeds alone are not his aim. He wants the feel of past minds at work, and he chases it through long quotes and free retelling. The air of an age matters more to him than its bare chronicle.

Stamp taxes, tea, and troops fill the tale, but ideas lead. Becker wrote for the series' Abraham Lincoln edition. His light touch made him a model for later historians of the founding.
the-fifth-string:
John Philip Sousa, famed for marches, wrote The Fifth String as a short novel of music and love, paired here with his tale The Conspirators. A violinist named Diotti stands at the center.

Diotti comes to America after triumphs in the great halls of Europe. The agent Perkins books him for a short run of concerts and talks him up without shame. On the night before his New York debut, Diotti shines at a rich hostess's reception, praised by men and women alike. A young woman in white catches his eye. Love and art pull at the star as his fame grows.
the-first-book-of-farming: Charles L. Goodrich, a farmer and expert in the Bureau of Plant Industry, wrote The First Book of Farming, printed at Garden City in 1923 from a first edition of 1905. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. The contents open with the broad rules of plant culture, starting with plants and then roots, their uses and habits of growth. No chapter text is included in this portion.
the-flag-raising:
Kate Douglas Wiggin wrote The Flag-Raising as a tale of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, in five chapters that end with The State o' Maine. Aunts Miranda and Jane Sawyer stand at the start.

Miranda grumbles that she never planned to raise any child, and that Rebecca's mother has palmed off the wild young one on them. Jane hopes the girl has had time to mend her ways. Miranda fears she has had time to grow worse. As the day of Rebecca's coming dawns, the stern farmhouse braces for a child whose bright talk and quick heart will shake its stiff rules.
the-good-time-coming:
T. S. Arthur wrote The Good Time Coming. It is dated 1855 at Boston and Philadelphia. His preface says life is a mystery. All men fix their eyes on the future. They wait for a good time that never comes. Years begin in hope and end in disappointment. Men gain little wisdom from the sharp lessons at every turn.

Arthur says he too has waited long for that good time. But hope should not die. A good time is coming for each person who works and waits for it. It must be sought in the right direction. Chapter I opens on a bright evening. It shows the lovely home of Edward Markland. Love and peace seem to dwell there. The tale will test that calm home. It will test it against the waiting and wanting of the preface.
the-grizzly-king: James Oliver Curwood wrote The Grizzly King, a romance of the wild. Frank B. Hoffman made the pictures. It is dedicated to the author's boy. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a list of illustrations. The captions are drawn from the tale. They tell of Thor, a great grizzly who has met porcupine quills before. Thor bears down on a caribou herd. Hunters read tracks in the sand and cry that if they hustle they can get their grizzly. No chapter text is present.
the-head-voice-and-other-problems-practi: D. A. Clippinger wrote The Head Voice and Other Problems, subtitled practical talks on singing, published in Boston by Oliver Ditson Company with a 1917 copyright. Clippinger is named as the author of Systematic Voice Training and The Elements of Voice Culture. A note explains that the musical examples were gathered into two PDF files, with the exercises following chapter two, The Head Voice. Only the title page and that note are present here, so the talks themselves do not appear.
the-house-of-the-wolfings-a-tale-of-the-:
William Morris wrote this tale of the Wolfing kindreds. It mixes prose and verse on purpose. The text follows the 1904 Longmans, Green edition. A prefatory poem frames the story. A traveler passes a homestead at night. Its candlelight shines beside the door. He can never enter it again. Chapter I then describes Mid-Mark. Men dwell in a clearing beside a great wood. Trees ring the plain on every side. A swift river cuts through it. The river matches the Thames at Sheene in width.

Morris stresses that men made the clearing. It was no accident of nature. They held ground between the forest and the river banks. Winter floods marked the stones each year. The archaic voice builds a tribal world from the ground up. Landscape and kinship are the real subjects. Morris wrote the language to feel centuries old.
the-ladder-to-learning:
Miss Lovechild's Ladder to Learning appears here in Marks' edition. R. H. Pease of Albany published it in 1852. Page images survive through a Florida children's literature project. The book teaches the alphabet in pictures and couplets. A stands for ape, for Arthur, and air. B stands for bullock, for bird, and for bear. C stands for cat, for Charles, and for cry. Each letter gets its picture and both its forms.

Such primers were a child's first ladder indeed. They climb from letters to words through familiar creatures. The Lovechild name promised parents a gentle method. It borrowed from a celebrated earlier teacher of children. Surviving copies are rare now. Small hands wore them out in use. Page images in Florida's library preserve this one. That library covers American and British children's books from 1850 to 1869.
the-laws-of-war-affecting-commerce-and-s:
H. Byerley Thomson, a Cambridge barrister of the Inner Temple, enlarged his treatise for a new edition in 1854. His preface says the first edition success among merchants encouraged large additions. He kept the plan and the concise, popular style that readers had welcomed.

A new introduction treats the origin of the laws of war in general, and an index aids reference. Contents open with the immediate effects of war and with enemies and hostile property. Thomson aimed at a working guide for traders whose ships and goods faced capture, blockade, and seizure.
the-library-of-work-and-play-gardening-a: Ellen Eddy Shaw wrote her gardening and farming book for young people in 1911, dedicating it to the boys of her club and to girls just as good as boys. Only the title page and contents of part one are present here. A garden club, indoor experiments, and a workshop end of the garden open the list. Later chapters cover strawberries, drainage, cabbage troubles, potatoes, and a corn contest. The lessons and club story themselves do not appear here.
the-life-and-work-of-susan-b-anthony-vol:
Ida Husted Harper wrote the life and work of Susan B. Anthony while Anthony still lived, and volume one appeared in Indianapolis in 1899. Her preface calls a lifetime biography unusual. Friends wanted the woman suffrage reform placed in history from unpublished records and living memory while correction stayed possible.

Harper admits Anthony often gave a different reading of letters and scenes than papers alone suggested. The volume holds public addresses, Anthony own letters, and letters from her contemporaries across fifty years. A dedication honors woman, for whose freedom Anthony gave those fifty years.
the-mad-king:
Edgar Rice Burroughs's The Mad King is a two-part adventure set in the kingdom of Lutha. The contents promise runaway horses, escapes, a king's ransom, a coronation day, and a battlefield. In part two they promise Barney condemned to death before a firing squad, a traitor king, and two kings face to face. Part one opens in uproar: all Lustadt is excited because the mad king has escaped, and crowds surge before the palace awaiting they know not what. The hero threaded through the chapter titles is Barney, an outsider caught up in Luthan royalty.

He finds a friend, wins a king's gratitude, returns to Lutha, and races to the rescue more than once. Burroughs sets mistaken identity and a vacant throne in a small European kingdom, with war and coronation pageantry around them.
the-man-of-feeling:
Henry Mackenzie's The Man of Feeling is presented here in the 1886 Cassell's National Library edition, whose editor's introduction tells the book's story. Mackenzie, an Edinburgh lawyer born in August 1745, read Sterne while studying law in London, caught the tone of sentiment from Tristram Shandy and The Sentimental Journey, and wrote his novel. It appeared without his name in 1771 and proved so popular that a young clergyman forged a marked-up copy and claimed to be its author, forcing Mackenzie to declare himself. The introduction follows his later career: The Man of the World in 1773 and Julia de Roubigné in 1777.

Then came the Edinburgh weekly The Mirror, which he edited from 1779 to 1780, followed by The Lounger. Mackenzie contributed forty-two papers to the first and fifty-seven to the second. The novel that made him famous began as an anonymous experiment in Sterne's manner.
the-man-who-would-be-king:
Rudyard Kipling's The Man Who Would Be King was published in New York by Brentano's. Its narrator opens with a motto: brother to a prince and fellow to a beggar, if he be found worthy. He has been fellow to beggars often, he says. Once he came near kinship with a veritable king, promised the reversion of a kingdom complete with army, law-courts, revenue, and policy. Today, he fears, his king is dead. The beginning of everything was a railway train on the road to Mhow from Ajmir.

A budget deficit forced him to travel Intermediate class, which he describes with comic disgust: no cushions, food in bundles, and travelers taken out dead in hot weather. At Nasirabad a huge gentleman in shirt-sleeves entered, a wanderer and vagabond like himself, with an educated taste for whiskey and tales of out-of-the-way corners of the Empire.
the-master-s-indwelling:
Andrew Murray's The Master's Indwelling grew out of addresses he delivered at the Northfield Conference of 1895. Murray later rewrote and revised the talks for this authorized publication, printed here in a 1953 edition. The contents move from Carnal Christians through The Self Life and Waiting on God. Later chapters treat complete surrender, joy in the Holy Ghost, and the source of power in prayer.

The first chapter opens on Paul's words in First Corinthians about speaking to believers as carnal rather than spiritual. Murray draws from that verse two stages, or types, of the Christian life. His chapters press readers to pass from the lower stage into rest and full surrender. Chapter titles promise that God may be all in all. Readers seeking devotional instruction get a plain, ordered path from self-rule toward Christ living within.
the-misses-mallett-the-bridge-dividing:
E. H. Young's novel The Misses Mallett, also titled The Bridge Dividing, is built in three books. Book I belongs to Rose, Book II to Henrietta, and Book III joins Rose and Henrietta together. That structure is set out in a short contents list before the story starts.

Book I opens on high land above a distant channel on a spring day thick with gorse, larch tassels, and celandines. A woman rides a horse along a broad grassy track, holding him in lightly while lambs play in the fields below. Ahead, the chimneys of Sales Hall rise over elm trees holding rooks' nests. Something in the sight amuses her, yet the person she seems to look for along the lane does not appear.
the-path-of-the-king: John Buchan wrote The Path of the King. He dedicated the chapters to his wife, who first heard them by a Cotswold fire. The header dates the book 1920. Only the dedication and contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The contents list a prologue, fourteen chapters, and an epilogue. Titles run from Hightown under Sunfell through The Englishman, The Wife of Flanders, and The Maid. The Regicide, The Marplot, and The End of the Road close the list.
the-perfect-wagnerite-a-commentary-on-th:
Bernard Shaw wrote The Perfect Wagnerite, a commentary on Wagner's Nibelung's Ring. The pages present give his preface to the first German edition, in Siegfried Trebitsch's translation. Shaw says the German version struck him as weak in explaining why Night Falls On The Gods departs from the Ring's philosophic scheme, so he added a new section.

The new chapter reads the Ring against Europe's revolutionary history from 1848 to the Paris Commune of 1871. Shaw thanks Trebitsch for making him a living German author rather than merely a translated one, and warns that the translator shares neither his views nor Wagner's. The preface is Shaw at his most combative and playful.
the-plattsburg-manual-a-handbook-for-mil: The Plattsburg Manual, a handbook for military training, was written by Major O. O. Ellis and Major E. B. Garey of the United States Infantry. Both men instructed at Plattsburg in 1916 and at officers' camps at Fort McPherson and Fort Oglethorpe in 1917. The Century Company published it at New York, with more than 220 illustrations. The edition shown is the tenth, dated May 1918. Here only the title pages, dedication, and the first contents entry, General Advice, appear, so the training lessons themselves are absent.
the-poetry-of-robert-browning: Stopford A. Brooke's The Poetry of Robert Browning was published by Isbister and Company at London. It was first issued in September 1902 and reprinted into January 1903. Here only the title page and contents appear, so the criticism itself is absent. Chapters open with Browning and Tennyson and treat his handling of nature. They turn to his theory of human life in Pauline and Paracelsus. Later chapters cover the poet of art, Sordello, the dramas, and poems of the passion of love.
the-practice-and-science-of-drawing: Harold Speed's The Practice and Science of Drawing was published in London by Seeley, Service and Co. in 1913, with 93 illustrations and diagrams. Speed is styled an associate of the national society of fine arts in Paris and a member of the Royal Society of Portrait Painters. The pages shown give the title page and contents, not the lessons themselves. Chapters move from vision and line drawing to mass drawing, then through a long run on rhythm in line and mass. Portrait drawing, the visual memory, and procedure close the list.
the-primrose-ring:
Ruth Sawyer's The Primrose Ring was published by Harper and Brothers at New York and London in 1915. Sawyer dedicates it to the Little Mother, in memory of a primrose ring woven once on a time. Chapter I, Concerning Fancy and Saint Margaret's, opens with a question. Would any of it have happened if Trustee Day had not fallen on April 30, which is May Eve?

The narrator calls herself only a story-teller passing on the tale. May Eve, she notes, is among the most bewitched times of the year. Margaret MacLean, in charge of Ward C at Saint Margaret's, found the flower-seller's basket full of primroses that morning. Primroses are gentle flowers, worked by faeries for thousands of years, and Margaret bought the full of her hands. Saint Margaret's itself is a free hospital for children, built by a wealthy man in memory of his dead son.
the-quickening: Francis Lynde, author of The Grafters and The Master of Appleby, published his novel with the Bobbs-Merrill Company in 1906, illustrated by E. M. Ashe and dedicated to his mother. Early chapters carry titles from Bethesda and cedars of Lebanon through family burdens and a newer exodus to the Dabneys of Deer Trace and a contrast of blue blood and red. A frontispiece caption shows Tom facing the firebrand Dabney. Only the title pages and opening of the chapter list are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-reporter-who-made-himself-king:
Richard Harding Davis opens by mocking an old creed. Old-time journalists say a reporter must rise slowly. The ladder runs from printer's devil to office boy. It runs from compositor to stenographer. Only then does a man earn a fire badge. Only then does he know police captains by name. Such training, Davis argues, traps a man. At sixty he is still a reporter.

A reporter raised inside the office learns one lesson too well. He learns that the pay is poor. He does only what the pay covers. A good reporter works for the paper itself. He gives time, health, and brains to get news. He sometimes gives his life for it. The contrast sets up Davis's hero. Readers get journalism lore told as adventure ethics.
the-rose-and-the-ring:
William Makepeace Thackeray signed the prelude to The Rose and the Ring in December 1854, calling the tale a fireside pantomime. He explains that he spent the previous Christmas in a foreign city full of English children, where Twelfth-Night character pictures could not be bought for a party.

His friend Miss Bunch, governess in the Palazzo Poniatowski at Rome, asked him to draw a set of those characters instead. Together they composed a history about the drawings, recited to the children at night, following Giglio and Bulbo, Rosalba and Angelica, a hall porter and the wrathful Countess Gruffanuff. Thackeray offers the printed version as brief holiday fooling for young and elder readers alike.
the-rose-in-the-ring: George Barr McCutcheon's The Rose in the Ring carries four illustrations in color by A. I. Keller, and the portion preserved here stops at the title page and contents, so none of the story's prose appears. Book one opens with a fugitive, moves into a dressing tent and the sawdust ring, and introduces David Jenison, the Braddocks and the brothers Cronk. Its later chapters promise a thief in the night and a sale. Book two begins with the daughter of Colonel Grand and a stranger at the hall.
the-rover-boys-at-college-or-the-right-r: The Right Road and the Wrong is the subtitle of The Rover Boys at College. Arthur M. Winfield wrote it, dated 1910. Seven earlier Rover Boys books by him are listed. What survives here is the title matter and contents alone. No opening chapter follows, so the college adventures are not shown. The headings move from a train journey to the Sanderson house. They promise a hazing, a colors contest, and a rowing race. A great football game comes later. The list ends with a haunted house.
the-shipwreck-a-story-for-the-young: The Rev. Joseph Spillmann, S. J., wrote The Shipwreck, a story for the young. Mary Richards Gray translated it from the German. B. Herder published the second edition at St. Louis and Freiburg in 1910. The book is volume seven of Tales of Foreign Lands, a series Spillmann edited. Its contents list twelve chapters. Two young friends open the tale, and sad tidings follow. A hurricane, stranding, and at last close the list. The pages shown stop at the contents.
the-sky-is-falling:
Lester del Rey's The Sky Is Falling reached this Ace Books edition after a layered history, its copyright page says. A shorter, earlier version appeared as No More Stars. It ran under the name Charles Satterfield in Beyond Fantasy Fiction for July 1954. Galaxy Publishing held copyrights of 1954 and 1963. The first Ace printing came in January 1973.

A teaser passage shows Dave staring around an office. He goes to the window and stares up at the crazy patchwork of the sky. In such a sky there might be cracks, he thinks. He makes out a rift, and beyond it a hole. That small patch has no color, yet it is not black. No stars appear there, though points of light cluster around its edges, apparently retreating.
the-social-cancer-a-complete-english-ver:
Charles Derbyshire translated José Rizal's Noli Me Tangere as The Social Cancer. The Philippine Education Company published it at Manila in 1912. The World Book Company handled New York. Derbyshire also translated Rizal's The Reign of Greed, a companion list notes. His translator's introduction opens the volume.

That introduction begins with a quoted meditation on institutions. Societies travel rapidly in historical sketches, it says. Institutions grow and win loyal obedience, then forfeit allegiance by their shortcomings. Wealth and greatness appear, and corruption and vice follow close upon them. One fancies they must always have co-existed, the passage observes. A steadier look perceives long periods of growth and then decay, like a tree's, it continues.
the-social-history-of-smoking: G. L. Apperson, I.S.O., wrote The Social History of Smoking. Martin Secker published it at London, first published in 1914. The book is dedicated to J.H.M. and R.W.B., by initials only. The pages shown give two title pages, the author's other work, and that dedication. No preface, contents, or chapter on smoking itself appears in the portion shown. Aperson's history of the habit therefore cannot be described from these pages.
the-story-of-sigurd-the-volsung:
William Morris's verse epic of Sigurd the Volsung appears here in a 1922 school edition. Winifred Turner and Helen Scott condensed portions into prose. J. W. Mackail wrote a biographical introduction. Mackail presents Morris, born in 1834, as an eminent Victorian imaginative writer who did great work in many fields besides literature and held beliefs about life very different from ordinary people's.

The introduction follows Morris from his Essex childhood on the edge of Epping Forest to Marlborough school among the Wiltshire downs and then Exeter College, Oxford. There his closest friend was the painter Edward Burne-Jones. Study of Ruskin deepened their love of medieval life and art. A summer in northern France in 1855 settled both friends. They would become artists.
the-strength-of-the-strong:
Jack London gathers seven stories in this volume. Mills and Boon published it in London in 1919. South of the Slot stands among the tales. The Unparalleled Invasion and The Enemy of All the World follow. The Dream of Debs, The Sea-Farmer, and Samuel close the list. The title story opens as a cave parable, under a motto that parables do not lie, though liars will parable.

Old Long-Beard pauses in his narrative. He licks his greasy fingers. He wipes them on his bare sides. His one piece of ragged bearskin fails to cover him there. Three listeners crouch around him on their hams in the firelight. The old man's tale of strength gets under way. Its voice is a primitive world's voice. Bearskins and greedy fingers fill that world.
the-tinker-s-wedding:
J. M. Synge's Tinker's Wedding, a comedy in two acts, is prefaced here by a famous essay on what drama should be. Drama is made serious, the preface argues, not by serious problems but by nourishment for the imagination. We should go to the theatre as to a dinner, not a chemist's shop. In an age of problem plays and musical comedy absinthe, Ben Jonson and Molière stay fresh as blackberries on hedges.

Humour, the essay insists, is among the most needful foods of the imagination, and Ireland still overflows with it, from tinkers to clergy. These country people, rich and genial in humour themselves, will not mind being laughed at without malice. That defence frames Synge's comedy of tinkers seeking a priest's blessing for a bargain marriage, a play once considered too rough for the Irish stage.
the-uncrowned-king: Harold Bell Wright, author of The Shepherd of the Hills, published The Uncrowned King in 1910 with illustrations by John Rea Neill. The pages present here stop at the front matter, so the tale itself does not appear. Wright dedicates the story to his publisher Elsbery W. Reynolds, crediting his belief for making the work possible. A short verse warns that eyes blinded by the fog of Things cannot see Truth. Contents name three parts: the pilgrim's pilgrimage, the voice of the waves, and the voice of the evening wind.
the-uttermost-farthing:
Mrs. Belloc Lowndes published her novel The Uttermost Farthing in 1910, in a Leipzig copyright edition for British authors. Its motto quotes the warning that no one leaves prison until the uttermost farthing is paid. Chapter one puts Laurence Vanderlyn, an unpaid attaché at the American Embassy, on a near-empty platform at Paris's Gare de Lyon.

Vanderlyn, an American diplomat, has chosen an unfashionable train south to hide a great adventure. He and Margaret Pargeter, an Englishwoman loved for seven years with unsatisfied devotion, mean to steal a few days of free happiness together. She risks the most by coming. Lowndes opens with secrecy, longing, and a departure timed for seven in the evening.
the-wallet-of-kai-lung:
Ernest Bramah introduces Kai Lung as a wandering Chinese storyteller who spreads his embroidered mat under a mulberry tree. Kai Lung calls himself insignificant and deformed, yet his tales entertained market crowds and sometimes diverted enemies intent on torturing him. The first story, The Transmutation of Ling, opens in a camphor-laurel forest at sunset.

Kai Lung still has twenty li to travel before reaching Knei Yang, and the gloomy forest aisles make him vow extra prayer-paper for safe arrival. At a turn in the glade he stops: a matchlock barrel points from behind a tree. Smiling with spread hands, he waits for its owner, the scarred brigand Lin Yi, to step out.
the-wings-of-the-morning: Louis Tracy published The Wings of the Morning with Edward J. Clode in New York, and the transcribers say the text was taken from a listing of that edition. A library stamp dates this copy's use to December 23, 1910. The pages present here give a long contents list of twenty-nine chapters, so the novel itself does not appear. Opening chapters follow a wreck, a missing boat, the first day, and a schooner flying the British flag. Later headings promise boat building and the tauranga pirates.
the-young-seigneur-or-nation-making:
Wilfrid Châteauclair, a pen name for William Douw Lighthall, published The Young Seigneur in Montreal in 1888. His preface states a bold chief aim outright. He hopes to chart a future for Canada as a nation. Canada, he says, has drifted without any plan. A lesser purpose is explaining French Canada's atmosphere to English speakers. His hero is a French-Canadian seigneur of lofty character.

Lighthall insists the book is not a political tract. It must not be read as a Grit diatribe, he warns. He calls himself an old-fashioned Tory instead. The novel argues nation-making through story rather than party pamphlets. Readers interested in early Canadian nationalism will find its vision stated plainly.
there-is-no-harm-in-dancing:
W. E. Penn published There Is No Harm in Dancing at St. Louis in 1884, with an introduction by the Rev. J. H. Stribling. Despite the title, Penn argues against dancing. He dedicated the book to husbands, fathers, and brothers who love the women in their families.

His preface says the lecture reached at least one hundred thousand people over seven years of evangelist work. Parents, pastors, and young people asked him to print it. Penn claims eyewitness knowledge of dance halls and hopes to halt readers before they go further down the broad road.
they-call-me-carpenter-a-tale-of-the-sec:
Upton Sinclair published They Call Me Carpenter, a tale of the second coming, at New York in 1922. The narrator begins with a German motion picture shown three years after the war ended. A mob in Western City tried to block the theatre, and other mobs followed.

He introduces Dr. Karl Henner, a Berlin literary critic whose talk started the adventure. Henner's quiet remarks about Prussian militarism unsettle the narrator's clubman's confidence. Readers get a satirical novel where a foreign visitor's ideas open the door to a strange religious encounter in an American city.
thomas-hart-benton-s-remarks-to-the-sena:
Thomas Hart Benton addressed the United States Senate on January 12, 1837, moving to expunge a censure resolution from its journal. Three years earlier the Senate had adopted the resolve against President Jackson. Benton had promised then that his motion would eventually prevail.

He argues the people have already decided, through state instructions, elections, and Jackson's chosen successor's victory. The Bank of the United States, once powerful on the Senate floor, now holds few friends. Readers get a famous congressional speech about public will, presidential honour, and erasing a record rather than merely repealing it.
tieck-the-pictures-the-betrothing:
Two novellas by Ludwig Tieck share this English volume: The Pictures and The Betrothing. Art and illusion drive the first, a story of paintings and the lives they distort. Love and misunderstanding drive the second, where a betrothal tangles on pride and mistaken readings of hearts.

Both tales show the German Romantic at his most characteristic. The everyday and the uncanny keep trading places, and mystery hides inside ordinary drawing rooms. Tieck's irony stays gentle; his strangeness creeps rather than leaps. Elegant and quietly unsettling, the pair suits readers who like their Romanticism in a minor key. The volume makes a fine doorway into his shorter fiction.
tom-swift-and-the-electronic-hydrolung: Victor Appleton II wrote Tom Swift and the Electronic Hydrolung for the new Tom Swift Jr. adventures, published by Grosset and Dunlap at New York in 1961 and illustrated by Charles Brey. Fourteen chapter headings are listed. Titles promise a pirate missile, an undersea survey, an invisible submarine, an aerial attack, and a caisson clue. Porpoise tag, a magnetic kidnapping, enemy frogmen, and a propaganda blitz follow. The title pages and partial contents are what is present here, so Appleton's underwater adventure itself does not appear.
twenty-two-years-a-slave-and-forty-years: Austin Steward's Twenty-Two Years a Slave, and Forty Years a Freeman, dated 1856, opens with letters of encouragement rather than narrative. Governor Myron H. Clark of New York writes from Albany, offering his name as a subscriber. Rochester acquaintances add testimony to Steward's high character from his years as a businessman there. The title page promises his correspondence as president of Wilberforce Colony, Canada West. Only these front pages are present here, so the life story itself does not appear.
uller-uprising:
H. Beam Piper's Uller Uprising appears in the 1983 Ace edition, with a new introduction by John F. Carr. The introduction records that the novel first appeared in 1952 in a Twayne triplet, bound with Judith Merril's Daughters of Earth and Fletcher Pratt's The Long View. It reached magazine readers a year later in Space Science Fiction.

The Ace printing reprints the complete hardcover text in a fresh typeface. Introductions from 1952 and 1983 frame the story, one by John D. Clark and one by Carr. A transcriber's note reports that research found no evidence of a United States copyright renewal. Piper's tale of revolt on a silicon-life world thus returns with its publishing history laid out.
ullr-uprising:
Ullr Uprising, spelled with the double l, comes from the magazine Space Science Fiction of February and March 1953. H. Beam Piper's story ran in two parts, illustrated by Orban. A headnote jokes about the heathen geeks who wear no breeks, warning that on Ullr both red and yellow mean danger and blood.

Part one opens aboard an armor-tender riding a contragravity field above Niflheim. That world's air is free fluorine, its river hydrofluoric acid, and no human has ever breathed it and lived. Men mine uranium there inside power-driven armor. The companion record in this set carries the later book edition, spelled Uller, with its own publishing history.
un-un-res-united-nations-declaration-on-:
Human cloning is condemned in this United Nations declaration, adopted by the General Assembly in 2005. States had argued for years over a cloning treaty and split over research uses of cloned embryos. In the end they settled for a non-binding declaration that passed by a divided vote.

The text calls on states to ban all forms of human cloning that clash with human dignity. It also urges laws against genetic work that threatens human life. Supporters saw a moral stand. Critics said the wording swept too wide. The declaration records where the world argument stood in 2005.
united-states-dept-of-state-corresponden: Correspondence in relation to the killing of prisoners in New Orleans. The State Department file. This book preserves that correspondence. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
vanished-arizona-recollections-of-the-ar:
Martha Summerhayes wrote Vanished Arizona at the urging of her children. They kept asking her to set down the tales of army life they had heard so often. She built the book with help from old letters sent home from Arizona. An uncle in New England had kept those letters for her. She dedicated the book to her son Harry, who shared the ups and downs of that life.

Summerhayes is clear about what she leaves out. She does not retell her husband's Civil War service or his Indian campaigns. She leaves the deeds of the old Eighth Infantry to historians. Her subject is her own view. In the early seventies she left a snug New England home to follow a second lieutenant into the army's wildest camps. Readers get an officer's wife's daily Arizona, told from her own letters and memory.
walking:
Henry David Thoreau's essay Walking speaks a word for nature, for absolute freedom and wildness. He sets that freedom against the mere freedom of civil life. He asks readers to see man as an inhabitant of nature, part and parcel of it, rather than as a member of society. Champions of civilization, he says, are many enough. He will make an extreme statement, so as to make an emphatic one.

Few people, Thoreau finds, understand the art of walking, the genius for sauntering. He traces that word to idle folk of the Middle Ages. True saunterers do go to a holy land in their walks; the rest are mere idlers. Or the word may come from having no home, and being at home everywhere. The essay turns a daily walk into a pilgrimage and a creed.
washington-irving:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote this life of Washington Irving for the American Men of Letters series. An editor's note says it was the first biography the series published, in December 1881. The note traces the book's growth. It began as a sketch prefixed to the Geoffrey Crayon edition of Irving's works in 1880. Then it stood again in Studies of Irving, beside Bryant's oration and George P. Putnam's personal memories.

Warner begins with the lapse of time. More than twenty years have passed since Irving's death took away the personal presence that sells an author's books. That presence colors the judgment of his own age. Irving's birth, he adds, was almost of a date with the Republic's. It fell in the year the British troops left New York.
weighed-and-wanting: George MacDonald wrote Weighed and Wanting, and its frontispiece shows Hester at her piano. Pages present here hold the title page and contents only, so the novel itself is not shown. Twenty chapters named here sketch the tale. Bad weather, father, mother and son, and the magic lantern come first. Hester alone, an aquarium, and Amy Amber follow. Cornelius and Vavasor, songs and singers, and a private exhibition come next. A small failure, the concert room, an uninvited guest, and a catastrophe close the list shown.
wild-flowers-worth-knowing: The pages here give the title page and a plant list for Wild Flowers Worth Knowing, with no flower entries shown. Asa Don Dickinson adapted the book in 1917 from Neltje Blanchan's Nature's Garden. The contents sort plants by family, starting with the water-plantain and arum groups. Jack-in-the-pulpit and skunk cabbage appear under the arum family. The lily family list is long, with white hellebore, Canada lily, and trilliums. Latin family names sit beside the common names throughout the list.
words-of-cheer-for-the-tempted-the-toili:
T. S. Arthur edited this 1856 gathering of comforting pieces for hard-pressed readers. His preface compares life to a road that shifts from smooth to rugged. Skies turn from gold to storm, he writes, and hearts sink. Yet the road still climbs, and light waits past the clouds. Arthur urges faith in a God who binds up broken hearts.

The contents list sketches and poems with titles like Aunt Mary, Wealth, and How to Be Happy. Pieces address grief, work, and temptation directly. Readers get short readings meant to steady them. Comfort, not argument, is the volume's clear purpose.
wreaths-of-friendship-a-gift-for-the-you:
T. S. Arthur and F. C. Woodworth made this gift book for young readers, published in New York in 1851. Their preface speaks straight to young friends. The writers joke that the preface is a toll gate between the title page and the first story. They ask only for a few words of attention. The wreaths of the title are the tales and poems twined together here.

Gift books mixed stories, verse, and pictures for holidays and rewards. This one promises tokens of affection, as a listed plate is called. Readers get gentle moral pieces shaped for children. Friendship and kindness form the binding theme.
